“Heerfather here at home would I keep, Where the gods together dwell; Amid all the giants an equal in might To Vafthruthnir know I none.”
lines: “Heerfather here at home would I keep,
Where the gods together dwell;
Amid all the giants an equal in might
To Vafthruthnir know I none.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Much have I fared, much have I found, Much have I got from the gods; And fain would I know how Vafthruthnir now Lives in his lofty hall.”
lines: “Much have I fared, much have I found,
Much have I got from the gods;
And fain would I know how Vafthruthnir now
Lives in his lofty hall.”

items.text: Frigg spake:
“Safe mayst thou go, safe come again, And safe be the way thou wendest! Father of men, let thy mind be keen When speech with the giant thou seekest.”
lines: “Safe mayst thou go, safe come again,
And safe be the way thou wendest!
Father of men, let thy mind be keen
When speech with the giant thou seekest.”

items.text: The wisdom then of the giant wise Forth did he fare to try; He found the hall of the father of Im, And in forthwith went Ygg.
lines: The wisdom then of the giant wise
Forth did he fare to try;
He found the hall of the father of Im,
And in forthwith went Ygg.

items.text: Othin spake:
“Vafthruthnir, hail! to thy hall am I come, For thyself I fain would see; And first would I ask if wise thou art, Or, giant, all wisdom hast won.”
lines: “Vafthruthnir, hail! to thy hall am I come,
For thyself I fain would see;
And first would I ask if wise thou art,
Or, giant, all wisdom hast won.”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“Who is the man that speaks to me, Here in my lofty hall? Forth from our dwelling thou never shalt fare, Unless wiser than I thou art.”
lines: “Who is the man that speaks to me,
Here in my lofty hall?
Forth from our dwelling thou never shalt fare,
Unless wiser than I thou art.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Gagnrath they call me, and thirsty I come From a journey hard to thy hall; Welcome I look for, for long have I fared, And gentle greeting, giant.”
lines: “Gagnrath they call me, and thirsty I come
From a journey hard to thy hall;
Welcome I look for, for long have I fared,
And gentle greeting, giant.”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“Why standest thou there on the floor whilst thou speakest? A seat shalt thou have in my hall; Then soon shall we know whose knowledge is more, The guest’s or the sage’s gray.”
lines: “Why standest thou there on the floor whilst thou
speakest?
A seat shalt thou have in my hall;
Then soon shall we know whose knowledge is more,
The guest’s or the sage’s gray.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“If a poor man reaches the home of the rich, Let him wisely speak or be still; For to him who speaks with the hard of heart Will chattering ever work ill.”
lines: “If a poor man reaches the home of the rich,
Let him wisely speak or be still;
For to him who speaks with the hard of heart
Will chattering ever work ill.”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“Speak forth now, Gagnrath, if there from the floor Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known: What name has the steed that each morn anew The day for mankind doth draw?”
lines: “Speak forth now, Gagnrath, if there from the floor
Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known:
What name has the steed that each morn anew
The day for mankind doth draw?”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Skinfaxi is he, the steed who for men The glittering day doth draw; The best of horses to heroes he seems, And brightly his mane doth burn.”
lines: “Skinfaxi is he, the steed who for men
The glittering day doth draw;
The best of horses to heroes he seems,
And brightly his mane doth burn.”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“Speak forth now, Gagnrath, if there from the floor Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known: What name has the steed that from East anew Brings night for the noble gods?”
lines: “Speak forth now, Gagnrath, if there from the floor
Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known:
What name has the steed that from East anew
Brings night for the noble gods?”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Hrimfaxi name they the steed that anew Brings night for the noble gods; Each morning foam from his bit there falls, And thence come the dews in the dales.”
lines: “Hrimfaxi name they the steed that anew
Brings night for the noble gods;
Each morning foam from his bit there falls,
And thence come the dews in the dales.”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“Speak forth now, Gagnrath, if there from the floor Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known: What name has the river that ’twixt the realms Of the gods and the giants goes?”
lines: “Speak forth now, Gagnrath, if there from the floor
Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known:
What name has the river that ’twixt the realms
Of the gods and the giants goes?”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Ifing is the river that ’twixt the realms Of the gods and the giants goes; For all time ever open it flows, No ice on the river there is.”
lines: “Ifing is the river that ’twixt the realms
Of the gods and the giants goes;
For all time ever open it flows,
No ice on the river there is.”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“Speak forth now, Gagnrath, if there from the floor Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known: What name has the field where in fight shall meet Surt and the gracious gods?”
lines: “Speak forth now, Gagnrath, if there from the floor
Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known:
What name has the field where in fight shall meet
Surt and the gracious gods?”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Vigrith is the field where in fight shall meet Surt and the gracious gods; A hundred miles each way does it measure, And so are its boundaries set.”
lines: “Vigrith is the field where in fight shall meet
Surt and the gracious gods;
A hundred miles each way does it measure,
And so are its boundaries set.”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“Wise art thou, guest! To my bench shalt thou go, In our seats let us speak together; Here in the hall our heads, O guest, hall we wager our wisdom upon.”
lines: “Wise art thou, guest! To my bench shalt thou go,
In our seats let us speak together;
Here in the hall our heads, O guest,
hall we wager our wisdom upon.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“First answer me well, if thy wisdom avails, And thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now: In earliest time whence came the earth, Or the sky, thou giant sage?”
lines: “First answer me well, if thy wisdom avails,
And thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
In earliest time whence came the earth,
Or the sky, thou giant sage?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“Out of Ymir’s flesh was fashioned the earth, And the mountains were made of his bones; The sky from the frost-cold giant’s skull, And the ocean out of his blood.”
lines: “Out of Ymir’s flesh was fashioned the earth,
And the mountains were made of his bones;
The sky from the frost-cold giant’s skull,
And the ocean out of his blood.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Next answer me well, if thy wisdom avails, And thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now: Whence came the moon, o’er the world of men That fares, and the flaming sun?”
lines: “Next answer me well, if thy wisdom avails,
And thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
Whence came the moon, o’er the world of men
That fares, and the flaming sun?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“Mundilferi is he who begat the moon, And fathered the flaming sun; The round of heaven each day they run, To tell the time for men.”
lines: “Mundilferi is he who begat the moon,
And fathered the flaming sun;
The round of heaven each day they run,
To tell the time for men.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Third answer me well, if wise thou art called, If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now: Whence came the day, o’er mankind that fares, Or night with the narrowing moon?”
lines: “Third answer me well, if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
Whence came the day, o’er mankind that fares,
Or night with the narrowing moon?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“The father of day is Delling called, And the night was begotten by Nor; Full moon and old by the gods were fashioned, To tell the time for men.”
lines: “The father of day is Delling called,
And the night was begotten by Nor;
Full moon and old by the gods were fashioned,
To tell the time for men.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Fourth answer me well, if wise thou art called, If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now: Whence did winter come, or the summer warm, First with the gracious gods?”
lines: “Fourth answer me well, if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
Whence did winter come, or the summer warm,
First with the gracious gods?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“Vindsval he was who was winter’s father, And Svosuth summer begat;” . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: “Vindsval he was who was winter’s father,
And Svosuth summer begat;”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Fifth answer me well, if wise thou art called, If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now: What giant first was fashioned of old, And the eldest of Ymir’s kin?”
lines: “Fifth answer me well, if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
What giant first was fashioned of old,
And the eldest of Ymir’s kin?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“Winters unmeasured ere earth was made Was the birth of Bergelmir; Thruthgelmir’s son was the giant strong, And Aurgelmir’s grandson of old.”
lines: “Winters unmeasured ere earth was made
Was the birth of Bergelmir;
Thruthgelmir’s son was the giant strong,
And Aurgelmir’s grandson of old.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Sixth answer me well, if wise thou art called, If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now: Whence did Aurgelmir come with the giants’ kin, Long since, thou giant sage?”
lines: “Sixth answer me well, if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
Whence did Aurgelmir come with the giants’ kin,
Long since, thou giant sage?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“Down from Elivagar did venom drop, And waxed till a giant it was; And thence arose our giants’ race, And thus so fierce are we found.”
lines: “Down from Elivagar did venom drop,
And waxed till a giant it was;
And thence arose our giants’ race,
And thus so fierce are we found.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Seventh answer me well, if wise thou art called, If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now: How begat he children, the giant grim, Who never a giantess knew?”
lines: “Seventh answer me well, if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
How begat he children, the giant grim,
Who never a giantess knew?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“They say ’neath the arms of the giant of ice Grew man-child and maid together; And foot with foot did the wise one fashion A son that six heads bore.”
lines: “They say ’neath the arms of the giant of ice
Grew man-child and maid together;
And foot with foot did the wise one fashion
A son that six heads bore.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Eighth answer me well, if wise thou art called, If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now: What farthest back dost thou bear in mind? For wide is thy wisdom, giant!”
lines: “Eighth answer me well, if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
What farthest back dost thou bear in mind?
For wide is thy wisdom, giant!”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“Winters unmeasured ere earth was made Was the birth of Bergelmir; This first knew I well, when the giant wise In a boat of old was borne.”
lines: “Winters unmeasured ere earth was made
Was the birth of Bergelmir;
This first knew I well, when the giant wise
In a boat of old was borne.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Ninth answer me well, if wise thou art called, If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now: Whence comes the wind that fares o’er the waves Yet never itself is seen?”
lines: “Ninth answer me well, if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
Whence comes the wind that fares o’er the waves
Yet never itself is seen?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“In an eagle’s guise at the end of heaven Hræsvelg sits, they say; And from his wings does the wind come forth To move o’er the world of men.”
lines: “In an eagle’s guise at the end of heaven
Hræsvelg sits, they say;
And from his wings does the wind come forth
To move o’er the world of men.”

items.text: Othin spake:

“Tenth answer me now, if thou knowest all The fate that is fixed for the gods: Whence came up Njorth to the kin of the gods,— (Rich in temples and shrines he rules,—) Though of gods he was never begot?”
lines: “Tenth answer me now, if thou knowest all
The fate that is fixed for the gods:
Whence came up Njorth to the kin of the gods,—
(Rich in temples and shrines he rules,—)
Though of gods he was never begot?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“In the home of the Wanes did the wise ones create him, And gave him as pledge to the gods; At the fall of the world shall he fare once more Home to the Wanes so wise.”
lines: “In the home of the Wanes did the wise ones create him,
And gave him as pledge to the gods;
At the fall of the world shall he fare once more
Home to the Wanes so wise.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Eleventh answer me well, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . What men . . . . . . in . . . . . . home Each day to fight go forth?”
lines: “Eleventh answer me well, . . . . . . . .
What men . . . . . . in . . . . . . home
Each day to fight go forth?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“The heroes all in Othin’s hall Each day to fight go forth; They fell each other, and fare from the fight All healed full soon to sit.”
lines: “The heroes all in Othin’s hall
Each day to fight go forth;
They fell each other, and fare from the fight
All healed full soon to sit.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Twelfth answer me now how all thou knowest Of the fate that is fixed for the gods; Of the runes of the gods and the giants’ race The truth indeed dost thou tell, (And wide is thy wisdom, giant!)”
lines: “Twelfth answer me now how all thou knowest
Of the fate that is fixed for the gods;
Of the runes of the gods and the giants’ race
The truth indeed dost thou tell,
(And wide is thy wisdom, giant!)”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“Of the runes of the gods and the giants’ race The truth indeed can I tell, (For to every world have I won;) To nine worlds came I, to Niflhel beneath, The home where dead men dwell.”
lines: “Of the runes of the gods and the giants’ race
The truth indeed can I tell,
(For to every world have I won;)
To nine worlds came I, to Niflhel beneath,
The home where dead men dwell.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Much have I fared, much have I found, Much have I got of the gods: What shall live of mankind when at last there comes The mighty winter to men?”
lines: “Much have I fared, much have I found,
Much have I got of the gods:
What shall live of mankind when at last there comes
The mighty winter to men?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“In Hoddmimir’s wood shall hide themselves Lif and Lifthrasir then; The morning dews for meat shall they have, Such food shall men then find.”
lines: “In Hoddmimir’s wood shall hide themselves
Lif and Lifthrasir then;
The morning dews for meat shall they have,
Such food shall men then find.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Much have I fared, much have I found, Much have I got of the gods: Whence comes the sun to the smooth sky back, When Fenrir has snatched it forth?”
lines: “Much have I fared, much have I found,
Much have I got of the gods:
Whence comes the sun to the smooth sky back,
When Fenrir has snatched it forth?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“A daughter bright Alfrothul bears Ere Fenrir snatches her forth; Her mother’s paths shall the maiden tread When the gods to death have gone.”
lines: “A daughter bright Alfrothul bears
Ere Fenrir snatches her forth;
Her mother’s paths shall the maiden tread
When the gods to death have gone.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Much have I fared, much have I found, Much have I got of the gods: What maidens are they, so wise of mind, That forth o’er the sea shall fare?”
lines: “Much have I fared, much have I found,
Much have I got of the gods:
What maidens are they, so wise of mind,
That forth o’er the sea shall fare?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“O’er Mogthrasir’s hill shall the maidens pass, And three are their throngs that come; They all shall protect the dwellers on earth, Though they come of the giants’ kin.”
lines: “O’er Mogthrasir’s hill shall the maidens pass,
And three are their throngs that come;
They all shall protect the dwellers on earth,
Though they come of the giants’ kin.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Much have I fared, much have I found, Much have I got of the gods: Who then shall rule the realm of the gods, When the fires of Surt have sunk?”
lines: “Much have I fared, much have I found,
Much have I got of the gods:
Who then shall rule the realm of the gods,
When the fires of Surt have sunk?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“In the gods’ home Vithar and Vali shall dwell, When the fires of Surt have sunk; Mothi and Magni shall Mjollnir have When Vingnir falls in fight.”
lines: “In the gods’ home Vithar and Vali shall dwell,
When the fires of Surt have sunk;
Mothi and Magni shall Mjollnir have
When Vingnir falls in fight.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Much have I fared, much have I found, Much have I got of the gods: What shall bring the doom of death to Othin, When the gods to destruction go?”
lines: “Much have I fared, much have I found,
Much have I got of the gods:
What shall bring the doom of death to Othin,
When the gods to destruction go?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:
“The wolf shall fell the father of men, And this shall Vithar avenge; The terrible jaws shall he tear apart, And so the wolf shall he slay.”
lines: “The wolf shall fell the father of men,
And this shall Vithar avenge;
The terrible jaws shall he tear apart,
And so the wolf shall he slay.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Much have I fared, much have I found, Much have I got from the gods: What spake Othin himself in the ears of his son, Ere in the bale-fire he burned?”
lines: “Much have I fared, much have I found,
Much have I got from the gods:
What spake Othin himself in the ears of his son,
Ere in the bale-fire he burned?”

items.text: Vafthruthnir spake:

“No man can tell what in olden time Thou spak’st in the ears of thy son; With fated mouth the fall of the gods And mine olden tales have I told; With Othin in knowledge now have I striven, And ever the wiser thou art.”
lines: “No man can tell what in olden time
Thou spak’st in the ears of thy son;
With fated mouth the fall of the gods
And mine olden tales have I told;
With Othin in knowledge now have I striven,
And ever the wiser thou art.”

items.text: King Hrauthung had two sons: one was called Agnar, and the other Geirröth. Agnar was ten winters old, and Geirröth eight. Once they both rowed in a boat with their fishing-gear to catch little fish; and the wind drove them out into the sea. In the darkness of the night they were wrecked on the shore; and going up, they found a poor peasant, with whom they stayed through the winter. The housewife took care of Agnar, and the peasant cared for Geirröth, and taught him wisdom. In the spring the peasant gave him a boat; and when the couple led them to the shore, the peasant spoke secretly with Geirröth. They had a fair wind, and came to their father’s landing-place. Geirröth was forward in the boat; he leaped up on land, but pushed out the boat and said, “Go thou now where evil may have thee!” The boat drifted out to sea. Geirröth, however, went up to the house, and was well received, but his father was dead. Then Geirröth was made king, and became a renowned man.

Othin and Frigg sat in Hlithskjolf and looked over all the worlds. Othin said: “Seest thou Agnar, thy fosterling, how he begets children with a giantess in the cave? But Geirröth, my fosterling, is a king, and now rules over his land.” Frigg said: “He is so miserly that he tortures his guests if he thinks that too many of them come to him.” Othin replied that this was the greatest of lies; and they made a wager about this matter. Frigg sent her maid-servant, Fulla, to Geirröth. She bade the king beware lest a magician who was come thither to his land should bewitch him, and told this sign concerning him, that no dog was so fierce as to leap at him. Now it was a very great slander that King Geirröth was not hospitable; but nevertheless he had them take the man whom the dogs would not attack. He wore a dark-blue mantle and called himself Grimnir, but said no more about himself, though he was questioned. The king had him tortured to make him speak, and set him between two fires, and he sat there eight nights. King Geirröth had a son ten winters old, and called Agnar after his father’s brother. Agnar went to Grimnir, and gave him a full horn to drink from, and said that the king did ill in letting him be tormented without cause. Grimnir drank from the horn; the fire had come so near that the mantle burned on Grimnir’s back. He spake:
Hot art thou, fire! too fierce by far; Get ye now gone, ye flames! The mantle is burnt, though I bear it aloft, And the fire scorches the fur.
lines: Hot art thou, fire! too fierce by far;
Get ye now gone, ye flames!
The mantle is burnt, though I bear it aloft,
And the fire scorches the fur.

items.text: ’Twixt the fires now eight nights have I sat, And no man brought meat to me, Save Agnar alone, and alone shall rule Geirröth’s son o’er the Goths.
lines: ’Twixt the fires now eight nights have I sat,
And no man brought meat to me,
Save Agnar alone, and alone shall rule
Geirröth’s son o’er the Goths.

items.text: Hail to thee, Agnar! for hailed thou art By the voice of Veratyr; For a single drink shalt thou never receive A greater gift as reward.
lines: Hail to thee, Agnar! for hailed thou art
By the voice of Veratyr;
For a single drink shalt thou never receive
A greater gift as reward.

items.text: The land is holy that lies hard by The gods and the elves together; And Thor shall ever in Thruthheim dwell, Till the gods to destruction go.
lines: The land is holy that lies hard by
The gods and the elves together;
And Thor shall ever in Thruthheim dwell,
Till the gods to destruction go.

items.text: Ydalir call they the place where Ull A hall for himself hath set; And Alfheim the gods to Freyr once gave As a tooth-gift in ancient times.
lines: Ydalir call they the place where Ull
A hall for himself hath set;
And Alfheim the gods to Freyr once gave
As a tooth-gift in ancient times.

items.text: A third home is there, with silver thatched By the hands of the gracious gods: Valaskjolf is it, in days of old Set by a god for himself.
lines: A third home is there, with silver thatched
By the hands of the gracious gods:
Valaskjolf is it, in days of old
Set by a god for himself.

items.text: Sökkvabekk is the fourth, where cool waves flow, And amid their murmur it stands; There daily do Othin and Saga drink In gladness from cups of gold.
lines: Sökkvabekk is the fourth, where cool waves flow,
And amid their murmur it stands;
There daily do Othin and Saga drink
In gladness from cups of gold.

items.text: The fifth is Glathsheim, and gold-bright there Stands Valhall stretching wide; And there does Othin each day choose The men who have fallen in fight.
lines: The fifth is Glathsheim, and gold-bright there
Stands Valhall stretching wide;
And there does Othin each day choose
The men who have fallen in fight.

items.text: Easy is it to know for him who to Othin Comes and beholds the hall; Its rafters are spears, with shields is it roofed, On its benches are breastplates strewn.
lines: Easy is it to know for him who to Othin
Comes and beholds the hall;
Its rafters are spears, with shields is it roofed,
On its benches are breastplates strewn.

items.text: Easy is it to know for him who to Othin Comes and beholds the hall; There hangs a wolf by the western door, And o’er it an eagle hovers.
lines: Easy is it to know for him who to Othin
Comes and beholds the hall;
There hangs a wolf by the western door,
And o’er it an eagle hovers.

items.text: The sixth is Thrymheim, where Thjazi dwelt, The giant of marvelous might; Now Skathi abides, the god’s fair bride, In the home that her father had.
lines: The sixth is Thrymheim, where Thjazi dwelt,
The giant of marvelous might;
Now Skathi abides, the god’s fair bride,
In the home that her father had.

items.text: The seventh is Breithablik; Baldr has there For himself a dwelling set, In the land I know that lies so fair, And from evil fate is free.
lines: The seventh is Breithablik; Baldr has there
For himself a dwelling set,
In the land I know that lies so fair,
And from evil fate is free.

items.text: Himinbjorg is the eighth, and Heimdall there O’er men holds sway, it is said; In his well-built house does the warder of heaven The good mead gladly drink.
lines: Himinbjorg is the eighth, and Heimdall there
O’er men holds sway, it is said;
In his well-built house does the warder of heaven
The good mead gladly drink.

items.text: The ninth is Folkvang, where Freyja decrees Who shall have seats in the hall; The half of the dead each day does she choose, And half does Othin have.
lines: The ninth is Folkvang, where Freyja decrees
Who shall have seats in the hall;
The half of the dead each day does she choose,
And half does Othin have.

items.text: The tenth is Glitnir; its pillars are gold, And its roof with silver is set; There most of his days does Forseti dwell, And sets all strife at end.
lines: The tenth is Glitnir; its pillars are gold,
And its roof with silver is set;
There most of his days does Forseti dwell,
And sets all strife at end.

items.text: The eleventh is Noatun; there has Njorth For himself a dwelling set; The sinless ruler of men there sits In his temple timbered high.
lines: The eleventh is Noatun; there has Njorth
For himself a dwelling set;
The sinless ruler of men there sits
In his temple timbered high.

items.text: Filled with growing trees and high-standing grass Is Vithi, Vithar’s land; But there did the son from his steed leap down, When his father he fain would avenge.
lines: Filled with growing trees and high-standing grass
Is Vithi, Vithar’s land;
But there did the son from his steed leap down,
When his father he fain would avenge.

items.text: In Eldhrimnir Andhrimnir cooks Sæhrimnir’s seething flesh,— The best of food, but few men know On what fare the warriors feast.
lines: In Eldhrimnir Andhrimnir cooks
Sæhrimnir’s seething flesh,—
The best of food, but few men know
On what fare the warriors feast.

items.text: Freki and Geri does Heerfather feed, The far-famed fighter of old: But on wine alone does the weapon-decked god, Othin, forever live.
lines: Freki and Geri does Heerfather feed,
The far-famed fighter of old:
But on wine alone does the weapon-decked god,
Othin, forever live.

items.text: O’er Mithgarth Hugin and Munin both Each day set forth to fly; For Hugin I fear lest he come not home, But for Munin my care is more.
lines: O’er Mithgarth Hugin and Munin both
Each day set forth to fly;
For Hugin I fear lest he come not home,
But for Munin my care is more.

items.text: Loud roars Thund, and Thjothvitnir’s fish Joyously fares in the flood; Hard does it seem to the host of the slain To wade the torrent wild.
lines: Loud roars Thund, and Thjothvitnir’s fish
Joyously fares in the flood;
Hard does it seem to the host of the slain
To wade the torrent wild.

items.text: There Valgrind stands, the sacred gate, And behind are the holy doors; Old is the gate, but few there are Who can tell how it tightly is locked.
lines: There Valgrind stands, the sacred gate,
And behind are the holy doors;
Old is the gate, but few there are
Who can tell how it tightly is locked.

items.text: Five hundred doors and forty there are, I ween, in Valhall’s walls; Eight hundred fighters through one door fare When to war with the wolf they go.
lines: Five hundred doors and forty there are,
I ween, in Valhall’s walls;
Eight hundred fighters through one door fare
When to war with the wolf they go.

items.text: Five hundred rooms and forty there are I ween, in Bilskirnir built; Of all the homes whose roofs I beheld, My son’s the greatest meseemed.
lines: Five hundred rooms and forty there are
I ween, in Bilskirnir built;
Of all the homes whose roofs I beheld,
My son’s the greatest meseemed.

items.text: Heithrun is the goat who stands by Heerfather’s hall, And the branches of Lærath she bites; The pitcher she fills with the fair, clear mead, Ne’er fails the foaming drink.
lines: Heithrun is the goat who stands by Heerfather’s hall,
And the branches of Lærath she bites;
The pitcher she fills with the fair, clear mead,
Ne’er fails the foaming drink.

items.text: Eikthyrnir is the hart who stands by Heerfather’s hall And the branches of Lærath he bites; From his horns a stream into Hvergelmir drops, Thence all the rivers run.
lines: Eikthyrnir is the hart who stands by Heerfather’s hall
And the branches of Lærath he bites;
From his horns a stream into Hvergelmir drops,
Thence all the rivers run.

items.text: Sith and Vith, Sækin and Ækin, Svol and Fimbulthul, Gunnthro and Fjorm, Rin and Rinnandi, Gipul and Gopul, Gomul and Geirvimul, That flow through the fields of the gods; Thyn and Vin, Thol and Hol, Groth and Gunnthorin.
lines: Sith and Vith, Sækin and Ækin,
Svol and Fimbulthul, Gunnthro and Fjorm,
Rin and Rinnandi,
Gipul and Gopul, Gomul and Geirvimul,
That flow through the fields of the gods;
Thyn and Vin, Thol and Hol,
Groth and Gunnthorin.

items.text: Vino is one, Vegsvin another, And Thjothnuma a third; Nyt and Not, Non and Hron, Slith and Hrith, Sylg and Ylg, Vith and Von, Vond and Strond, Gjol and Leipt, that go among men, And hence they fall to Hel.
lines: Vino is one, Vegsvin another,
And Thjothnuma a third;
Nyt and Not, Non and Hron,
Slith and Hrith, Sylg and Ylg,
Vith and Von, Vond and Strond,
Gjol and Leipt, that go among men,
And hence they fall to Hel.

items.text: Kormt and Ormt and the Kerlaugs twain Shall Thor each day wade through, (When dooms to give he forth shall go To the ash-tree Yggdrasil;) For heaven’s bridge burns all in flame, And the sacred waters seethe.
lines: Kormt and Ormt and the Kerlaugs twain
Shall Thor each day wade through,
(When dooms to give he forth shall go
To the ash-tree Yggdrasil;)
For heaven’s bridge burns all in flame,
And the sacred waters seethe.

items.text: Glath and Gyllir, Gler and Skeithbrimir, Silfrintopp and Sinir, Gisl and Falhofnir, Golltopp and Lettfeti, On these steeds the gods shall go When dooms to give each day they ride To the ash-tree Yggdrasil.
lines: Glath and Gyllir, Gler and Skeithbrimir,
Silfrintopp and Sinir,
Gisl and Falhofnir, Golltopp and Lettfeti,
On these steeds the gods shall go
When dooms to give each day they ride
To the ash-tree Yggdrasil.

items.text: Three roots there are that three ways run ’Neath the ash-tree Yggdrasil; ’Neath the first lives Hel, ’neath the second the frost-giants, ’Neath the last are the lands of men.
lines: Three roots there are that three ways run
’Neath the ash-tree Yggdrasil;
’Neath the first lives Hel, ’neath the second the
frost-giants,
’Neath the last are the lands of men.

items.text: Ratatosk is the squirrel who there shall run On the ash-tree Yggdrasil; From above the words of the eagle he bears, And tells them to Nithhogg beneath.
lines: Ratatosk is the squirrel who there shall run
On the ash-tree Yggdrasil;
From above the words of the eagle he bears,
And tells them to Nithhogg beneath.

items.text: Four harts there are, that the highest twigs Nibble with necks bent back; Dain and Dvalin, . . . . . . . . Duneyr and Dyrathror.
lines: Four harts there are, that the highest twigs
Nibble with necks bent back;
Dain and Dvalin, . . . . . . . .
Duneyr and Dyrathror.

items.text: More serpents there are beneath the ash Than an unwise ape would think; Goin and Moin, Grafvitnir’s sons, Grabak and Grafvolluth, Ofnir and Svafnir shall ever, methinks, Gnaw at the twigs of the tree.
lines: More serpents there are beneath the ash
Than an unwise ape would think;
Goin and Moin, Grafvitnir’s sons,
Grabak and Grafvolluth,
Ofnir and Svafnir shall ever, methinks,
Gnaw at the twigs of the tree.

items.text: Yggdrasil’s ash great evil suffers, Far more than men do know; The hart bites its top, its trunk is rotting, And Nithhogg gnaws beneath.
lines: Yggdrasil’s ash great evil suffers,
Far more than men do know;
The hart bites its top, its trunk is rotting,
And Nithhogg gnaws beneath.

items.text: Hrist and Mist bring the horn at my will, Skeggjold and Skogul; Hild and Thruth, Hlokk and Herfjotur, Gol and Geironul, Randgrith and Rathgrith and Reginleif Beer to the warriors bring.
lines: Hrist and Mist bring the horn at my will,
Skeggjold and Skogul;
Hild and Thruth, Hlokk and Herfjotur,
Gol and Geironul,
Randgrith and Rathgrith and Reginleif
Beer to the warriors bring.

items.text: Arvak and Alsvith up shall drag Weary the weight of the sun; But an iron cool have the kindly gods Of yore set under their yokes.
lines: Arvak and Alsvith up shall drag
Weary the weight of the sun;
But an iron cool have the kindly gods
Of yore set under their yokes.

items.text: In front of the sun does Svalin stand, The shield for the shining god; Mountains and sea would be set in flames If it fell from before the sun.
lines: In front of the sun does Svalin stand,
The shield for the shining god;
Mountains and sea would be set in flames
If it fell from before the sun.

items.text: Skoll is the wolf that to Ironwood Follows the glittering god, And the son of Hrothvitnir, Hati, awaits The burning bride of heaven.
lines: Skoll is the wolf that to Ironwood
Follows the glittering god,
And the son of Hrothvitnir, Hati, awaits
The burning bride of heaven.

items.text: Out of Ymir’s flesh was fashioned the earth, And the ocean out of his blood; Of his bones the hills, of his hair the trees, Of his skull the heavens high.
lines: Out of Ymir’s flesh was fashioned the earth,
And the ocean out of his blood;
Of his bones the hills, of his hair the trees,
Of his skull the heavens high.

items.text: Mithgarth the gods from his eyebrows made, And set for the sons of men; And out of his brain the baleful clouds They made to move on high.
lines: Mithgarth the gods from his eyebrows made,
And set for the sons of men;
And out of his brain the baleful clouds
They made to move on high.

items.text: His the favor of Ull and of all the gods Who first in the flames will reach; For the house can be seen by the sons of the gods If the kettle aside were cast.
lines: His the favor of Ull and of all the gods
Who first in the flames will reach;
For the house can be seen by the sons of the gods
If the kettle aside were cast.

items.text: In days of old did Ivaldi’s sons Skithblathnir fashion fair, The best of ships for the bright god Freyr, The noble son of Njorth.
lines: In days of old did Ivaldi’s sons
Skithblathnir fashion fair,
The best of ships for the bright god Freyr,
The noble son of Njorth.

items.text: The best of trees must Yggdrasil be, Skithblathnir best of boats; Of all the gods is Othin the greatest, And Sleipnir the best of steeds; Bilrost of bridges, Bragi of skalds, Hobrok of hawks, and Garm of hounds.
lines: The best of trees must Yggdrasil be,
Skithblathnir best of boats;
Of all the gods is Othin the greatest,
And Sleipnir the best of steeds;
Bilrost of bridges, Bragi of skalds,
Hobrok of hawks, and Garm of hounds.

items.text: To the race of the gods my face have I raised, And the wished-for aid have I waked; For to all the gods has the message gone That sit in Ægir’s seats, That drink within Ægir’s doors.
lines: To the race of the gods my face have I raised,
And the wished-for aid have I waked;
For to all the gods has the message gone
That sit in Ægir’s seats,
That drink within Ægir’s doors.

items.text: Grim is my name, Gangleri am I, Herjan and Hjalmberi, Thekk and Thrithi, Thuth and Uth, Helblindi and Hor;
lines: Grim is my name, Gangleri am I,
Herjan and Hjalmberi,
Thekk and Thrithi, Thuth and Uth,
Helblindi and Hor;

items.text: Sath and Svipal and Sanngetal, Herteit and Hnikar, Bileyg, Baleyg, Bolverk, Fjolnir, Grim and Grimnir, Glapsvith, Fjolsvith.
lines: Sath and Svipal and Sanngetal,
Herteit and Hnikar,
Bileyg, Baleyg, Bolverk, Fjolnir,
Grim and Grimnir, Glapsvith, Fjolsvith.

items.text: Sithhott, Sithskegg, Sigfather, Hnikuth, Allfather, Valfather, Atrith, Farmatyr: A single name have I never had Since first among men I fared.
lines: Sithhott, Sithskegg, Sigfather, Hnikuth,
Allfather, Valfather, Atrith, Farmatyr:
A single name have I never had
Since first among men I fared.

items.text: Grimnir they call me in Geirröth’s hall, With Asmund Jalk am I; Kjalar I was when I went in a sledge, At the council Thror am I called, As Vithur I fare to the fight; Oski, Biflindi, Jafnhor and Omi, Gondlir and Harbarth midst gods.
lines: Grimnir they call me in Geirröth’s hall,
With Asmund Jalk am I;
Kjalar I was when I went in a sledge,
At the council Thror am I called,
As Vithur I fare to the fight;
Oski, Biflindi, Jafnhor and Omi,
Gondlir and Harbarth midst gods.

items.text: I deceived the giant Sokkmimir old As Svithur and Svithrir of yore; Of Mithvitnir’s son the slayer I was When the famed one found his doom.
lines: I deceived the giant Sokkmimir old
As Svithur and Svithrir of yore;
Of Mithvitnir’s son the slayer I was
When the famed one found his doom.

items.text: Drunk art thou, Geirröth, too much didst thou drink, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Much hast thou lost, for help no more From me or my heroes thou hast.
lines: Drunk art thou, Geirröth, too much didst thou drink,
Much hast thou lost, for help no more
From me or my heroes thou hast.

items.text: Small heed didst thou take to all that I told, And false were the words of thy friends; For now the sword of my friend I see, That waits all wet with blood.
lines: Small heed didst thou take to all that I told,
And false were the words of thy friends;
For now the sword of my friend I see,
That waits all wet with blood.

items.text: Thy sword-pierced body shall Ygg have soon, For thy life is ended at last; The maids are hostile; now Othin behold! Now come to me if thou canst!
lines: Thy sword-pierced body shall Ygg have soon,
For thy life is ended at last;
The maids are hostile; now Othin behold!
Now come to me if thou canst!

items.text: Now am I Othin, Ygg was I once, Ere that did they call me Thund; Vak and Skilfing, Vofuth and Hroptatyr, Gaut and Jalk midst the gods; Ofnir and Svafnir, and all, methinks, Are names for none but me.
lines: Now am I Othin, Ygg was I once,
Ere that did they call me Thund;
Vak and Skilfing, Vofuth and Hroptatyr,
Gaut and Jalk midst the gods;
Ofnir and Svafnir, and all, methinks,
Are names for none but me.

items.text: King Geirröth sat and had his sword on his knee, half drawn from its sheath. But when he heard that Othin was come thither, then he rose up and sought to take Othin from the fire. The sword slipped from his hand, and fell with the hilt down. The king stumbled and fell forward, and the sword pierced him through, and slew him. Then Othin vanished, but Agnar long ruled there as king.

Freyr, the son of Njorth, had sat one day in Hlithskjolf, and looked over all the worlds. He looked into Jotunheim, and saw there a fair maiden, as she went from her father’s house to her bower. Forthwith he felt a mighty love-sickness. Skirnir was the name of Freyr’s servant; Njorth bade him ask speech of Freyr. He said:
“Go now, Skirnir! and seek to gain Speech from my son; And answer to win, for whom the wise one Is mightily moved.”
lines: “Go now, Skirnir! and seek to gain
Speech from my son;
And answer to win, for whom the wise one
Is mightily moved.”

items.text: Skirnir spake:
“Ill words do I now await from thy son, If I seek to get speech with him, And answer to win, for whom the wise one Is mightily moved.”
lines: “Ill words do I now await from thy son,
If I seek to get speech with him,
And answer to win, for whom the wise one
Is mightily moved.”

items.text: Skirnir spake:
“Speak prithee, Freyr, foremost of the gods, For now I fain would know; Why sittest thou here in the wide halls, Days long, my prince, alone?”
lines: “Speak prithee, Freyr, foremost of the gods,
For now I fain would know;
Why sittest thou here in the wide halls,
Days long, my prince, alone?”

items.text: Freyr spake:
“How shall I tell thee, thou hero young, Of all my grief so great? Though every day the elfbeam dawns, It lights my longing never.”
lines: “How shall I tell thee, thou hero young,
Of all my grief so great?
Though every day the elfbeam dawns,
It lights my longing never.”

items.text: Skirnir spake:
“Thy longings, methinks, are not so large That thou mayst not tell them to me; Since in days of yore we were young together, We two might each other trust.”
lines: “Thy longings, methinks, are not so large
That thou mayst not tell them to me;
Since in days of yore we were young together,
We two might each other trust.”

items.text: Freyr spake:
“From Gymir’s house I beheld go forth A maiden dear to me; Her arms glittered, and from their gleam Shone all the sea and sky.
lines: “From Gymir’s house I beheld go forth
A maiden dear to me;
Her arms glittered, and from their gleam
Shone all the sea and sky.

items.text: “To me more dear than in days of old Was ever maiden to man; But no one of gods or elves will grant That we both together should be.”
lines: “To me more dear than in days of old
Was ever maiden to man;
But no one of gods or elves will grant
That we both together should be.”

items.text: Skirnir spake:
“Then give me the horse that goes through the dark And magic flickering flames; And the sword as well that fights of itself Against the giants grim.”
lines: “Then give me the horse that goes through the dark
And magic flickering flames;
And the sword as well that fights of itself
Against the giants grim.”

items.text: Freyr spake:
“The horse will I give thee that goes through the dark And magic flickering flames, And the sword as well that will fight of itself If a worthy hero wields it.”
lines: “The horse will I give thee that goes through the dark
And magic flickering flames,
And the sword as well that will fight of itself
If a worthy hero wields it.”

items.text: Skirnir spake to the horse:
“Dark is it without, and I deem it time To fare through the wild fells, (To fare through the giants’ fastness;) We shall both come back, or us both together The terrible giant will take.”
lines: “Dark is it without, and I deem it time
To fare through the wild fells,
(To fare through the giants’ fastness;)
We shall both come back, or us both together
The terrible giant will take.”

items.text: Skirnir rode into Jotunheim to Gymir’s house. There were fierce dogs bound before the gate of the fence which was around Gerth’s hall. He rode to where a herdsman sat on a hill, and said:
“Tell me, herdsman, sitting on the hill, And watching all the ways, How may I win a word with the maid Past the hounds of Gymir here?”
lines: “Tell me, herdsman, sitting on the hill,
And watching all the ways,
How may I win a word with the maid
Past the hounds of Gymir here?”

items.text: The herdsman spake:
“Art thou doomed to die or already dead, Thou horseman that ridest hither? Barred from speech shalt thou ever be With Gymir’s daughter good.”
lines: “Art thou doomed to die or already dead,
Thou horseman that ridest hither?
Barred from speech shalt thou ever be
With Gymir’s daughter good.”

items.text: Skirnir spake:
“Boldness is better than plaints can be For him whose feet must fare; To a destined day has mine age been doomed, And my life’s span thereto laid.”
lines: “Boldness is better than plaints can be
For him whose feet must fare;
To a destined day has mine age been doomed,
And my life’s span thereto laid.”

items.text: Gerth spake:
“What noise is that which now so loud I hear within our house? The ground shakes, and the home of Gymir Around me trembles too.”
lines: “What noise is that which now so loud
I hear within our house?
The ground shakes, and the home of Gymir
Around me trembles too.”

items.text: The Serving-Maid spake:
“One stands without who has leapt from his steed, And lets his horse loose to graze;” . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: “One stands without who has leapt from his steed,
And lets his horse loose to graze;”

items.text: Gerth spake:
“Bid the man come in, and drink good mead Here within our hall; Though this I fear, that there without My brother’s slayer stands.
lines: “Bid the man come in, and drink good mead
Here within our hall;
Though this I fear, that there without
My brother’s slayer stands.

items.text: “Art thou of the elves or the offspring of gods, Or of the wise Wanes? How camst thou alone through the leaping flame Thus to behold our home?”
lines: “Art thou of the elves or the offspring of gods,
Or of the wise Wanes?
How camst thou alone through the leaping flame
Thus to behold our home?”

items.text: Skirnir spake:
“I am not of the elves, nor the offspring of gods, Nor of the wise Wanes; Though I came alone through the leaping flame Thus to behold thy home.
lines: “I am not of the elves, nor the offspring of gods,
Nor of the wise Wanes;
Though I came alone through the leaping flame
Thus to behold thy home.

items.text: “Eleven apples, all of gold, Here will I give thee, Gerth, To buy thy troth that Freyr shall be Deemed to be dearest to you.”
lines: “Eleven apples, all of gold,
Here will I give thee, Gerth,
To buy thy troth that Freyr shall be
Deemed to be dearest to you.”

items.text: Gerth spake:
“I will not take at any man’s wish These eleven apples ever; Nor shall Freyr and I one dwelling find So long as we two live.”
lines: “I will not take at any man’s wish
These eleven apples ever;
Nor shall Freyr and I one dwelling find
So long as we two live.”

items.text: Skirnir spake:
“Then do I bring thee the ring that was burned Of old with Othin’s son; From it do eight of like weight fall On every ninth night.”
lines: “Then do I bring thee the ring that was burned
Of old with Othin’s son;
From it do eight of like weight fall
On every ninth night.”

items.text: Gerth spake:
“The ring I wish not, though burned it was Of old with Othin’s son; In Gymir’s home is no lack of gold In the wealth my father wields.”
lines: “The ring I wish not, though burned it was
Of old with Othin’s son;
In Gymir’s home is no lack of gold
In the wealth my father wields.”

items.text: Skirnir spake:
“Seest thou, maiden, this keen, bright sword That I hold here in my hand? Thy head from thy neck shall I straightway hew, If thou wilt not do my will.”
lines: “Seest thou, maiden, this keen, bright sword
That I hold here in my hand?
Thy head from thy neck shall I straightway hew,
If thou wilt not do my will.”

items.text: Gerth spake:
“For no man’s sake will I ever suffer To be thus moved by might; But gladly, methinks, will Gymir seek To fight if he finds thee here.”
lines: “For no man’s sake will I ever suffer
To be thus moved by might;
But gladly, methinks, will Gymir seek
To fight if he finds thee here.”

items.text: Skirnir spake:
“Seest thou, maiden, this keen, bright sword That I hold here in my hand? Before its blade the old giant bends,— Thy father is doomed to die.
lines: “Seest thou, maiden, this keen, bright sword
That I hold here in my hand?
Before its blade the old giant bends,—
Thy father is doomed to die.

items.text: “I strike thee, maid, with my magic staff, To tame thee to work my will; There shalt thou go where never again The sons of men shall see thee.
lines: “I strike thee, maid, with my magic staff,
To tame thee to work my will;
There shalt thou go where never again
The sons of men shall see thee.

items.text: “On the eagle’s hill shalt thou ever sit, And gaze on the gates of Hel; More loathsome to thee than the light-hued snake To men, shall thy meat become.
lines: “On the eagle’s hill shalt thou ever sit,
And gaze on the gates of Hel;
More loathsome to thee than the light-hued snake
To men, shall thy meat become.

items.text: “Fearful to see, if thou comest forth, Hrimnir will stand and stare, (Men will marvel at thee;) More famed shalt thou grow than the watchman of the gods! Peer forth, then, from thy prison.
lines: “Fearful to see, if thou comest forth,
Hrimnir will stand and stare,
(Men will marvel at thee;)
More famed shalt thou grow than the watchman of the gods!
Peer forth, then, from thy prison.

items.text: “Rage and longing, fetters and wrath, Tears and torment are thine; Where thou sittest down my doom is on thee Of heavy heart And double dole.
lines: “Rage and longing, fetters and wrath,
Tears and torment are thine;
Where thou sittest down my doom is on thee
Of heavy heart
And double dole.

items.text: “In the giants’ home shall vile things harm thee Each day with evil deeds; Grief shalt thou get instead of gladness, And sorrow to suffer with tears.
lines: “In the giants’ home shall vile things harm thee
Each day with evil deeds;
Grief shalt thou get instead of gladness,
And sorrow to suffer with tears.

items.text: “With three-headed giants thou shalt dwell ever, Or never know a husband; (Let longing grip thee, let wasting waste thee,—) Be like to the thistle that in the loft Was cast and there was crushed.
lines: “With three-headed giants thou shalt dwell ever,
Or never know a husband;
(Let longing grip thee, let wasting waste thee,—)
Be like to the thistle that in the loft
Was cast and there was crushed.

items.text: “I go to the wood, and to the wet forest, To win a magic wand; . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . I won a magic wand.
lines: “I go to the wood, and to the wet forest,
To win a magic wand;
I won a magic wand.

items.text: “Othin grows angry, angered is the best of the gods, Freyr shall be thy foe, Most evil maid, who the magic wrath Of gods hast got for thyself.
lines: “Othin grows angry, angered is the best of the gods,
Freyr shall be thy foe,
Most evil maid, who the magic wrath
Of gods hast got for thyself.

items.text: “Give heed, frost-rulers, hear it, giants, Sons of Suttung, And gods, ye too, How I forbid and how I ban The meeting of men with the maid, (The joy of men with the maid.)
lines: “Give heed, frost-rulers, hear it, giants,
Sons of Suttung,
And gods, ye too,
How I forbid and how I ban
The meeting of men with the maid,
(The joy of men with the maid.)

items.text: “Hrimgrimnir is he, the giant who shall have thee In the depth by the doors of Hel; To the frost-giants’ halls each day shalt thou fare, Crawling and craving in vain, (Crawling and having no hope.)
lines: “Hrimgrimnir is he, the giant who shall have thee
In the depth by the doors of Hel;
To the frost-giants’ halls each day shalt thou fare,
Crawling and craving in vain,
(Crawling and having no hope.)

items.text: “Base wretches there by the root of the tree Will hold for thee horns of filth; A fairer drink shalt thou never find, Maid, to meet thy wish, (Maid, to meet my wish.)
lines: “Base wretches there by the root of the tree
Will hold for thee horns of filth;
A fairer drink shalt thou never find,
Maid, to meet thy wish,
(Maid, to meet my wish.)

items.text: “I write thee a charm and three runes therewith, Longing and madness and lust; But what I have writ I may yet unwrite If I find a need therefor.”
lines: “I write thee a charm and three runes therewith,
Longing and madness and lust;
But what I have writ I may yet unwrite
If I find a need therefor.”

items.text: Gerth spake:
“Find welcome rather, and with it take The frost-cup filled with mead; Though I did not believe that I should so love Ever one of the Wanes.”
lines: “Find welcome rather, and with it take
The frost-cup filled with mead;
Though I did not believe that I should so love
Ever one of the Wanes.”

items.text: Skirnir spake:
“My tidings all must I truly learn Ere homeward hence I ride: How soon thou wilt with the mighty son Of Njorth a meeting make.”
lines: “My tidings all must I truly learn
Ere homeward hence I ride:
How soon thou wilt with the mighty son
Of Njorth a meeting make.”

items.text: Gerth spake:
“Barri there is, which we both know well, A forest fair and still; And nine nights hence to the son of Njorth Will Gerth there grant delight.”
lines: “Barri there is, which we both know well,
A forest fair and still;
And nine nights hence to the son of Njorth
Will Gerth there grant delight.”

items.text: Then Skirnir rode home. Freyr stood without, and spoke to him, and asked for tidings:
“Tell me, Skirnir, ere thou take off the saddle, Or farest forward a step: What hast thou done in the giants’ dwelling To make glad thee or me?”
lines: “Tell me, Skirnir, ere thou take off the saddle,
Or farest forward a step:
What hast thou done in the giants’ dwelling
To make glad thee or me?”

items.text: Skirnir spake:
“Barri there is, which we both know well, A forest fair and still; And nine nights hence to the son of Njorth Will Gerth there grant delight.”
lines: “Barri there is, which we both know well,
A forest fair and still;
And nine nights hence to the son of Njorth
Will Gerth there grant delight.”

items.text: Freyr spake:
“Long is one night, longer are two; How then shall I bear three? Often to me has a month seemed less Than now half a night of desire.”
lines: “Long is one night, longer are two;
How then shall I bear three?
Often to me has a month seemed less
Than now half a night of desire.”

items.text: Thor was on his way back from a journey in the East, and came to a sound; on the other side of the sound was a ferryman with a boat. Thor called out:
“Who is the fellow yonder, on the farther shore of the sound?”
lines: “Who is the fellow yonder, on the farther shore of the
sound?”

items.text: The ferryman spake:
“What kind of a peasant is yon, that calls o’er the bay?”
lines: “What kind of a peasant is yon, that calls o’er the bay?”

items.text: Thor spake:

“Ferry me over the sound; I will feed thee therefor in the morning; A basket I have on my back, and food therein, none better; At leisure I ate, ere the house I left, Of herrings and porridge, so plenty I had.”
lines: “Ferry me over the sound; I will feed thee therefor in the
morning;
A basket I have on my back, and food therein, none better;
At leisure I ate, ere the house I left,
Of herrings and porridge, so plenty I had.”

items.text: The ferryman spake:
“Of thy morning feats art thou proud, but the future thou knowest not wholly; Doleful thine home-coming is: thy mother, methinks, is dead.”
lines: “Of thy morning feats art thou proud, but the future thou
knowest not wholly;
Doleful thine home-coming is: thy mother, methinks, is dead.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Now hast thou said what to each must seem The mightiest grief, that my mother is dead.”
lines: “Now hast thou said what to each must seem
The mightiest grief, that my mother is dead.”

items.text: The ferryman spake:
“Three good dwellings, methinks, thou hast not; Barefoot thou standest, and wearest a beggar’s dress; Not even hose dost thou have.”
lines: “Three good dwellings, methinks, thou hast not;
Barefoot thou standest, and wearest a beggar’s dress;
Not even hose dost thou have.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Steer thou hither the boat; the landing here shall I show thee; But whose the craft that thou keepest on the shore?”
lines: “Steer thou hither the boat; the landing here shall I show
thee;
But whose the craft that thou keepest on the shore?”

items.text: The ferryman spake:

“Hildolf is he who bade me have it, A hero wise; his home is at Rathsey’s sound. He bade me no robbers to steer, nor stealers of steeds, But worthy men, and those whom well do I know. Say now thy name, if over the sound thou wilt fare.”
lines: “Hildolf is he who bade me have it,
A hero wise; his home is at Rathsey’s sound.
He bade me no robbers to steer, nor stealers of steeds,
But worthy men, and those whom well do I know.
Say now thy name, if over the sound thou wilt fare.”

items.text: Thor spake:

“My name indeed shall I tell, though in danger I am, And all my race; I am Othin’s son, Meili’s brother, and Magni’s father, The strong one of the gods; with Thor now speech canst thou get. And now would I know what name thou hast.”
lines: “My name indeed shall I tell, though in danger I am,
And all my race; I am Othin’s son,
Meili’s brother, and Magni’s father,
The strong one of the gods; with Thor now speech canst thou
get.
And now would I know what name thou hast.”

items.text: The ferryman spake:
“Harbarth am I, and seldom I hide my name.”
lines: “Harbarth am I, and seldom I hide my name.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Why shouldst thou hide thy name, if quarrel thou hast not?”
lines: “Why shouldst thou hide thy name, if quarrel thou hast
not?”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“And though I had a quarrel, from such as thou art Yet none the less my life would I guard, Unless I be doomed to die.”
lines: “And though I had a quarrel, from such as thou art
Yet none the less my life would I guard,
Unless I be doomed to die.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Great trouble, methinks, would it be to come to thee, To wade the waters across, and wet my middle; Weakling, well shall I pay thy mocking words, If across the sound I come.”
lines: “Great trouble, methinks, would it be to come to thee,
To wade the waters across, and wet my middle;
Weakling, well shall I pay thy mocking words,
If across the sound I come.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“Here shall I stand and await thee here; Thou hast found since Hrungnir died no fiercer man.”
lines: “Here shall I stand and await thee here;
Thou hast found since Hrungnir died no fiercer man.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Fain art thou to tell how with Hrungnir I fought, The haughty giant, whose head of stone was made; And yet I felled him, and stretched him before me. What, Harbarth, didst thou the while?”
lines: “Fain art thou to tell how with Hrungnir I fought,
The haughty giant, whose head of stone was made;
And yet I felled him, and stretched him before me.
What, Harbarth, didst thou the while?”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“Five full winters with Fjolvar was I, And dwelt in the isle that is Algrön called; There could we fight, and fell the slain, Much could we seek, and maids could master.”
lines: “Five full winters with Fjolvar was I,
And dwelt in the isle that is Algrön called;
There could we fight, and fell the slain,
Much could we seek, and maids could master.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“How won ye success with your women?”
lines: “How won ye success with your women?”

items.text: Harbarth spake:

“Lively women we had, if they wise for us were; Wise were the women we had, if they kind for us were; For ropes of sand they would seek to wind, And the bottom to dig from the deepest dale. Wiser than all in counsel I was, And there I slept by the sisters seven, And joy full great did I get from each. What, Thor, didst thou the while?”
lines: “Lively women we had, if they wise for us were;
Wise were the women we had, if they kind for us were;
For ropes of sand they would seek to wind,
And the bottom to dig from the deepest dale.
Wiser than all in counsel I was,
And there I slept by the sisters seven,
And joy full great did I get from each.
What, Thor, didst thou the while?”

items.text: Thor spake:

“Thjazi I felled, the giant fierce, And I hurled the eyes of Alvaldi’s son To the heavens hot above; Of my deeds the mightiest marks are these, That all men since can see. What, Harbarth, didst thou the while?”
lines: “Thjazi I felled, the giant fierce,
And I hurled the eyes of Alvaldi’s son
To the heavens hot above;
Of my deeds the mightiest marks are these,
That all men since can see.
What, Harbarth, didst thou the while?”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“Much love-craft I wrought with them who ride by night, When I stole them by stealth from their husbands; A giant hard was Hlebarth, methinks: His wand he gave me as gift, And I stole his wits away.”
lines: “Much love-craft I wrought with them who ride by night,
When I stole them by stealth from their husbands;
A giant hard was Hlebarth, methinks:
His wand he gave me as gift,
And I stole his wits away.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Thou didst repay good gifts with evil mind.”
lines: “Thou didst repay good gifts with evil mind.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“The oak must have what it shaves from another; In such things each for himself. What, Thor, didst thou the while?”
lines: “The oak must have what it shaves from another;
In such things each for himself.
What, Thor, didst thou the while?”

items.text: Thor spake:

“Eastward I fared, of the giants I felled Their ill-working women who went to the mountain; And large were the giants’ throng if all were alive; No men would there be in Mithgarth more. What, Harbarth, didst thou the while?”
lines: “Eastward I fared, of the giants I felled
Their ill-working women who went to the mountain;
And large were the giants’ throng if all were
alive;
No men would there be in Mithgarth more.
What, Harbarth, didst thou the while?”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“In Valland I was, and wars I raised, Princes I angered, and peace brought never; The noble who fall in the fight hath Othin, And Thor hath the race of the thralls.”
lines: “In Valland I was, and wars I raised,
Princes I angered, and peace brought never;
The noble who fall in the fight hath Othin,
And Thor hath the race of the thralls.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Unequal gifts of men wouldst thou give to the gods, If might too much thou shouldst have.”
lines: “Unequal gifts of men wouldst thou give to the gods,
If might too much thou shouldst have.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:

“Thor has might enough, but never a heart; For cowardly fear in a glove wast thou fain to crawl, And there forgot thou wast Thor; Afraid there thou wast, thy fear was such, To fart or sneeze lest Fjalar should hear.”
lines: “Thor has might enough, but never a heart;
For cowardly fear in a glove wast thou fain to crawl,
And there forgot thou wast Thor;
Afraid there thou wast, thy fear was such,
To fart or sneeze lest Fjalar should hear.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Thou womanish Harbarth, to hell would I smite thee straight, Could mine arm reach over the sound.”
lines: “Thou womanish Harbarth, to hell would I smite thee
straight,
Could mine arm reach over the sound.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“Wherefore reach over the sound, since strife we have none? What, Thor, didst thou do then?”
lines: “Wherefore reach over the sound, since strife we have
none?
What, Thor, didst thou do then?”

items.text: Thor spake:

“Eastward I was, and the river I guarded well, Where the sons of Svarang sought me there; Stones did they hurl; small joy did they have of winning; Before me there to ask for peace did they fare. What, Harbarth, didst thou the while?”
lines: “Eastward I was, and the river I guarded well,
Where the sons of Svarang sought me there;
Stones did they hurl; small joy did they have of winning;
Before me there to ask for peace did they fare.
What, Harbarth, didst thou the while?”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“Eastward I was, and spake with a certain one, I played with the linen-white maid, and met her by stealth; I gladdened the gold-decked one, and she granted me joy.”
lines: “Eastward I was, and spake with a certain one,
I played with the linen-white maid, and met her by stealth;
I gladdened the gold-decked one, and she granted me joy.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Full fair was thy woman-finding.”
lines: “Full fair was thy woman-finding.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“Thy help did I need then, Thor, to hold the white maid fast.”
lines: “Thy help did I need then, Thor, to hold the white maid
fast.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Gladly, had I been there, my help to thee had been given.”
lines: “Gladly, had I been there, my help to thee had been
given.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“I might have trusted thee then, didst thou not betray thy troth.”
lines: “I might have trusted thee then, didst thou not betray
thy troth.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“No heel-biter am I, in truth, like an old leather shoe in spring.”
lines: “No heel-biter am I, in truth, like an old leather shoe
in spring.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“What, Thor, didst thou the while?”
lines: “What, Thor, didst thou the while?”

items.text: Thor spake:
“In Hlesey the brides of the Berserkers slew I; Most evil they were, and all they betrayed.”
lines: “In Hlesey the brides of the Berserkers slew I;
Most evil they were, and all they betrayed.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“Shame didst thou win, that women thou slewest, Thor.”
lines: “Shame didst thou win, that women thou slewest, Thor.”

items.text: Thor spake:

“She-wolves they were like, and women but little; My ship, which well I had trimmed, did they shake; With clubs of iron they threatened, and Thjalfi they drove off. What, Harbarth, didst thou the while?”
lines: “She-wolves they were like, and women but little;
My ship, which well I had trimmed, did they shake;
With clubs of iron they threatened, and Thjalfi they drove
off.
What, Harbarth, didst thou the while?”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“In the host I was that hither fared, The banners to raise, and the spear to redden.”
lines: “In the host I was that hither fared,
The banners to raise, and the spear to redden.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Wilt thou now say that hatred thou soughtest to bring us?”
lines: “Wilt thou now say that hatred thou soughtest to bring
us?”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“A ring for thy hand shall make all right for thee, As the judge decides who sets us two at peace.”
lines: “A ring for thy hand shall make all right for thee,
As the judge decides who sets us two at peace.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Where foundest thou so foul and scornful a speech? More foul a speech I never before have heard.”
lines: “Where foundest thou so foul and scornful a speech?
More foul a speech I never before have heard.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“I learned it from men, the men so old, Who dwell in the hills of home.”
lines: “I learned it from men, the men so old,
Who dwell in the hills of home.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“A name full good to heaps of stones thou givest When thou callest them hills of home.”
lines: “A name full good to heaps of stones thou givest
When thou callest them hills of home.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“Of such things speak I so.”
lines: “Of such things speak I so.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Ill for thee comes thy keenness of tongue, If the water I choose to wade; Louder, I ween, than a wolf thou cryest, If a blow of my hammer thou hast.”
lines: “Ill for thee comes thy keenness of tongue,
If the water I choose to wade;
Louder, I ween, than a wolf thou cryest,
If a blow of my hammer thou hast.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“Sif has a lover at home, and him shouldst thou meet; More fitting it were on him to put forth thy strength.”
lines: “Sif has a lover at home, and him shouldst thou meet;
More fitting it were on him to put forth thy strength.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Thy tongue still makes thee say what seems most ill to me, Thou witless man! Thou liest, I ween.”
lines: “Thy tongue still makes thee say what seems most ill to
me,
Thou witless man! Thou liest, I ween.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“Truth do I speak, but slow on thy way thou art; Far hadst thou gone if now in the boat thou hadst fared.”
lines: “Truth do I speak, but slow on thy way thou art;
Far hadst thou gone if now in the boat thou hadst fared.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Thou womanish Harbarth! here hast thou held me too long.”
lines: “Thou womanish Harbarth! here hast thou held me too
long.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“I thought not ever that Asathor would be hindered By a ferryman thus from faring.”
lines: “I thought not ever that Asathor would be hindered
By a ferryman thus from faring.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“One counsel I bring thee now: row hither thy boat; No more of scoffing; set Magni’s father across.”
lines: “One counsel I bring thee now: row hither thy boat;
No more of scoffing; set Magni’s father across.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“From the sound go hence; the passage thou hast not.”
lines: “From the sound go hence; the passage thou hast not.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“The way now show me, since thou takest me not o’er the water.”
lines: “The way now show me, since thou takest me not o’er the
water.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:

“To refuse it is little, to fare it is long; A while to the stock, and a while to the stone; Then the road to thy left, till Verland thou reachest; And there shall Fjorgyn her son Thor find, And the road of her children she shows him to Othin’s realm.”
lines: “To refuse it is little, to fare it is long;
A while to the stock, and a while to the stone;
Then the road to thy left, till Verland thou reachest;
And there shall Fjorgyn her son Thor find,
And the road of her children she shows him to Othin’s realm.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“May I come so far in a day?”
lines: “May I come so far in a day?”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“With toil and trouble perchance, While the sun still shines, or so I think.”
lines: “With toil and trouble perchance,
While the sun still shines, or so I think.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Short now shall be our speech, for thou speakest in mockery only; The passage thou gavest me not I shall pay thee if ever we meet.”
lines: “Short now shall be our speech, for thou speakest in
mockery only;
The passage thou gavest me not I shall pay thee if ever we
meet.”

items.text: Harbarth spake:
“Get hence where every evil thing shall have thee!”
lines: “Get hence where every evil thing shall have thee!”

items.text: Of old the gods made feast together, And drink they sought ere sated they were; Twigs they shook, and blood they tried: Rich fare in Ægir’s hall they found.
lines: Of old the gods made feast together,
And drink they sought ere sated they were;
Twigs they shook, and blood they tried:
Rich fare in Ægir’s hall they found.

items.text: The mountain-dweller sat merry as boyhood, But soon like a blinded man he seemed; The son of Ygg gazed in his eyes: “For the gods a feast shalt thou forthwith get.”
lines: The mountain-dweller sat merry as boyhood,
But soon like a blinded man he seemed;
The son of Ygg gazed in his eyes:
“For the gods a feast shalt thou forthwith get.”

items.text: The word-wielder toil for the giant worked, And so revenge on the gods he sought; He bade Sif’s mate the kettle bring: “Therein for ye all much ale shall I brew.”
lines: The word-wielder toil for the giant worked,
And so revenge on the gods he sought;
He bade Sif’s mate the kettle bring:
“Therein for ye all much ale shall I brew.”

items.text: The far-famed ones could find it not, And the holy gods could get it nowhere; Till in truthful wise did Tyr speak forth, And helpful counsel to Hlorrithi gave.
lines: The far-famed ones could find it not,
And the holy gods could get it nowhere;
Till in truthful wise did Tyr speak forth,
And helpful counsel to Hlorrithi gave.

items.text: “There dwells to the east of Elivagar Hymir the wise at the end of heaven; A kettle my father fierce doth own, A mighty vessel a mile in depth.”
lines: “There dwells to the east of Elivagar
Hymir the wise at the end of heaven;
A kettle my father fierce doth own,
A mighty vessel a mile in depth.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“May we win, dost thou think, this whirler of water?”
lines: “May we win, dost thou think, this whirler of water?”

items.text: Tyr spake:
“Aye, friend, we can, if cunning we are.”
lines: “Aye, friend, we can, if cunning we are.”

items.text: Forward that day with speed they fared, From Asgarth came they to Egil’s home; The goats with horns bedecked he guarded; Then they sped to the hall where Hymir dwelt.
lines: Forward that day with speed they fared,
From Asgarth came they to Egil’s home;
The goats with horns bedecked he guarded;
Then they sped to the hall where Hymir dwelt.

items.text: The youth found his grandam, that greatly he loathed, And full nine hundred heads she had; But the other fair with gold came forth, And the bright-browed one brought beer to her son.
lines: The youth found his grandam, that greatly he loathed,
And full nine hundred heads she had;
But the other fair with gold came forth,
And the bright-browed one brought beer to her son.

items.text: “Kinsman of giants, beneath the kettle Will I set ye both, ye heroes bold; For many a time my dear-loved mate To guests is wrathful and grim of mind.”
lines: “Kinsman of giants, beneath the kettle
Will I set ye both, ye heroes bold;
For many a time my dear-loved mate
To guests is wrathful and grim of mind.”

items.text: Late to his home the misshapen Hymir, The giant harsh, from his hunting came; The icicles rattled as in he came, For the fellow’s chin-forest frozen was.
lines: Late to his home the misshapen Hymir,
The giant harsh, from his hunting came;
The icicles rattled as in he came,
For the fellow’s chin-forest frozen was.

items.text: “Hail to thee, Hymir! good thoughts mayst thou have; Here has thy son to thine hall now come; (For him have we waited, his way was long;) And with him fares the foeman of Hroth, The friend of mankind, and Veur they call him.
lines: “Hail to thee, Hymir! good thoughts mayst thou have;
Here has thy son to thine hall now come;
(For him have we waited, his way was long;)
And with him fares the foeman of Hroth,
The friend of mankind, and Veur they call him.

items.text: “See where under the gable they sit! Behind the beam do they hide themselves.” The beam at the glance of the giant broke, And the mighty pillar in pieces fell.
lines: “See where under the gable they sit!
Behind the beam do they hide themselves.”
The beam at the glance of the giant broke,
And the mighty pillar in pieces fell.

items.text: Eight fell from the ledge, and one alone, The hard-hammered kettle, of all was whole; Forth came they then, and his foes he sought, The giant old, and held with his eyes.
lines: Eight fell from the ledge, and one alone,
The hard-hammered kettle, of all was whole;
Forth came they then, and his foes he sought,
The giant old, and held with his eyes.

items.text: Much sorrow his heart foretold when he saw The giantess’ foeman come forth on the floor; Then of the steers did they bring in three; Their flesh to boil did the giant bid.
lines: Much sorrow his heart foretold when he saw
The giantess’ foeman come forth on the floor;
Then of the steers did they bring in three;
Their flesh to boil did the giant bid.

items.text: By a head was each the shorter hewed, And the beasts to the fire straight they bore; The husband of Sif, ere to sleep he went, Alone two oxen of Hymir’s ate.
lines: By a head was each the shorter hewed,
And the beasts to the fire straight they bore;
The husband of Sif, ere to sleep he went,
Alone two oxen of Hymir’s ate.

items.text: To the comrade hoary of Hrungnir then Did Hlorrithi’s meal full mighty seem; “Next time at eve we three must eat The food we have as the hunting’s spoil.”
lines: To the comrade hoary of Hrungnir then
Did Hlorrithi’s meal full mighty seem;
“Next time at eve we three must eat
The food we have as the hunting’s spoil.”

items.text: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Fain to row on the sea was Veur, he said, If the giant bold would give him bait.
lines: Fain to row on the sea was Veur, he said,
If the giant bold would give him bait.

items.text: Hymir spake:
“Go to the herd, if thou hast it in mind, Thou slayer of giants, thy bait to seek; For there thou soon mayst find, methinks, Bait from the oxen easy to get.”
lines: “Go to the herd, if thou hast it in mind,
Thou slayer of giants, thy bait to seek;
For there thou soon mayst find, methinks,
Bait from the oxen easy to get.”

items.text: Swift to the wood the hero went, Till before him an ox all black he found; From the beast the slayer of giants broke The fortress high of his double horns.
lines: Swift to the wood the hero went,
Till before him an ox all black he found;
From the beast the slayer of giants broke
The fortress high of his double horns.

items.text: Hymir spake:
“Thy works, methinks, are worse by far, Thou steerer of ships, than when still thou sittest.” . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: “Thy works, methinks, are worse by far,
Thou steerer of ships, than when still thou sittest.”

items.text: The lord of the goats bade the ape-begotten Farther to steer the steed of the rollers; But the giant said that his will, forsooth, Longer to row was little enough.
lines: The lord of the goats bade the ape-begotten
Farther to steer the steed of the rollers;
But the giant said that his will, forsooth,
Longer to row was little enough.

items.text: Two whales on his hook did the mighty Hymir Soon pull up on a single cast; In the stern the kinsman of Othin sat, And Veur with cunning his cast prepared.
lines: Two whales on his hook did the mighty Hymir
Soon pull up on a single cast;
In the stern the kinsman of Othin sat,
And Veur with cunning his cast prepared.

items.text: The warder of men, the worm’s destroyer, Fixed on his hook the head of the ox; There gaped at the bait the foe of the gods, The girdler of all the earth beneath.
lines: The warder of men, the worm’s destroyer,
Fixed on his hook the head of the ox;
There gaped at the bait the foe of the gods,
The girdler of all the earth beneath.

items.text: The venomous serpent swiftly up To the boat did Thor, the bold one, pull; With his hammer the loathly hill of the hair Of the brother of Fenrir he smote from above.
lines: The venomous serpent swiftly up
To the boat did Thor, the bold one, pull;
With his hammer the loathly hill of the hair
Of the brother of Fenrir he smote from above.

items.text: The monsters roared, and the rocks resounded, And all the earth so old was shaken; . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Then sank the fish in the sea forthwith.
lines: The monsters roared, and the rocks resounded,
And all the earth so old was shaken;
Then sank the fish in the sea forthwith.

items.text: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Joyless as back they rowed was the giant; Speechless did Hymir sit at the oars, With the rudder he sought a second wind.
lines: Joyless as back they rowed was the giant;
Speechless did Hymir sit at the oars,
With the rudder he sought a second wind.

items.text: Hymir spake:
“The half of our toil wilt thou have with me, And now make fast our goat of the flood; Or home wilt thou bear the whales to the house, Across the gorge of the wooded glen?”
lines: “The half of our toil wilt thou have with me,
And now make fast our goat of the flood;
Or home wilt thou bear the whales to the house,
Across the gorge of the wooded glen?”

items.text: Hlorrithi stood and the stem he gripped, And the sea-horse with water awash he lifted; Oars and bailer and all he bore With the surf-swine home to the giant’s house.
lines: Hlorrithi stood and the stem he gripped,
And the sea-horse with water awash he lifted;
Oars and bailer and all he bore
With the surf-swine home to the giant’s house.

items.text: His might the giant again would match, For stubborn he was, with the strength of Thor; None truly strong, though stoutly he rowed, Would he call save one who could break the cup.
lines: His might the giant again would match,
For stubborn he was, with the strength of Thor;
None truly strong, though stoutly he rowed,
Would he call save one who could break the cup.

items.text: Hlorrithi then, when the cup he held, Struck with the glass the pillars of stone; As he sat the posts in pieces he shattered, Yet the glass to Hymir whole they brought.
lines: Hlorrithi then, when the cup he held,
Struck with the glass the pillars of stone;
As he sat the posts in pieces he shattered,
Yet the glass to Hymir whole they brought.

items.text: But the loved one fair of the giant found A counsel true, and told her thought: “Smite the skull of Hymir, heavy with food, For harder it is than ever was glass.”
lines: But the loved one fair of the giant found
A counsel true, and told her thought:
“Smite the skull of Hymir, heavy with food,
For harder it is than ever was glass.”
