items.text: The goats’ mighty ruler then rose on his knee, And with all the strength of a god he struck; Whole was the fellow’s helmet-stem, But shattered the wine-cup rounded was.
lines: The goats’ mighty ruler then rose on his knee,
And with all the strength of a god he struck;
Whole was the fellow’s helmet-stem,
But shattered the wine-cup rounded was.

items.text: Hymir spake:
“Fair is the treasure that from me is gone, Since now the cup on my knees lies shattered;” So spake the giant: “No more can I say In days to be, ‘Thou art brewed, mine ale.’
lines: “Fair is the treasure that from me is gone,
Since now the cup on my knees lies shattered;”
So spake the giant: “No more can I say
In days to be, ‘Thou art brewed, mine ale.’

items.text: “Enough shall it be if out ye can bring Forth from our house the kettle here.” Tyr then twice to move it tried, But before him the kettle twice stood fast.
lines: “Enough shall it be if out ye can bring
Forth from our house the kettle here.”
Tyr then twice to move it tried,
But before him the kettle twice stood fast.

items.text: The father of Mothi the rim seized firm, And before it stood on the floor below; Up on his head Sif’s husband raised it, And about his heels the handles clattered.
lines: The father of Mothi the rim seized firm,
And before it stood on the floor below;
Up on his head Sif’s husband raised it,
And about his heels the handles clattered.

items.text: Not long had they fared, ere backwards looked The son of Othin, once more to see; From their caves in the east beheld he coming With Hymir the throng of the many-headed.
lines: Not long had they fared, ere backwards looked
The son of Othin, once more to see;
From their caves in the east beheld he coming
With Hymir the throng of the many-headed.

items.text: He stood and cast from his back the kettle, And Mjollnir, the lover of murder, he wielded; . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . So all the whales of the waste he slew.
lines: He stood and cast from his back the kettle,
And Mjollnir, the lover of murder, he wielded;
So all the whales of the waste he slew.

items.text: Not long had they fared ere one there lay Of Hlorrithi’s goats half-dead on the ground; In his leg the pole-horse there was lame; The deed the evil Loki had done.
lines: Not long had they fared ere one there lay
Of Hlorrithi’s goats half-dead on the ground;
In his leg the pole-horse there was lame;
The deed the evil Loki had done.

items.text: But ye all have heard,— for of them who have The tales of the gods, who better can tell?— What prize he won from the wilderness-dweller, Who both his children gave him to boot.
lines: But ye all have heard,— for of them who have
The tales of the gods, who better can tell?—
What prize he won from the wilderness-dweller,
Who both his children gave him to boot.

items.text: The mighty one came to the council of gods, And the kettle he had that Hymir’s was; So gladly their ale the gods could drink In Ægir’s hall at the autumn-time.
lines: The mighty one came to the council of gods,
And the kettle he had that Hymir’s was;
So gladly their ale the gods could drink
In Ægir’s hall at the autumn-time.

items.text: Ægir, who was also called Gymir, had prepared ale for the gods, after he had got the mighty kettle, as now has been told. To this feast came Othin and Frigg, his wife. Thor came not, as he was on a journey in the East. Sif, Thor’s wife, was there, and Bragi with Ithun, his wife. Tyr, who had but one hand, was there; the wolf Fenrir had bitten off his other hand when they had bound him. There were Njorth and Skathi his wife, Freyr and Freyja, and Vithar, the son of Othin. Loki was there, and Freyr’s servants Byggvir and Beyla. Many were there of the gods and elves.

Ægir had two serving-men, Fimafeng and Eldir. Glittering gold they had in place of firelight; the ale came in of itself; and great was the peace. The guests praised much the ability of Ægir’s serving-men. Loki might not endure that, and he slew Fimafeng. Then the gods shook their shields and howled at Loki and drove him away to the forest, and thereafter set to drinking again. Loki turned back, and outside he met Eldir. Loki spoke to him:
“Speak now, Eldir, for not one step Farther shalt thou fare; What ale-talk here do they have within, The sons of the glorious gods?”
lines: “Speak now, Eldir, for not one step
Farther shalt thou fare;
What ale-talk here do they have within,
The sons of the glorious gods?”

items.text: Eldir spake:
“Of their weapons they talk, and their might in war, The sons of the glorious gods; From the gods and elves who are gathered here No friend in words shalt thou find.”
lines: “Of their weapons they talk, and their might in war,
The sons of the glorious gods;
From the gods and elves who are gathered here
No friend in words shalt thou find.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“In shall I go into Ægir’s hall, For the feast I fain would see; Bale and hatred I bring to the gods, And their mead with venom I mix.”
lines: “In shall I go into Ægir’s hall,
For the feast I fain would see;
Bale and hatred I bring to the gods,
And their mead with venom I mix.”

items.text: Eldir spake:
“If in thou goest to Ægir’s hall, And fain the feast wouldst see, And with slander and spite wouldst sprinkle the gods, Think well lest they wipe it on thee.”
lines: “If in thou goest to Ægir’s hall,
And fain the feast wouldst see,
And with slander and spite wouldst sprinkle the gods,
Think well lest they wipe it on thee.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Bethink thee, Eldir, if thou and I Shall strive with spiteful speech; Richer I grow in ready words If thou speakest too much to me.”
lines: “Bethink thee, Eldir, if thou and I
Shall strive with spiteful speech;
Richer I grow in ready words
If thou speakest too much to me.”

items.text: Then Loki went into the hall, but when they who were there saw who had entered, they were all silent.
Loki spake:
“Thirsty I come into this thine hall, I, Lopt, from a journey long, To ask of the gods that one should give Fair mead for a drink to me.
lines: “Thirsty I come into this thine hall,
I, Lopt, from a journey long,
To ask of the gods that one should give
Fair mead for a drink to me.

items.text: “Why sit ye silent, swollen with pride, Ye gods, and no answer give? At your feast a place and a seat prepare me, Or bid me forth to fare.”
lines: “Why sit ye silent, swollen with pride,
Ye gods, and no answer give?
At your feast a place and a seat prepare me,
Or bid me forth to fare.”

items.text: Bragi spake:
“A place and a seat will the gods prepare No more in their midst for thee; For the gods know well what men they wish To find at their mighty feasts.”
lines: “A place and a seat will the gods prepare
No more in their midst for thee;
For the gods know well what men they wish
To find at their mighty feasts.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Remember, Othin, in olden days That we both our blood have mixed; Then didst thou promise no ale to pour, Unless it were brought for us both.”
lines: “Remember, Othin, in olden days
That we both our blood have mixed;
Then didst thou promise no ale to pour,
Unless it were brought for us both.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Stand forth then, Vithar, and let the wolf’s father Find a seat at our feast; Lest evil should Loki speak aloud Here within Ægir’s hall.”
lines: “Stand forth then, Vithar, and let the wolf’s father
Find a seat at our feast;
Lest evil should Loki speak aloud
Here within Ægir’s hall.”

items.text: Then Vithar arose and poured drink for Loki; but before he drank he spoke to the gods:
“Hail to you, gods! ye goddesses, hail! Hail to the holy throng! Save for the god who yonder sits, Bragi there on the bench.”
lines: “Hail to you, gods! ye goddesses, hail!
Hail to the holy throng!
Save for the god who yonder sits,
Bragi there on the bench.”

items.text: Bragi spake:
“A horse and a sword from my hoard will I give, And a ring gives Bragi to boot, That hatred thou makst not among the gods; So rouse not the great ones to wrath.”
lines: “A horse and a sword from my hoard will I give,
And a ring gives Bragi to boot,
That hatred thou makst not among the gods;
So rouse not the great ones to wrath.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“In horses and rings thou shalt never be rich, Bragi, but both shalt thou lack; Of the gods and elves here together met Least brave in battle art thou, (And shyest thou art of the shot.)”
lines: “In horses and rings thou shalt never be rich,
Bragi, but both shalt thou lack;
Of the gods and elves here together met
Least brave in battle art thou,
(And shyest thou art of the shot.)”

items.text: Bragi spake:
“Now were I without as I am within, And here in Ægir’s hall, Thine head would I bear in mine hands away, And pay thee the price of thy lies.”
lines: “Now were I without as I am within,
And here in Ægir’s hall,
Thine head would I bear in mine hands away,
And pay thee the price of thy lies.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“In thy seat art thou bold, not so are thy deeds, Bragi, adorner of benches! Go out and fight if angered thou feelest, No hero such forethought has.”
lines: “In thy seat art thou bold, not so are thy deeds,
Bragi, adorner of benches!
Go out and fight if angered thou feelest,
No hero such forethought has.”

items.text: Ithun spake:
“Well, prithee, Bragi, his kinship weigh, Since chosen as wish-son he was; And speak not to Loki such words of spite Here within Ægir’s hall.”
lines: “Well, prithee, Bragi, his kinship weigh,
Since chosen as wish-son he was;
And speak not to Loki such words of spite
Here within Ægir’s hall.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Be silent, Ithun! thou art, I say, Of women most lustful in love, Since thou thy washed-bright arms didst wind About thy brother’s slayer.”
lines: “Be silent, Ithun! thou art, I say,
Of women most lustful in love,
Since thou thy washed-bright arms didst wind
About thy brother’s slayer.”

items.text: Ithun spake:
“To Loki I speak not with spiteful words Here within Ægir’s hall; And Bragi I calm, who is hot with beer, For I wish not that fierce they should fight.”
lines: “To Loki I speak not with spiteful words
Here within Ægir’s hall;
And Bragi I calm, who is hot with beer,
For I wish not that fierce they should fight.”

items.text: Gefjun spake:
“Why, ye gods twain, with bitter tongues Raise hate among us here? Loki is famed for his mockery foul, And the dwellers in heaven he hates.”
lines: “Why, ye gods twain, with bitter tongues
Raise hate among us here?
Loki is famed for his mockery foul,
And the dwellers in heaven he hates.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Be silent, Gefjun! for now shall I say Who led thee to evil life; The boy so fair gave a necklace bright, And about him thy leg was laid.”
lines: “Be silent, Gefjun! for now shall I say
Who led thee to evil life;
The boy so fair gave a necklace bright,
And about him thy leg was laid.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Mad art thou, Loki, and little of wit, The wrath of Gefjun to rouse; For the fate that is set for all she sees, Even as I, methinks.”
lines: “Mad art thou, Loki, and little of wit,
The wrath of Gefjun to rouse;
For the fate that is set for all she sees,
Even as I, methinks.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Be silent, Othin! not justly thou settest The fate of the fight among men; Oft gavst thou to him who deserved not the gift, To the baser, the battle’s prize.”
lines: “Be silent, Othin! not justly thou settest
The fate of the fight among men;
Oft gavst thou to him who deserved not the gift,
To the baser, the battle’s prize.”

items.text: Othin spake:

“Though I gave to him who deserved not the gift, To the baser, the battle’s prize; Winters eight wast thou under the earth, Milking the cows as a maid, (Ay, and babes didst thou bear; Unmanly thy soul must seem.)”
lines: “Though I gave to him who deserved not the gift,
To the baser, the battle’s prize;
Winters eight wast thou under the earth,
Milking the cows as a maid,
(Ay, and babes didst thou bear;
Unmanly thy soul must seem.)”

items.text: Loki spake:
“They say that with spells in Samsey once Like witches with charms didst thou work; And in witch’s guise among men didst thou go; Unmanly thy soul must seem.”
lines: “They say that with spells in Samsey once
Like witches with charms didst thou work;
And in witch’s guise among men didst thou go;
Unmanly thy soul must seem.”

items.text: Frigg spake:
“Of the deeds ye two of old have done Ye should make no speech among men; Whate’er ye have done in days gone by, Old tales should ne’er be told.”
lines: “Of the deeds ye two of old have done
Ye should make no speech among men;
Whate’er ye have done in days gone by,
Old tales should ne’er be told.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Be silent, Frigg! thou art Fjorgyn’s wife, But ever lustful in love; For Vili and Ve, thou wife of Vithrir, Both in thy bosom have lain.”
lines: “Be silent, Frigg! thou art Fjorgyn’s wife,
But ever lustful in love;
For Vili and Ve, thou wife of Vithrir,
Both in thy bosom have lain.”

items.text: Frigg spake:
“If a son like Baldr were by me now, Here within Ægir’s hall, From the sons of the gods thou shouldst go not forth Till thy fierceness in fight were tried.”
lines: “If a son like Baldr were by me now,
Here within Ægir’s hall,
From the sons of the gods thou shouldst go not forth
Till thy fierceness in fight were tried.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Thou wilt then, Frigg, that further I tell Of the ill that now I know; Mine is the blame that Baldr no more Thou seest ride home to the hall.”
lines: “Thou wilt then, Frigg, that further I tell
Of the ill that now I know;
Mine is the blame that Baldr no more
Thou seest ride home to the hall.”

items.text: Freyja spake:
“Mad art thou, Loki, that known thou makest The wrong and shame thou hast wrought; The fate of all does Frigg know well, Though herself she says it not.”
lines: “Mad art thou, Loki, that known thou makest
The wrong and shame thou hast wrought;
The fate of all does Frigg know well,
Though herself she says it not.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Be silent, Freyja! for fully I know thee, Sinless thou art not thyself; Of the gods and elves who are gathered here, Each one as thy lover has lain.”
lines: “Be silent, Freyja! for fully I know thee,
Sinless thou art not thyself;
Of the gods and elves who are gathered here,
Each one as thy lover has lain.”

items.text: Freyja spake:
“False is thy tongue, and soon shalt thou find That it sings thee an evil song; The gods are wroth, and the goddesses all, And in grief shalt thou homeward go.”
lines: “False is thy tongue, and soon shalt thou find
That it sings thee an evil song;
The gods are wroth, and the goddesses all,
And in grief shalt thou homeward go.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Be silent, Freyja! thou foulest witch, And steeped full sore in sin; In the arms of thy brother the bright gods caught thee When Freyja her wind set free.”
lines: “Be silent, Freyja! thou foulest witch,
And steeped full sore in sin;
In the arms of thy brother the bright gods caught thee
When Freyja her wind set free.”

items.text: Njorth spake:
“Small ill does it work though a woman may have A lord or a lover or both; But a wonder it is that this womanish god Comes hither, though babes he has borne.”
lines: “Small ill does it work though a woman may have
A lord or a lover or both;
But a wonder it is that this womanish god
Comes hither, though babes he has borne.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Be silent, Njorth; thou wast eastward sent, To the gods as a hostage given; And the daughters of Hymir their privy had When use did they make of thy mouth.”
lines: “Be silent, Njorth; thou wast eastward sent,
To the gods as a hostage given;
And the daughters of Hymir their privy had
When use did they make of thy mouth.”

items.text: Njorth spake:
“Great was my gain, though long was I gone, To the gods as a hostage given; The son did I have whom no man hates, And foremost of gods is found.”
lines: “Great was my gain, though long was I gone,
To the gods as a hostage given;
The son did I have whom no man hates,
And foremost of gods is found.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Give heed now, Njorth, nor boast too high, No longer I hold it hid; With thy sister hadst thou so fair a son, Thus hadst thou no worse a hope.”
lines: “Give heed now, Njorth, nor boast too high,
No longer I hold it hid;
With thy sister hadst thou so fair a son,
Thus hadst thou no worse a hope.”

items.text: Tyr spake:
“Of the heroes brave is Freyr the best Here in the home of the gods; He harms not maids nor the wives of men, And the bound from their fetters he frees.”
lines: “Of the heroes brave is Freyr the best
Here in the home of the gods;
He harms not maids nor the wives of men,
And the bound from their fetters he frees.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Be silent, Tyr! for between two men Friendship thou ne’er couldst fashion; Fain would I tell how Fenrir once Thy right hand rent from thee.”
lines: “Be silent, Tyr! for between two men
Friendship thou ne’er couldst fashion;
Fain would I tell how Fenrir once
Thy right hand rent from thee.”

items.text: Tyr spake:
“My hand do I lack, but Hrothvitnir thou, And the loss brings longing to both; Ill fares the wolf who shall ever await In fetters the fall of the gods.”
lines: “My hand do I lack, but Hrothvitnir thou,
And the loss brings longing to both;
Ill fares the wolf who shall ever await
In fetters the fall of the gods.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Be silent, Tyr! for a son with me Thy wife once chanced to win; Not a penny, methinks, wast thou paid for the wrong, Nor wast righted an inch, poor wretch.”
lines: “Be silent, Tyr! for a son with me
Thy wife once chanced to win;
Not a penny, methinks, wast thou paid for the wrong,
Nor wast righted an inch, poor wretch.”

items.text: Freyr spake:
“By the mouth of the river the wolf remains Till the gods to destruction go; Thou too shalt soon, if thy tongue is not stilled, Be fettered, thou forger of ill.”
lines: “By the mouth of the river the wolf remains
Till the gods to destruction go;
Thou too shalt soon, if thy tongue is not stilled,
Be fettered, thou forger of ill.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“The daughter of Gymir with gold didst thou buy, And sold thy sword to boot; But when Muspell’s sons through Myrkwood ride, Thou shalt weaponless wait, poor wretch.”
lines: “The daughter of Gymir with gold didst thou buy,
And sold thy sword to boot;
But when Muspell’s sons through Myrkwood ride,
Thou shalt weaponless wait, poor wretch.”

items.text: Byggvir spake:
“Had I birth so famous as Ingunar-Freyr, And sat in so lofty a seat, I would crush to marrow this croaker of ill, And beat all his body to bits.”
lines: “Had I birth so famous as Ingunar-Freyr,
And sat in so lofty a seat,
I would crush to marrow this croaker of ill,
And beat all his body to bits.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“What little creature goes crawling there, Snuffling and snapping about? At Freyr’s ears ever wilt thou be found, Or muttering hard at the mill.”
lines: “What little creature goes crawling there,
Snuffling and snapping about?
At Freyr’s ears ever wilt thou be found,
Or muttering hard at the mill.”

items.text: Byggvir spake:
“Byggvir my name, and nimble am I, As gods and men do grant; And here am I proud that the children of Hropt Together all drink ale.”
lines: “Byggvir my name, and nimble am I,
As gods and men do grant;
And here am I proud that the children of Hropt
Together all drink ale.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Be silent, Byggvir! thou never couldst set Their shares of the meat for men; Hid in straw on the floor, they found thee not When heroes were fain to fight.”
lines: “Be silent, Byggvir! thou never couldst set
Their shares of the meat for men;
Hid in straw on the floor, they found thee not
When heroes were fain to fight.”

items.text: Heimdall spake:
“Drunk art thou, Loki, and mad are thy deeds, Why, Loki, leavst thou this not? For drink beyond measure will lead all men No thought of their tongues to take.”
lines: “Drunk art thou, Loki, and mad are thy deeds,
Why, Loki, leavst thou this not?
For drink beyond measure will lead all men
No thought of their tongues to take.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Be silent, Heimdall! in days long since Was an evil fate for thee fixed; With back held stiff must thou ever stand, As warder of heaven to watch.”
lines: “Be silent, Heimdall! in days long since
Was an evil fate for thee fixed;
With back held stiff must thou ever stand,
As warder of heaven to watch.”

items.text: Skathi spake:
“Light art thou, Loki, but longer thou mayst not In freedom flourish thy tail; On the rocks the gods bind thee with bowels torn Forth from thy frost-cold son.”
lines: “Light art thou, Loki, but longer thou mayst not
In freedom flourish thy tail;
On the rocks the gods bind thee with bowels torn
Forth from thy frost-cold son.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Though on rocks the gods bind me with bowels torn Forth from my frost-cold son, I was first and last at the deadly fight There where Thjazi we caught.”
lines: “Though on rocks the gods bind me with bowels torn
Forth from my frost-cold son,
I was first and last at the deadly fight
There where Thjazi we caught.”

items.text: Skathi spake:
“Wert thou first and last at the deadly fight There where Thjazi was caught, From my dwellings and fields shall ever come forth A counsel cold for thee.”
lines: “Wert thou first and last at the deadly fight
There where Thjazi was caught,
From my dwellings and fields shall ever come forth
A counsel cold for thee.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“More lightly thou spakest with Laufey’s son, When thou badst me come to thy bed; Such things must be known if now we two Shall seek our sins to tell.”
lines: “More lightly thou spakest with Laufey’s son,
When thou badst me come to thy bed;
Such things must be known if now we two
Shall seek our sins to tell.”

items.text: Then Sif came forward and poured mead for Loki in a crystal cup, and said:
“Hail to thee, Loki, and take thou here The crystal cup of old mead; For me at least, alone of the gods, Blameless thou knowest to be.”
lines: “Hail to thee, Loki, and take thou here
The crystal cup of old mead;
For me at least, alone of the gods,
Blameless thou knowest to be.”

items.text: He took the horn, and drank therefrom:
“Alone thou wert if truly thou wouldst All men so shyly shun; But one do I know full well, methinks, Who had thee from Hlorrithi’s arms,— (Loki the crafty in lies.)”
lines: “Alone thou wert if truly thou wouldst
All men so shyly shun;
But one do I know full well, methinks,
Who had thee from Hlorrithi’s arms,—
(Loki the crafty in lies.)”

items.text: Beyla spake:
“The mountains shake, and surely I think From his home comes Hlorrithi now; He will silence the man who is slandering here Together both gods and men.”
lines: “The mountains shake, and surely I think
From his home comes Hlorrithi now;
He will silence the man who is slandering here
Together both gods and men.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Be silent, Beyla! thou art Byggvir’s wife, And deep art thou steeped in sin; A greater shame to the gods came ne’er, Befouled thou art with thy filth.”
lines: “Be silent, Beyla! thou art Byggvir’s wife,
And deep art thou steeped in sin;
A greater shame to the gods came ne’er,
Befouled thou art with thy filth.”

items.text: Then came Thor forth, and spake:
“Unmanly one, cease, or the mighty hammer, Mjollnir, shall close thy mouth; Thy shoulder-cliff shall I cleave from thy neck, And so shall thy life be lost.”
lines: “Unmanly one, cease, or the mighty hammer,
Mjollnir, shall close thy mouth;
Thy shoulder-cliff shall I cleave from thy neck,
And so shall thy life be lost.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Lo, in has come the son of Earth: Why threaten so loudly, Thor? Less fierce thou shalt go to fight with the wolf When he swallows Sigfather up.”
lines: “Lo, in has come the son of Earth:
Why threaten so loudly, Thor?
Less fierce thou shalt go to fight with the wolf
When he swallows Sigfather up.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Unmanly one, cease, or the mighty hammer, Mjollnir, shall close thy mouth; I shall hurl thee up and out in the East, Where men shall see thee no more.”
lines: “Unmanly one, cease, or the mighty hammer,
Mjollnir, shall close thy mouth;
I shall hurl thee up and out in the East,
Where men shall see thee no more.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“That thou hast fared on the East-road forth To men shouldst thou say no more; In the thumb of a glove didst thou hide, thou great one, And there forgot thou wast Thor.”
lines: “That thou hast fared on the East-road forth
To men shouldst thou say no more;
In the thumb of a glove didst thou hide, thou great one,
And there forgot thou wast Thor.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Unmanly one, cease, or the mighty hammer, Mjollnir, shall close thy mouth; My right hand shall smite thee with Hrungnir’s slayer, Till all thy bones are broken.”
lines: “Unmanly one, cease, or the mighty hammer,
Mjollnir, shall close thy mouth;
My right hand shall smite thee with Hrungnir’s slayer,
Till all thy bones are broken.”

items.text: Loki spake:

“A long time still do I think to live, Though thou threatenest thus with thy hammer; Rough seemed the straps of Skrymir’s wallet, When thy meat thou mightest not get, (And faint from hunger didst feel.)”
lines: “A long time still do I think to live,
Though thou threatenest thus with thy hammer;
Rough seemed the straps of Skrymir’s wallet,
When thy meat thou mightest not get,
(And faint from hunger didst feel.)”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Unmanly one, cease, or the mighty hammer, Mjollnir, shall close thy mouth; The slayer of Hrungnir shall send thee to hell, And down to the gate of death.”
lines: “Unmanly one, cease, or the mighty hammer,
Mjollnir, shall close thy mouth;
The slayer of Hrungnir shall send thee to hell,
And down to the gate of death.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“I have said to the gods and the sons of the gods The things that whetted my thoughts; But before thee alone do I now go forth, For thou fightest well, I ween.
lines: “I have said to the gods and the sons of the gods
The things that whetted my thoughts;
But before thee alone do I now go forth,
For thou fightest well, I ween.

items.text: “Ale hast thou brewed, but, Ægir, now Such feasts shalt thou make no more; O’er all that thou hast which is here within Shall play the flickering flames, (And thy back shall be burnt with fire.)”
lines: “Ale hast thou brewed, but, Ægir, now
Such feasts shalt thou make no more;
O’er all that thou hast which is here within
Shall play the flickering flames,
(And thy back shall be burnt with fire.)”

items.text: And after that Loki hid himself in Franang’s waterfall in the guise of a salmon, and there the gods took him. He was bound with the bowels of his son Vali, but his son Narfi was changed to a wolf. Skathi took a poison-snake and fastened it up over Loki’s face, and the poison dropped thereon. Sigyn, Loki’s wife, sat there and held a shell under the poison, but when the shell was full she bore away the poison, and meanwhile the poison dropped on Loki. Then he struggled so hard that the whole earth shook therewith; and now that is called an earthquake.
Wild was Vingthor when he awoke, And when his mighty hammer he missed; He shook his beard, his hair was bristling, As the son of Jorth about him sought.
lines: Wild was Vingthor when he awoke,
And when his mighty hammer he missed;
He shook his beard, his hair was bristling,
As the son of Jorth about him sought.

items.text: Hear now the speech that first he spake: “Harken, Loki, and heed my words, Nowhere on earth is it known to man, Nor in heaven above: our hammer is stolen.”
lines: Hear now the speech that first he spake:
“Harken, Loki, and heed my words,
Nowhere on earth is it known to man,
Nor in heaven above: our hammer is stolen.”

items.text: To the dwelling fair of Freyja went they, Hear now the speech that first he spake: “Wilt thou, Freyja, thy feather-dress lend me, That so my hammer I may seek?”
lines: To the dwelling fair of Freyja went they,
Hear now the speech that first he spake:
“Wilt thou, Freyja, thy feather-dress lend me,
That so my hammer I may seek?”

items.text: Freyja spake:

“Thine should it be though of silver bright, And I would give it though ’twere of gold.” Then Loki flew, and the feather-dress whirred, Till he left behind him the home of the gods, And reached at last the realm of the giants.
lines: “Thine should it be though of silver bright,
And I would give it though ’twere of gold.”
Then Loki flew, and the feather-dress whirred,
Till he left behind him the home of the gods,
And reached at last the realm of the giants.

items.text: Thrym sat on a mound, the giants’ master, Leashes of gold he laid for his dogs, And stroked and smoothed the manes of his steeds.
lines: Thrym sat on a mound, the giants’ master,
Leashes of gold he laid for his dogs,
And stroked and smoothed the manes of his steeds.

items.text: Thrym spake:
“How fare the gods, how fare the elves? Why comst thou alone to the giants’ land?”
lines: “How fare the gods, how fare the elves?
Why comst thou alone to the giants’ land?”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Ill fare the gods, ill fare the elves! Hast thou hidden Hlorrithi’s hammer?”
lines: “Ill fare the gods, ill fare the elves!
Hast thou hidden Hlorrithi’s hammer?”

items.text: Thrym spake:
“I have hidden Hlorrithi’s hammer, Eight miles down deep in the earth; And back again shall no man bring it If Freyja I win not to be my wife.”
lines: “I have hidden Hlorrithi’s hammer,
Eight miles down deep in the earth;
And back again shall no man bring it
If Freyja I win not to be my wife.”

items.text: Then Loki flew, and the feather-dress whirred, Till he left behind him the home of the giants, And reached at last the realm of the gods. There in the courtyard Thor he met: Hear now the speech that first he spake:
lines: Then Loki flew, and the feather-dress whirred,
Till he left behind him the home of the giants,
And reached at last the realm of the gods.
There in the courtyard Thor he met:
Hear now the speech that first he spake:

items.text: “Hast thou found tidings as well as trouble? Thy news in the air shalt thou utter now; Oft doth the sitter his story forget, And lies he speaks who lays himself down.”
lines: “Hast thou found tidings as well as trouble?
Thy news in the air shalt thou utter now;
Oft doth the sitter his story forget,
And lies he speaks who lays himself down.”

items.text: Loki spake:
“Trouble I have, and tidings as well: Thrym, king of the giants, keeps thy hammer, And back again shall no man bring it If Freyja he wins not to be his wife.”
lines: “Trouble I have, and tidings as well:
Thrym, king of the giants, keeps thy hammer,
And back again shall no man bring it
If Freyja he wins not to be his wife.”

items.text: Freyja the fair then went they to find; Hear now the speech that first he spake: “Bind on, Freyja, the bridal veil, For we two must haste to the giants’ home.”
lines: Freyja the fair then went they to find;
Hear now the speech that first he spake:
“Bind on, Freyja, the bridal veil,
For we two must haste to the giants’ home.”

items.text: Wrathful was Freyja, and fiercely she snorted, And the dwelling great of the gods was shaken, And burst was the mighty Brisings’ necklace: “Most lustful indeed should I look to all If I journeyed with thee to the giants’ home.”
lines: Wrathful was Freyja, and fiercely she snorted,
And the dwelling great of the gods was shaken,
And burst was the mighty Brisings’ necklace:
“Most lustful indeed should I look to all
If I journeyed with thee to the giants’ home.”

items.text: Then were the gods together met, And the goddesses came and council held, And the far-famed ones a plan would find, How they might Hlorrithi’s hammer win.
lines: Then were the gods together met,
And the goddesses came and council held,
And the far-famed ones a plan would find,
How they might Hlorrithi’s hammer win.

items.text: Then Heimdall spake, whitest of the gods, Like the Wanes he knew the future well: “Bind we on Thor the bridal veil, Let him bear the mighty Brisings’ necklace;
lines: Then Heimdall spake, whitest of the gods,
Like the Wanes he knew the future well:
“Bind we on Thor the bridal veil,
Let him bear the mighty Brisings’ necklace;

items.text: “Keys around him let there rattle, And down to his knees hang woman’s dress; With gems full broad upon his breast, And a pretty cap to crown his head.”
lines: “Keys around him let there rattle,
And down to his knees hang woman’s dress;
With gems full broad upon his breast,
And a pretty cap to crown his head.”

items.text: Then Thor the mighty his answer made: “Me would the gods unmanly call If I let bind the bridal veil.”
lines: Then Thor the mighty his answer made:
“Me would the gods unmanly call
If I let bind the bridal veil.”

items.text: Then Loki spake, the son of Laufey: “Be silent, Thor, and speak not thus; Else will the giants in Asgarth dwell If thy hammer is brought not home to thee.”
lines: Then Loki spake, the son of Laufey:
“Be silent, Thor, and speak not thus;
Else will the giants in Asgarth dwell
If thy hammer is brought not home to thee.”

items.text: Then bound they on Thor the bridal veil, And next the mighty Brisings’ necklace.
lines: Then bound they on Thor the bridal veil,
And next the mighty Brisings’ necklace.

items.text: Keys around him let they rattle, And down to his knees hung woman’s dress; With gems full broad upon his breast, And a pretty cap to crown his head.
lines: Keys around him let they rattle,
And down to his knees hung woman’s dress;
With gems full broad upon his breast,
And a pretty cap to crown his head.

items.text: Then Loki spake, the son of Laufey: “As thy maid-servant thither I go with thee; We two shall haste to the giants’ home.”
lines: Then Loki spake, the son of Laufey:
“As thy maid-servant thither I go with thee;
We two shall haste to the giants’ home.”

items.text: Then home the goats to the hall were driven, They wrenched at the halters, swift were they to run; The mountains burst, earth burned with fire, And Othin’s son sought Jotunheim.
lines: Then home the goats to the hall were driven,
They wrenched at the halters, swift were they to
run;
The mountains burst, earth burned with fire,
And Othin’s son sought Jotunheim.

items.text: Then loud spake Thrym, the giants’ leader: “Bestir ye, giants, put straw on the benches; Now Freyja they bring to be my bride, The daughter of Njorth out of Noatun.
lines: Then loud spake Thrym, the giants’ leader:
“Bestir ye, giants, put straw on the benches;
Now Freyja they bring to be my bride,
The daughter of Njorth out of Noatun.

items.text: “Gold-horned cattle go to my stables, Jet-black oxen, the giant’s joy; Many my gems, and many my jewels, Freyja alone did I lack, methinks.”
lines: “Gold-horned cattle go to my stables,
Jet-black oxen, the giant’s joy;
Many my gems, and many my jewels,
Freyja alone did I lack, methinks.”

items.text: Early it was to evening come, And forth was borne the beer for the giants; Thor alone ate an ox, and eight salmon, All the dainties as well that were set for the women; And drank Sif’s mate three tuns of mead.
lines: Early it was to evening come,
And forth was borne the beer for the giants;
Thor alone ate an ox, and eight salmon,
All the dainties as well that were set for the
women;
And drank Sif’s mate three tuns of mead.

items.text: Then loud spake Thrym, the giants’ leader: “Who ever saw bride more keenly bite? I ne’er saw bride with a broader bite, Nor a maiden who drank more mead than this!”
lines: Then loud spake Thrym, the giants’ leader:
“Who ever saw bride more keenly bite?
I ne’er saw bride with a broader bite,
Nor a maiden who drank more mead than this!”

items.text: Hard by there sat the serving-maid wise, So well she answered the giant’s words: “From food has Freyja eight nights fasted, So hot was her longing for Jotunheim.”
lines: Hard by there sat the serving-maid wise,
So well she answered the giant’s words:
“From food has Freyja eight nights fasted,
So hot was her longing for Jotunheim.”

items.text: Thrym looked ’neath the veil, for he longed to kiss, But back he leaped the length of the hall: “Why are so fearful the eyes of Freyja? Fire, methinks, from her eyes burns forth.”
lines: Thrym looked ’neath the veil, for he longed to kiss,
But back he leaped the length of the hall:
“Why are so fearful the eyes of Freyja?
Fire, methinks, from her eyes burns forth.”

items.text: Hard by there sat the serving-maid wise, So well she answered the giant’s words: “No sleep has Freyja for eight nights found, So hot was her longing for Jotunheim.”
lines: Hard by there sat the serving-maid wise,
So well she answered the giant’s words:
“No sleep has Freyja for eight nights found,
So hot was her longing for Jotunheim.”

items.text: Soon came the giant’s luckless sister, Who feared not to ask the bridal fee: “From thy hands the rings of red gold take, If thou wouldst win my willing love, (My willing love and welcome glad.)”
lines: Soon came the giant’s luckless sister,
Who feared not to ask the bridal fee:
“From thy hands the rings of red gold take,
If thou wouldst win my willing love,
(My willing love and welcome glad.)”

items.text: Then loud spake Thrym, the giants’ leader: “Bring in the hammer to hallow the bride; On the maiden’s knees let Mjollnir lie, That us both the hand of Vor may bless.”
lines: Then loud spake Thrym, the giants’ leader:
“Bring in the hammer to hallow the bride;
On the maiden’s knees let Mjollnir lie,
That us both the hand of Vor may bless.”

items.text: The heart in the breast of Hlorrithi laughed When the hard-souled one his hammer beheld; First Thrym, the king of the giants, he killed, Then all the folk of the giants he felled.
lines: The heart in the breast of Hlorrithi laughed
When the hard-souled one his hammer beheld;
First Thrym, the king of the giants, he killed,
Then all the folk of the giants he felled.

items.text: The giant’s sister old he slew, She who had begged the bridal fee; A stroke she got in the shilling’s stead. And for many rings the might of the hammer.
lines: The giant’s sister old he slew,
She who had begged the bridal fee;
A stroke she got in the shilling’s stead.
And for many rings the might of the hammer.

items.text: And so his hammer got Othin’s son.
lines: And so his hammer got Othin’s son.

items.text: Alvis spake:
“Now shall the bride my benches adorn, And homeward haste forthwith; Eager for wedlock to all shall I seem, Nor at home shall they rob me of rest.”
lines: “Now shall the bride my benches adorn,
And homeward haste forthwith;
Eager for wedlock to all shall I seem,
Nor at home shall they rob me of rest.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“What, pray, art thou? Why so pale round the nose? By the dead hast thou lain of late? To a giant like dost thou look, methinks; Thou wast not born for the bride.”
lines: “What, pray, art thou? Why so pale round the nose?
By the dead hast thou lain of late?
To a giant like dost thou look, methinks;
Thou wast not born for the bride.”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“Alvis am I, and under the earth My home ’neath the rocks I have; With the wagon-guider a word do I seek; Let the gods their bond not break.”
lines: “Alvis am I, and under the earth
My home ’neath the rocks I have;
With the wagon-guider a word do I seek;
Let the gods their bond not break.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Break it shall I, for over the bride Her father has foremost right; At home was I not when the promise thou hadst, And I give her alone of the gods.”
lines: “Break it shall I, for over the bride
Her father has foremost right;
At home was I not when the promise thou hadst,
And I give her alone of the gods.”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“What hero claims such right to hold O’er the bride that shines so bright? Not many will know thee, thou wandering man! Who was bought with rings to bear thee?”
lines: “What hero claims such right to hold
O’er the bride that shines so bright?
Not many will know thee, thou wandering man!
Who was bought with rings to bear thee?”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Vingthor, the wanderer wide, am I, And I am Sithgrani’s son; Against my will shalt thou get the maid, And win the marriage word.”
lines: “Vingthor, the wanderer wide, am I,
And I am Sithgrani’s son;
Against my will shalt thou get the maid,
And win the marriage word.”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“Thy good-will now shall I quickly get, And win the marriage word; I long to have, and I would not lack, This snow-white maid for mine.”
lines: “Thy good-will now shall I quickly get,
And win the marriage word;
I long to have, and I would not lack,
This snow-white maid for mine.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“The love of the maid I may not keep thee From winning, thou guest so wise, If of every world thou canst tell me all That now I wish to know.
lines: “The love of the maid I may not keep thee
From winning, thou guest so wise,
If of every world thou canst tell me all
That now I wish to know.

items.text: “Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all, Dwarf, of the doom of men: What call they the earth, that lies before all, In each and every world?”
lines: “Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the earth, that lies before all,
In each and every world?”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“‘Earth’ to men, ‘Field’ to the gods it is, ‘The Ways’ is it called by the Wanes; ‘Ever Green’ by the giants, ‘The Grower’ by elves, ‘The Moist’ by the holy ones high.”
lines: “‘Earth’ to men, ‘Field’ to the gods it is,
‘The Ways’ is it called by the Wanes;
‘Ever Green’ by the giants, ‘The Grower’ by elves,
‘The Moist’ by the holy ones high.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all, Dwarf, of the doom of men: What call they the heaven, beheld of the high one, In each and every world?”
lines: “Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the heaven, beheld of the high one,
In each and every world?”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“‘Heaven’ men call it, ‘The Height’ the gods, The Wanes ‘The Weaver of Winds’; Giants ‘The Up-World,’ elves ‘The Fair-Roof,’ The dwarfs ‘The Dripping Hall.’”
lines: “‘Heaven’ men call it, ‘The Height’ the gods,
The Wanes ‘The Weaver of Winds’;
Giants ‘The Up-World,’ elves ‘The Fair-Roof,’
The dwarfs ‘The Dripping Hall.’”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all, Dwarf, of the doom of men: What call they the moon, that men behold, In each and every world?”
lines: “Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the moon, that men behold,
In each and every world?”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“‘Moon’ with men, ‘Flame’ the gods among, ‘The Wheel’ in the house of hell; ‘The Goer’ the giants, ‘The Gleamer’ the dwarfs, The elves ‘The Teller of Time.’”
lines: “‘Moon’ with men, ‘Flame’ the gods among,
‘The Wheel’ in the house of hell;
‘The Goer’ the giants, ‘The Gleamer’ the dwarfs,
The elves ‘The Teller of Time.’”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all, Dwarf, of the doom of men: What call they the sun, that all men see, In each and every world?”
lines: “Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the sun, that all men see,
In each and every world?”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“Men call it ‘Sun,’ gods ‘Orb of the Sun,’ ‘The Deceiver of Dvalin’ the dwarfs; The giants ‘The Ever-Bright,’ elves ‘Fair Wheel,’ ‘All-Glowing’ the sons of the gods.”
lines: “Men call it ‘Sun,’ gods ‘Orb of the Sun,’
‘The Deceiver of Dvalin’ the dwarfs;
The giants ‘The Ever-Bright,’ elves ‘Fair Wheel,’
‘All-Glowing’ the sons of the gods.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all, Dwarf, of the doom of men: What call they the clouds, that keep the rains, In each and every world?”
lines: “Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the clouds, that keep the rains,
In each and every world?”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“‘Clouds’ men name them, ‘Rain-Hope’ gods call them, The Wanes call them ‘Kites of the Wind’; ‘Water-Hope’ giants, ‘Weather-Might’ elves, ‘The Helmet of Secrets’ in hell.”
lines: “‘Clouds’ men name them, ‘Rain-Hope’ gods call them,
The Wanes call them ‘Kites of the Wind’;
‘Water-Hope’ giants, ‘Weather-Might’ elves,
‘The Helmet of Secrets’ in hell.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all, Dwarf, of the doom of men: What call they the wind, that widest fares, In each and every world?”
lines: “Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the wind, that widest fares,
In each and every world?”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“‘Wind’ do men call it, the gods ‘The Waverer,’ ‘The Neigher’ the holy ones high; ‘The Wailer’ the giants, ‘Roaring Wender’ the elves, In hell ‘The Blustering Blast.’”
lines: “‘Wind’ do men call it, the gods ‘The Waverer,’
‘The Neigher’ the holy ones high;
‘The Wailer’ the giants, ‘Roaring Wender’ the elves,
In hell ‘The Blustering Blast.’”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all, Dwarf, of the doom of men: What call they the calm, that quiet lies, In each and every world?”
lines: “Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the calm, that quiet lies,
In each and every world?”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“‘Calm’ men call it, ‘The Quiet’ the gods, The Wanes ‘The Hush of the Winds’; ‘The Sultry’ the giants, elves ‘Day’s Stillness,’ The dwarfs ‘The Shelter of Day.’”
lines: “‘Calm’ men call it, ‘The Quiet’ the gods,
The Wanes ‘The Hush of the Winds’;
‘The Sultry’ the giants, elves ‘Day’s Stillness,’
The dwarfs ‘The Shelter of Day.’”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all, Dwarf, of the doom of men: What call they the sea, whereon men sail, In each and every world?”
lines: “Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the sea, whereon men sail,
In each and every world?”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“‘Sea’ men call it, gods ‘The Smooth-Lying,’ ‘The Wave’ is it called by the Wanes; ‘Eel-Home’ the giants, ‘Drink-Stuff’ the elves, For the dwarfs its name is ‘The Deep.’”
lines: “‘Sea’ men call it, gods ‘The Smooth-Lying,’
‘The Wave’ is it called by the Wanes;
‘Eel-Home’ the giants, ‘Drink-Stuff’ the elves,
For the dwarfs its name is ‘The Deep.’”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all, Dwarf, of the doom of men: What call they the fire, that flames for men, In each of all the worlds?”
lines: “Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the fire, that flames for men,
In each of all the worlds?”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“‘Fire’ men call it, and ‘Flame’ the gods, By the Wanes is it ‘Wildfire’ called; ‘The Biter’ by giants, ‘The Burner’ by dwarfs, ‘The Swift’ in the house of hell.”
lines: “‘Fire’ men call it, and ‘Flame’ the gods,
By the Wanes is it ‘Wildfire’ called;
‘The Biter’ by giants, ‘The Burner’ by dwarfs,
‘The Swift’ in the house of hell.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all, Dwarf, of the doom of men: What call they the wood, that grows for mankind, In each and every world?”
lines: “Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the wood, that grows for mankind,
In each and every world?”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“Men call it ‘The Wood,’ gods ‘The Mane of the Field,’ ‘Seaweed of Hills’ in hell; ‘Flame-Food’ the giants, ‘Fair-Limbed’ the elves, ‘The Wand’ is it called by the Wanes.”
lines: “Men call it ‘The Wood,’ gods ‘The Mane of the Field,’
‘Seaweed of Hills’ in hell;
‘Flame-Food’ the giants, ‘Fair-Limbed’ the elves,
‘The Wand’ is it called by the Wanes.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all, Dwarf, of the doom of men: What call they the night, the daughter of Nor, In each and every world?”
lines: “Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the night, the daughter of Nor,
In each and every world?”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“‘Night’ men call it, ‘Darkness’ gods name it, ‘The Hood’ the holy ones high; The giants ‘The Lightless,’ the elves ‘Sleep’s Joy,’ The dwarfs ‘The Weaver of Dreams.’”
lines: “‘Night’ men call it, ‘Darkness’ gods name it,
‘The Hood’ the holy ones high;
The giants ‘The Lightless,’ the elves ‘Sleep’s Joy,’
The dwarfs ‘The Weaver of Dreams.’”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all, Dwarf, of the doom of men: What call they the seed, that is sown by men, In each and every world?”
lines: “Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the seed, that is sown by men,
In each and every world?”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“Men call it ‘Grain,’ and ‘Corn’ the gods, ‘Growth’ in the world of the Wanes; ‘The Eaten’ by giants, ‘Drink-Stuff’ by elves, In hell ‘The Slender Stem.’”
lines: “Men call it ‘Grain,’ and ‘Corn’ the gods,
‘Growth’ in the world of the Wanes;
‘The Eaten’ by giants, ‘Drink-Stuff’ by elves,
In hell ‘The Slender Stem.’”

items.text: Thor spake:
“Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all, Dwarf, of the doom of men: What call they the ale, that is quaffed of men, In each and every world?”
lines: “Answer me, Alvis! thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the ale, that is quaffed of men,
In each and every world?”

items.text: Alvis spake:
“‘Ale’ among men, ‘Beer’ the gods among, In the world of the Wanes ‘The Foaming’; ‘Bright Draught’ with giants, ‘Mead’ with dwellers in hell, ‘The Feast-Draught’ with Suttung’s sons.”
lines: “‘Ale’ among men, ‘Beer’ the gods among,
In the world of the Wanes ‘The Foaming’;
‘Bright Draught’ with giants, ‘Mead’ with dwellers in hell,
‘The Feast-Draught’ with Suttung’s sons.”

items.text: Thor spake:
“In a single breast I never have seen More wealth of wisdom old; But with treacherous wiles must I now betray thee: The day has caught thee, dwarf! (Now the sun shines here in the hall.)”
lines: “In a single breast I never have seen
More wealth of wisdom old;
But with treacherous wiles must I now betray thee:
The day has caught thee, dwarf!
(Now the sun shines here in the hall.)”

items.text: Once were the gods together met, And the goddesses came and council held, And the far-famed ones the truth would find, Why baleful dreams to Baldr had come.
lines: Once were the gods together met,
And the goddesses came and council held,
And the far-famed ones the truth would find,
Why baleful dreams to Baldr had come.

items.text: Then Othin rose, the enchanter old, And the saddle he laid on Sleipnir’s back; Thence rode he down to Niflhel deep, And the hound he met that came from hell.
lines: Then Othin rose, the enchanter old,
And the saddle he laid on Sleipnir’s back;
Thence rode he down to Niflhel deep,
And the hound he met that came from hell.

items.text: Bloody he was on his breast before, At the father of magic he howled from afar; Forward rode Othin, the earth resounded Till the house so high of Hel he reached.
lines: Bloody he was on his breast before,
At the father of magic he howled from afar;
Forward rode Othin, the earth resounded
Till the house so high of Hel he reached.

items.text: Then Othin rode to the eastern door, There, he knew well, was the wise-woman’s grave; Magic he spoke and mighty charms, Till spell-bound she rose, and in death she spoke:
lines: Then Othin rode to the eastern door,
There, he knew well, was the wise-woman’s grave;
Magic he spoke and mighty charms,
Till spell-bound she rose, and in death she spoke:

items.text: “What is the man, to me unknown, That has made me travel the troublous road? I was snowed on with snow, and smitten with rain, And drenched with dew; long was I dead.”
lines: “What is the man, to me unknown,
That has made me travel the troublous road?
I was snowed on with snow, and smitten with rain,
And drenched with dew; long was I dead.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Vegtam my name, I am Valtam’s son; Speak thou of hell, for of heaven I know: For whom are the benches bright with rings, And the platforms gay bedecked with gold?”
lines: “Vegtam my name, I am Valtam’s son;
Speak thou of hell, for of heaven I know:
For whom are the benches bright with rings,
And the platforms gay bedecked with gold?”

items.text: The Wise-Woman spake:
“Here for Baldr the mead is brewed, The shining drink, and a shield lies o’er it; But their hope is gone from the mighty gods. Unwilling I spake, and now would be still.”
lines: “Here for Baldr the mead is brewed,
The shining drink, and a shield lies o’er it;
But their hope is gone from the mighty gods.
Unwilling I spake, and now would be still.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Wise-woman, cease not! I seek from thee All to know that I fain would ask: Who shall the bane of Baldr become, And steal the life from Othin’s son?”
lines: “Wise-woman, cease not! I seek from thee
All to know that I fain would ask:
Who shall the bane of Baldr become,
And steal the life from Othin’s son?”

items.text: The Wise-Woman spake:
“Hoth thither bears the far-famed branch, He shall the bane of Baldr become, And steal the life from Othin’s son. Unwilling I spake, and now would be still.”
lines: “Hoth thither bears the far-famed branch,
He shall the bane of Baldr become,
And steal the life from Othin’s son.
Unwilling I spake, and now would be still.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Wise-woman, cease not! I seek from thee All to know that I fain would ask: Who shall vengeance win for the evil work, Or bring to the flames the slayer of Baldr?”
lines: “Wise-woman, cease not! I seek from thee
All to know that I fain would ask:
Who shall vengeance win for the evil work,
Or bring to the flames the slayer of Baldr?”

items.text: The Wise-Woman spake:

“Rind bears Vali in Vestrsalir, And one night old fights Othin’s son; His hands he shall wash not, his hair he shall comb not, Till the slayer of Baldr he brings to the flames. Unwilling I spake, and now would be still.”
lines: “Rind bears Vali in Vestrsalir,
And one night old fights Othin’s son;
His hands he shall wash not, his hair he shall comb not,
Till the slayer of Baldr he brings to the flames.
Unwilling I spake, and now would be still.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“Wise-woman, cease not! I seek from thee All to know that I fain would ask: What maidens are they who then shall weep, And toss to the sky the yards of the sails?”
lines: “Wise-woman, cease not! I seek from thee
All to know that I fain would ask:
What maidens are they who then shall weep,
And toss to the sky the yards of the sails?”

items.text: The Wise-Woman spake:
“Vegtam thou art not, as erstwhile I thought; Othin thou art, the enchanter old.”
lines: “Vegtam thou art not, as erstwhile I thought;
Othin thou art, the enchanter old.”

items.text: Othin spake:
“No wise-woman art thou, nor wisdom hast; Of giants three the mother art thou.”
lines: “No wise-woman art thou, nor wisdom hast;
Of giants three the mother art thou.”

items.text: The Wise-Woman spake:
“Home ride, Othin, be ever proud; For no one of men shall seek me more Till Loki wanders loose from his bonds, And to the last strife the destroyers come.”
lines: “Home ride, Othin, be ever proud;
For no one of men shall seek me more
Till Loki wanders loose from his bonds,
And to the last strife the destroyers come.”

items.text: They tell in old stories that one of the gods, whose name was Heimdall, went on his way along a certain seashore, and came to a dwelling, where he called himself Rig. According to these stories is the following poem:
Men say there went by ways so green Of old the god, the aged and wise, Mighty and strong did Rig go striding. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: Men say there went by ways so green
Of old the god, the aged and wise,
Mighty and strong did Rig go striding.

items.text: Forward he went on the midmost way, He came to a dwelling, a door on its posts; In did he fare, on the floor was a fire, Two hoary ones by the hearth there sat, Ai and Edda, in olden dress.
lines: Forward he went on the midmost way,
He came to a dwelling, a door on its posts;
In did he fare, on the floor was a fire,
Two hoary ones by the hearth there sat,
Ai and Edda, in olden dress.

items.text: Rig knew well wise words to speak, Soon in the midst of the room he sat, And on either side the others were.
lines: Rig knew well wise words to speak,
Soon in the midst of the room he sat,
And on either side the others were.

items.text: A loaf of bread did Edda bring, Heavy and thick and swollen with husks; Forth on the table she set the fare, And broth for the meal in a bowl there was. (Calf’s flesh boiled was the best of the dainties.)
lines: A loaf of bread did Edda bring,
Heavy and thick and swollen with husks;
Forth on the table she set the fare,
And broth for the meal in a bowl there was.
(Calf’s flesh boiled was the best of the dainties.)

items.text: Rig knew well wise words to speak, Thence did he rise, made ready to sleep; Soon in the bed himself did he lay, And on either side the others were.
lines: Rig knew well wise words to speak,
Thence did he rise, made ready to sleep;
Soon in the bed himself did he lay,
And on either side the others were.

items.text: Thus was he there for three nights long, Then forward he went on the midmost way, And so nine months were soon passed by.
lines: Thus was he there for three nights long,
Then forward he went on the midmost way,
And so nine months were soon passed by.

items.text: A son bore Edda, with water they sprinkled him, With a cloth his hair so black they covered; Thræll they named him, . . . . . . . .
lines: A son bore Edda, with water they sprinkled him,
With a cloth his hair so black they covered;
Thræll they named him, . . . . . . . .

items.text: The skin was wrinkled and rough on his hands, Knotted his knuckles, . . . . . . . . Thick his fingers, and ugly his face, Twisted his back, and big his heels.
lines: The skin was wrinkled and rough on his hands,
Knotted his knuckles, . . . . . . . .
Thick his fingers, and ugly his face,
Twisted his back, and big his heels.

items.text: He began to grow, and to gain in strength, Soon of his might good use he made; With bast he bound, and burdens carried, Home bore faggots the whole day long.
lines: He began to grow, and to gain in strength,
Soon of his might good use he made;
With bast he bound, and burdens carried,
Home bore faggots the whole day long.

items.text: One came to their home, crooked her legs, Stained were her feet, and sunburned her arms, Flat was her nose; her name was Thir.
lines: One came to their home, crooked her legs,
Stained were her feet, and sunburned her arms,
Flat was her nose; her name was Thir.

items.text: Soon in the midst of the room she sat, By her side there sat the son of the house; They whispered both, and the bed made ready, Thræll and Thir, till the day was through.
lines: Soon in the midst of the room she sat,
By her side there sat the son of the house;
They whispered both, and the bed made ready,
Thræll and Thir, till the day was through.

items.text: Children they had, they lived and were happy, Fjosnir and Klur they were called, methinks, Hreim and Kleggi, Kefsir, Fulnir, Drumb, Digraldi, Drott and Leggjaldi, Lut and Hosvir; the house they cared for, Ground they dunged, and swine they guarded, Goats they tended, and turf they dug.
lines: Children they had, they lived and were happy,
Fjosnir and Klur they were called, methinks,
Hreim and Kleggi, Kefsir, Fulnir,
Drumb, Digraldi, Drott and Leggjaldi,
Lut and Hosvir; the house they cared for,
Ground they dunged, and swine they guarded,
Goats they tended, and turf they dug.

items.text: Daughters had they, Drumba and Kumba, Ökkvinkalfa, Arinnefja, Ysja and Ambott, Eikintjasna, Totrughypja and Tronubeina; And thence has risen the race of thralls.
lines: Daughters had they, Drumba and Kumba,
Ökkvinkalfa, Arinnefja,
Ysja and Ambott, Eikintjasna,
Totrughypja and Tronubeina;
And thence has risen the race of thralls.

items.text: Forward went Rig, his road was straight, To a hall he came, and a door there hung; In did he fare, on the floor was a fire: Afi and Amma owned the house.
lines: Forward went Rig, his road was straight,
To a hall he came, and a door there hung;
In did he fare, on the floor was a fire:
Afi and Amma owned the house.

items.text: There sat the twain, and worked at their tasks: The man hewed wood for the weaver’s beam; His beard was trimmed, o’er his brow a curl, His clothes fitted close; in the corner a chest.
lines: There sat the twain, and worked at their tasks:
The man hewed wood for the weaver’s beam;
His beard was trimmed, o’er his brow a curl,
His clothes fitted close; in the corner a chest.

items.text: The woman sat and the distaff wielded, At the weaving with arms outstretched she worked; On her head was a band, on her breast a smock; On her shoulders a kerchief with clasps there was.
lines: The woman sat and the distaff wielded,
At the weaving with arms outstretched she worked;
On her head was a band, on her breast a smock;
On her shoulders a kerchief with clasps there was.

items.text: Rig knew well wise words to speak, Soon in the midst of the room he sat, And on either side the others were.
lines: Rig knew well wise words to speak,
Soon in the midst of the room he sat,
And on either side the others were.

items.text: Then took Amma . . . . . . . . The vessels full with the fare she set, Calf’s flesh boiled was the best of the dainties.
lines: Then took Amma . . . . . . . .
The vessels full with the fare she set,
Calf’s flesh boiled was the best of the dainties.

items.text: Rig knew well wise words to speak, He rose from the board, made ready to sleep; Soon in the bed himself did he lay, And on either side the others were.
lines: Rig knew well wise words to speak,
He rose from the board, made ready to sleep;
Soon in the bed himself did he lay,
And on either side the others were.

items.text: Thus was he there for three nights long, Then forward he went on the midmost way, And so nine months were soon passed by.
lines: Thus was he there for three nights long,
Then forward he went on the midmost way,
And so nine months were soon passed by.

items.text: A son bore Amma, with water they sprinkled him, Karl they named him; in a cloth she wrapped him, He was ruddy of face, and flashing his eyes.
lines: A son bore Amma, with water they sprinkled him,
Karl they named him; in a cloth she wrapped him,
He was ruddy of face, and flashing his eyes.

items.text: He began to grow, and to gain in strength, Oxen he ruled, and plows made ready, Houses he built, and barns he fashioned, Carts he made, and the plow he managed.
lines: He began to grow, and to gain in strength,
Oxen he ruled, and plows made ready,
Houses he built, and barns he fashioned,
Carts he made, and the plow he managed.

items.text: Home did they bring the bride for Karl, In goatskins clad, and keys she bore; Snör was her name, ’neath the veil she sat; A home they made ready, and rings exchanged, The bed they decked, and a dwelling made.
lines: Home did they bring the bride for Karl,
In goatskins clad, and keys she bore;
Snör was her name, ’neath the veil she sat;
A home they made ready, and rings exchanged,
The bed they decked, and a dwelling made.

items.text: Sons they had, they lived and were happy: Hal and Dreng, Holth, Thegn and Smith, Breith and Bondi, Bundinskeggi, Bui and Boddi, Brattskegg and Segg.
lines: Sons they had, they lived and were happy:
Hal and Dreng, Holth, Thegn and Smith,
Breith and Bondi, Bundinskeggi,
Bui and Boddi, Brattskegg and Segg.

items.text: Daughters they had, and their names are here: Snot, Bruth, Svanni, Svarri, Sprakki, Fljoth, Sprund and Vif, Feima, Ristil: And thence has risen the yeomen’s race.
lines: Daughters they had, and their names are here:
Snot, Bruth, Svanni, Svarri, Sprakki,
Fljoth, Sprund and Vif, Feima, Ristil:
And thence has risen the yeomen’s race.

items.text: Thence went Rig, his road was straight, A hall he saw, the doors faced south; The portal stood wide, on the posts was a ring, Then in he fared; the floor was strewn.
lines: Thence went Rig, his road was straight,
A hall he saw, the doors faced south;
The portal stood wide, on the posts was a ring,
Then in he fared; the floor was strewn.

items.text: Within two gazed in each other’s eyes, Fathir and Mothir, and played with their fingers; There sat the house-lord, wound strings for the bow, Shafts he fashioned, and bows he shaped.
lines: Within two gazed in each other’s eyes,
Fathir and Mothir, and played with their fingers;
There sat the house-lord, wound strings for the bow,
Shafts he fashioned, and bows he shaped.

items.text: The lady sat, at her arms she looked, She smoothed the cloth, and fitted the sleeves; Gay was her cap, on her breast were clasps, Broad was her train, of blue was her gown, Her brows were bright, her breast was shining, Whiter her neck than new-fallen snow.
lines: The lady sat, at her arms she looked,
She smoothed the cloth, and fitted the sleeves;
Gay was her cap, on her breast were clasps,
Broad was her train, of blue was her gown,
Her brows were bright, her breast was shining,
Whiter her neck than new-fallen snow.

items.text: Rig knew well wise words to speak, Soon in the midst of the room he sat, And on either side the others were.
lines: Rig knew well wise words to speak,
Soon in the midst of the room he sat,
And on either side the others were.

items.text: Then Mothir brought a broidered cloth, Of linen bright, and the board she covered; And then she took the loaves so thin, And laid them, white from the wheat, on the cloth.
lines: Then Mothir brought a broidered cloth,
Of linen bright, and the board she covered;
And then she took the loaves so thin,
And laid them, white from the wheat, on the cloth.

items.text: Then forth she brought the vessels full, With silver covered, and set before them, Meat all browned, and well-cooked birds; In the pitcher was wine, of plate were the cups, So drank they and talked till the day was gone.
lines: Then forth she brought the vessels full,
With silver covered, and set before them,
Meat all browned, and well-cooked birds;
In the pitcher was wine, of plate were the cups,
So drank they and talked till the day was gone.

items.text: Rig knew well wise words to speak, Soon did he rise, made ready to sleep; So in the bed himself did he lay, And on either side the others were.
lines: Rig knew well wise words to speak,
Soon did he rise, made ready to sleep;
So in the bed himself did he lay,
And on either side the others were.

items.text: Thus was he there for three nights long, Then forward he went on the midmost way, And so nine months were soon passed by.
lines: Thus was he there for three nights long,
Then forward he went on the midmost way,
And so nine months were soon passed by.

items.text: A son had Mothir, in silk they wrapped him, With water they sprinkled him, Jarl he was; Blond was his hair, and bright his cheeks, Grim as a snake’s were his glowing eyes.
lines: A son had Mothir, in silk they wrapped him,
With water they sprinkled him, Jarl he was;
Blond was his hair, and bright his cheeks,
Grim as a snake’s were his glowing eyes.

items.text: To grow in the house did Jarl begin, Shields he brandished, and bow-strings wound, Bows he shot, and shafts he fashioned, Arrows he loosened, and lances wielded, Horses he rode, and hounds unleashed, Swords he handled, and sounds he swam.
lines: To grow in the house did Jarl begin,
Shields he brandished, and bow-strings wound,
Bows he shot, and shafts he fashioned,
Arrows he loosened, and lances wielded,
Horses he rode, and hounds unleashed,
Swords he handled, and sounds he swam.

items.text: Straight from the grove came striding Rig, Rig came striding, and runes he taught him; By his name he called him, as son he claimed him, And bade him hold his heritage wide, His heritage wide, the ancient homes.
lines: Straight from the grove came striding Rig,
Rig came striding, and runes he taught him;
By his name he called him, as son he claimed him,
And bade him hold his heritage wide,
His heritage wide, the ancient homes.

items.text: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Forward he rode through the forest dark, O’er the frosty crags, till a hall he found.
lines: Forward he rode through the forest dark,
O’er the frosty crags, till a hall he found.

items.text: His spear he shook, his shield he brandished, His horse he spurred, with his sword he hewed; Wars he raised, and reddened the field, Warriors slew he, and land he won.
lines: His spear he shook, his shield he brandished,
His horse he spurred, with his sword he hewed;
Wars he raised, and reddened the field,
Warriors slew he, and land he won.

items.text: Eighteen halls ere long did he hold, Wealth did he get, and gave to all, Stones and jewels and slim-flanked steeds, Rings he offered, and arm-rings shared.
lines: Eighteen halls ere long did he hold,
Wealth did he get, and gave to all,
Stones and jewels and slim-flanked steeds,
Rings he offered, and arm-rings shared.

items.text: His messengers went by the ways so wet, And came to the hall where Hersir dwelt; His daughter was fair and slender-fingered, Erna the wise the maiden was.
lines: His messengers went by the ways so wet,
And came to the hall where Hersir dwelt;
His daughter was fair and slender-fingered,
Erna the wise the maiden was.

items.text: Her hand they sought, and home they brought her, Wedded to Jarl the veil she wore; Together they dwelt, their joy was great, Children they had, and happy they lived.
lines: Her hand they sought, and home they brought her,
Wedded to Jarl the veil she wore;
Together they dwelt, their joy was great,
Children they had, and happy they lived.

items.text: Bur was the eldest, and Barn the next, Joth and Athal, Arfi, Mog, Nith and Svein, soon they began— Sun and Nithjung— to play and swim; Kund was one, and the youngest Kon.
lines: Bur was the eldest, and Barn the next,
Joth and Athal, Arfi, Mog,
Nith and Svein, soon they began—
Sun and Nithjung— to play and swim;
Kund was one, and the youngest Kon.

items.text: Soon grew up the sons of Jarl, Beasts they tamed, and bucklers rounded, Shafts they fashioned, and spears they shook.
lines: Soon grew up the sons of Jarl,
Beasts they tamed, and bucklers rounded,
Shafts they fashioned, and spears they shook.

items.text: But Kon the Young learned runes to use, Runes everlasting, the runes of life; Soon could he well the warriors shield, Dull the swordblade, and still the seas.
lines: But Kon the Young learned runes to use,
Runes everlasting, the runes of life;
Soon could he well the warriors shield,
Dull the swordblade, and still the seas.

items.text: Bird-chatter learned he, flames could he lessen, Minds could quiet, and sorrows calm; . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . The might and strength of twice four men.
lines: Bird-chatter learned he, flames could he lessen,
Minds could quiet, and sorrows calm;
The might and strength of twice four men.

items.text: With Rig-Jarl soon the runes he shared, More crafty he was, and greater his wisdom; The right he sought, and soon he won it, Rig to be called, and runes to know.
lines: With Rig-Jarl soon the runes he shared,
More crafty he was, and greater his wisdom;
The right he sought, and soon he won it,
Rig to be called, and runes to know.

items.text: Young Kon rode forth through forest and grove, Shafts let loose, and birds he lured; There spake a crow on a bough that sat: “Why lurest thou, Kon, the birds to come?
lines: Young Kon rode forth through forest and grove,
Shafts let loose, and birds he lured;
There spake a crow on a bough that sat:
“Why lurest thou, Kon, the birds to come?

items.text: “’Twere better forth on thy steed to fare, . . . . . . . . and the host to slay.
lines: “’Twere better forth on thy steed to fare,
. . . . . . . . and the host to slay.

items.text: “The halls of Dan and Danp are noble, Greater their wealth than thou hast gained; Good are they at guiding the keel, Trying of weapons, and giving of wounds.”
lines: “The halls of Dan and Danp are noble,
Greater their wealth than thou hast gained;
Good are they at guiding the keel,
Trying of weapons, and giving of wounds.”

items.text: Freyja spake:
“Maiden, awake! wake thee, my friend, My sister Hyndla, in thy hollow cave! Already comes darkness, and ride must we To Valhall to seek the sacred hall.
lines: “Maiden, awake! wake thee, my friend,
My sister Hyndla, in thy hollow cave!
Already comes darkness, and ride must we
To Valhall to seek the sacred hall.

items.text: “The favor of Heerfather seek we to find, To his followers gold he gladly gives; To Hermoth gave he helm and mail-coat, And to Sigmund he gave a sword as gift.
lines: “The favor of Heerfather seek we to find,
To his followers gold he gladly gives;
To Hermoth gave he helm and mail-coat,
And to Sigmund he gave a sword as gift.

items.text: “Triumph to some, and treasure to others, To many wisdom and skill in words, Fair winds to the sailor, to the singer his art, And a manly heart to many a hero.
lines: “Triumph to some, and treasure to others,
To many wisdom and skill in words,
Fair winds to the sailor, to the singer his art,
And a manly heart to many a hero.

items.text: “Thor shall I honor, and this shall I ask, That his favor true mayst thou ever find; . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Though little the brides of the giants he loves.
lines: “Thor shall I honor, and this shall I ask,
That his favor true mayst thou ever find;
Though little the brides of the giants he loves.

items.text: “From the stall now one of thy wolves lead forth, And along with my boar shalt thou let him run; For slow my boar goes on the road of the gods, And I would not weary my worthy steed.”
lines: “From the stall now one of thy wolves lead forth,
And along with my boar shalt thou let him run;
For slow my boar goes on the road of the gods,
And I would not weary my worthy steed.”

items.text: Hyndla spake:
“Falsely thou askest me, Freyja, to go, For so in the glance of thine eyes I see; On the way of the slain thy lover goes with thee, Ottar the young, the son of Instein.”
lines: “Falsely thou askest me, Freyja, to go,
For so in the glance of thine eyes I see;
On the way of the slain thy lover goes with thee,
Ottar the young, the son of Instein.”

items.text: Freyja spake:

“Wild dreams, methinks, are thine when thou sayest My lover is with me on the way of the slain; There shines the boar with bristles of gold, Hildisvini, he who was made By Dain and Nabbi, the cunning dwarfs.
lines: “Wild dreams, methinks, are thine when thou
sayest
My lover is with me on the way of the slain;
There shines the boar with bristles of gold,
Hildisvini, he who was made
By Dain and Nabbi, the cunning dwarfs.

items.text: “Now let us down from our saddles leap, And talk of the race of the heroes twain; The men who were born of the gods above, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: “Now let us down from our saddles leap,
And talk of the race of the heroes twain;
The men who were born of the gods above,

items.text: “A wager have made in the foreign metal Ottar the young and Angantyr; We must guard, for the hero young to have, His father’s wealth, the fruits of his race.
lines: “A wager have made in the foreign metal
Ottar the young and Angantyr;
We must guard, for the hero young to have,
His father’s wealth, the fruits of his race.

items.text: “For me a shrine of stones he made,— And now to glass the rock has grown;— Oft with the blood of beasts was it red; In the goddesses ever did Ottar trust.
lines: “For me a shrine of stones he made,—
And now to glass the rock has grown;—
Oft with the blood of beasts was it red;
In the goddesses ever did Ottar trust.

items.text: “Tell to me now the ancient names, And the races of all that were born of old: Who are of the Skjoldungs, who of the Skilfings, Who of the Othlings, who of the Ylfings, Who are the free-born, who are the high-born, The noblest of men that in Mithgarth dwell?”
lines: “Tell to me now the ancient names,
And the races of all that were born of old:
Who are of the Skjoldungs, who of the Skilfings,
Who of the Othlings, who of the Ylfings,
Who are the free-born, who are the high-born,
The noblest of men that in Mithgarth dwell?”

items.text: Hyndla spake:
“Thou art, Ottar, the son of Instein, And Instein the son of Alf the Old, Alf of Ulf, Ulf of Sæfari, And Sæfari’s father was Svan the Red.
lines: “Thou art, Ottar, the son of Instein,
And Instein the son of Alf the Old,
Alf of Ulf, Ulf of Sæfari,
And Sæfari’s father was Svan the Red.

items.text: “Thy mother, bright with bracelets fair, Hight, methinks, the priestess Hledis; Frothi her father, and Friaut her mother;— Her race of the mightiest men must seem.
lines: “Thy mother, bright with bracelets fair,
Hight, methinks, the priestess Hledis;
Frothi her father, and Friaut her mother;—
Her race of the mightiest men must seem.

items.text: “Of old the noblest of all was Ali, Before him Halfdan, foremost of Skjoldungs; Famed were the battles the hero fought, To the corners of heaven his deeds were carried.
lines: “Of old the noblest of all was Ali,
Before him Halfdan, foremost of Skjoldungs;
Famed were the battles the hero fought,
To the corners of heaven his deeds were carried.

items.text: “Strengthened by Eymund, the strongest of men, Sigtrygg he slew with the ice-cold sword; His bride was Almveig, the best of women, And eighteen boys did Almveig bear him.
lines: “Strengthened by Eymund, the strongest of men,
Sigtrygg he slew with the ice-cold sword;
His bride was Almveig, the best of women,
And eighteen boys did Almveig bear him.

items.text: “Hence come the Skjoldungs, hence the Skilfings, Hence the Othlings, hence the Ynglings, Hence come the free-born, hence the high-born, The noblest of men that in Mithgarth dwell: And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!
lines: “Hence come the Skjoldungs, hence the Skilfings,
Hence the Othlings, hence the Ynglings,
Hence come the free-born, hence the high-born,
The noblest of men that in Mithgarth dwell:
And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!

items.text: “Hildigun then her mother hight, The daughter of Svava and Sækonung; And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool! It is much to know,— wilt thou hear yet more?
lines: “Hildigun then her mother hight,
The daughter of Svava and Sækonung;
And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!
It is much to know,— wilt thou hear yet more?

items.text: “The mate of Dag was a mother of heroes, Thora, who bore him the bravest of fighters, Frathmar and Gyrth and the Frekis twain, Am and Jofurmar, Alf the Old; It is much to know,— wilt thou hear yet more?
lines: “The mate of Dag was a mother of heroes,
Thora, who bore him the bravest of fighters,
Frathmar and Gyrth and the Frekis twain,
Am and Jofurmar, Alf the Old;
It is much to know,— wilt thou hear yet more?

items.text: “Her husband was Ketil, the heir of Klypp, He was of thy mother the mother’s-father; Before the days of Kari was Frothi, And born of Hild was Hoalf then.
lines: “Her husband was Ketil, the heir of Klypp,
He was of thy mother the mother’s-father;
Before the days of Kari was Frothi,
And born of Hild was Hoalf then.

items.text: “Next was Nanna, daughter of Nokkvi, Thy father’s kinsman her son became; Old is the line, and longer still, And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!
lines: “Next was Nanna, daughter of Nokkvi,
Thy father’s kinsman her son became;
Old is the line, and longer still,
And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!

items.text: “Isolf and Osolf, the sons of Olmoth, Whose wife was Skurhild, the daughter of Skekkil, Count them among the heroes mighty, And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!
lines: “Isolf and Osolf, the sons of Olmoth,
Whose wife was Skurhild, the daughter of Skekkil,
Count them among the heroes mighty,
And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!

items.text: “Gunnar the Bulwark, Grim the Hardy, Thorir the Iron-shield, Ulf the Gaper, Brodd and Hörvir both did I know; In the household they were of Hrolf the Old.
lines: “Gunnar the Bulwark, Grim the Hardy,
Thorir the Iron-shield, Ulf the Gaper,
Brodd and Hörvir both did I know;
In the household they were of Hrolf the Old.
