items.text: “Hervarth, Hjorvarth, Hrani, Angantyr, Bui and Brami, Barri and Reifnir, Tind and Tyrfing, the Haddings twain,— And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!
lines: “Hervarth, Hjorvarth, Hrani, Angantyr,
Bui and Brami, Barri and Reifnir,
Tind and Tyrfing, the Haddings twain,—
And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!

items.text: “Eastward in Bolm were born of old The sons of Arngrim and Eyfura; With berserk-tumult and baleful deed Like fire o’er land and sea they fared,— And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!
lines: “Eastward in Bolm were born of old
The sons of Arngrim and Eyfura;
With berserk-tumult and baleful deed
Like fire o’er land and sea they fared,—
And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!

items.text: “The sons of Jormunrek all of yore To the gods in death were as offerings given; He was kinsman of Sigurth,— hear well what I say,— The foe of hosts, and Fafnir’s slayer.
lines: “The sons of Jormunrek all of yore
To the gods in death were as offerings given;
He was kinsman of Sigurth,— hear well what I say,—
The foe of hosts, and Fafnir’s slayer.

items.text: “From Volsung’s seed was the hero sprung, And Hjordis was born of Hrauthung’s race, And Eylimi from the Othlings came,— And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!
lines: “From Volsung’s seed was the hero sprung,
And Hjordis was born of Hrauthung’s race,
And Eylimi from the Othlings came,—
And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!

items.text: “Gunnar and Hogni, the heirs of Gjuki, And Guthrun as well, who their sister was; But Gotthorm was not of Gjuki’s race, Although the brother of both he was: And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!
lines: “Gunnar and Hogni, the heirs of Gjuki,
And Guthrun as well, who their sister was;
But Gotthorm was not of Gjuki’s race,
Although the brother of both he was:
And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!

items.text: “Of Hvethna’s sons was Haki the best, And Hjorvarth the father of Hvethna was; . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: “Of Hvethna’s sons was Haki the best,
And Hjorvarth the father of Hvethna was;

items.text: “Harald Battle-tooth of Auth was born, Hrörek the Ring-giver her husband was; Auth the Deep-minded was Ivar’s daughter, But Rathbarth the father of Randver was: And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!”
lines: “Harald Battle-tooth of Auth was born,
Hrörek the Ring-giver her husband was;
Auth the Deep-minded was Ivar’s daughter,
But Rathbarth the father of Randver was:
And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!”

items.text: FRAGMENT OF “THE SHORT VOLUSPO”
Eleven in number the gods were known, When Baldr o’er the hill of death was bowed; And this to avenge was Vali swift, When his brother’s slayer soon he slew.
lines: Eleven in number the gods were known,
When Baldr o’er the hill of death was bowed;
And this to avenge was Vali swift,
When his brother’s slayer soon he slew.

items.text: The father of Baldr was the heir of Bur, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: The father of Baldr was the heir of Bur,

items.text: Freyr’s wife was Gerth, the daughter of Gymir, Of the giants’ brood, and Aurbotha bore her; To these as well was Thjazi kin, The dark-loving giant; his daughter was Skathi.
lines: Freyr’s wife was Gerth, the daughter of Gymir,
Of the giants’ brood, and Aurbotha bore her;
To these as well was Thjazi kin,
The dark-loving giant; his daughter was Skathi.

items.text: Much have I told thee, and further will tell; There is much that I know;— wilt thou hear yet more?
lines: Much have I told thee, and further will tell;
There is much that I know;— wilt thou hear
yet more?

items.text: Heith and Hrossthjof, the children of Hrimnir. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: Heith and Hrossthjof, the children of Hrimnir.

items.text: The sybils arose from Vitholf’s race, From Vilmeith all the seers are, And the workers of charms are Svarthofthi’s children, And from Ymir sprang the giants all.
lines: The sybils arose from Vitholf’s race,
From Vilmeith all the seers are,
And the workers of charms are Svarthofthi’s children,
And from Ymir sprang the giants all.

items.text: Much have I told thee, and further will tell; There is much that I know;— wilt thou hear yet more?
lines: Much have I told thee, and further will tell;
There is much that I know;— wilt thou hear yet more?

items.text: One there was born in the bygone days, Of the race of the gods, and great was his might; Nine giant women, at the world’s edge, Once bore the man so mighty in arms.
lines: One there was born in the bygone days,
Of the race of the gods, and great was his might;
Nine giant women, at the world’s edge,
Once bore the man so mighty in arms.

items.text: Gjolp there bore him, Greip there bore him, Eistla bore him, and Eyrgjafa, Ulfrun bore him, and Angeyja, Imth and Atla, and Jarnsaxa.
lines: Gjolp there bore him, Greip there bore him,
Eistla bore him, and Eyrgjafa,
Ulfrun bore him, and Angeyja,
Imth and Atla, and Jarnsaxa.

items.text: Strong was he made with the strength of earth, With the ice-cold sea, and the blood of swine.
lines: Strong was he made with the strength of earth,
With the ice-cold sea, and the blood of swine.

items.text: One there was born, the best of all, And strong was he made with the strength of earth; The proudest is called the kinsman of men Of the rulers all throughout the world.
lines: One there was born, the best of all,
And strong was he made with the strength of earth;
The proudest is called the kinsman of men
Of the rulers all throughout the world.

items.text: Much have I told thee, and further will tell; There is much that I know;— wilt thou hear yet more?
lines: Much have I told thee, and further will tell;
There is much that I know;— wilt thou hear yet more?

items.text: The wolf did Loki with Angrbotha win, And Sleipnir bore he to Svathilfari; The worst of marvels seemed the one That sprang from the brother of Byleist then.
lines: The wolf did Loki with Angrbotha win,
And Sleipnir bore he to Svathilfari;
The worst of marvels seemed the one
That sprang from the brother of Byleist then.

items.text: A heart ate Loki,— in the embers it lay, And half-cooked found he the woman’s heart;— With child from the woman Lopt soon was, And thence among men came the monsters all.
lines: A heart ate Loki,— in the embers it lay,
And half-cooked found he the woman’s heart;—
With child from the woman Lopt soon was,
And thence among men came the monsters all.

items.text: The sea, storm-driven, seeks heaven itself, O’er the earth it flows, the air grows sterile; Then follow the snows and the furious winds, For the gods are doomed, and the end is death.
lines: The sea, storm-driven, seeks heaven itself,
O’er the earth it flows, the air grows sterile;
Then follow the snows and the furious winds,
For the gods are doomed, and the end is death.

items.text: Then comes another, a greater than all, Though never I dare his name to speak; Few are they now that farther can see Than the moment when Othin shall meet the wolf.
lines: Then comes another, a greater than all,
Though never I dare his name to speak;
Few are they now that farther can see
Than the moment when Othin shall meet the wolf.

items.text: Freyja spake:
“To my boar now bring the memory-beer, So that all thy words, that well thou hast spoken, The third morn hence he may hold in mind, When their races Ottar and Angantyr tell.”
lines: “To my boar now bring the memory-beer,
So that all thy words, that well thou hast spoken,
The third morn hence he may hold in mind,
When their races Ottar and Angantyr tell.”

items.text: Hyndla spake:
“Hence shalt thou fare, for fain would I sleep, From me thou gettest few favors good; My noble one, out in the night thou leapest As Heithrun goes the goats among.
lines: “Hence shalt thou fare, for fain would I sleep,
From me thou gettest few favors good;
My noble one, out in the night thou leapest
As Heithrun goes the goats among.

items.text: “To Oth didst thou run, who loved thee ever, And many under thy apron have crawled; My noble one, out in the night thou leapest, As Heithrun goes the goats among.”
lines: “To Oth didst thou run, who loved thee ever,
And many under thy apron have crawled;
My noble one, out in the night thou leapest,
As Heithrun goes the goats among.”

items.text: Freyja spake:
“Around the giantess flames shall I raise, So that forth unburned thou mayst not fare.”
lines: “Around the giantess flames shall I raise,
So that forth unburned thou mayst not fare.”

items.text: Hyndla spake:
“Flames I see burning, the earth is on fire, And each for his life the price must lose; Bring then to Ottar the draught of beer, Of venom full for an evil fate.”
lines: “Flames I see burning, the earth is on fire,
And each for his life the price must lose;
Bring then to Ottar the draught of beer,
Of venom full for an evil fate.”

items.text: Freyja spake:
“Thine evil words shall work no ill, Though, giantess, bitter thy baleful threats; A drink full fair shall Ottar find, If of all the gods the favor I get.”
lines: “Thine evil words shall work no ill,
Though, giantess, bitter thy baleful threats;
A drink full fair shall Ottar find,
If of all the gods the favor I get.”

items.text: I. GROUGALDR
GROA’S SPELL
Svipdag spake:
“Wake thee, Groa! wake, mother good! At the doors of the dead I call thee; Thy son, bethink thee, thou badst to seek Thy help at the hill of death.”
lines: “Wake thee, Groa! wake, mother good!
At the doors of the dead I call thee;
Thy son, bethink thee, thou badst to seek
Thy help at the hill of death.”

items.text: Groa spake:
“What evil vexes mine only son, What baleful fate hast thou found, That thou callest thy mother, who lies in the mould, And the world of the living has left?”
lines: “What evil vexes mine only son,
What baleful fate hast thou found,
That thou callest thy mother, who lies in the mould,
And the world of the living has left?”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“The woman false whom my father embraced Has brought me a baleful game; For she bade me go forth where none may fare, And Mengloth the maid to seek.”
lines: “The woman false whom my father embraced
Has brought me a baleful game;
For she bade me go forth where none may fare,
And Mengloth the maid to seek.”

items.text: Groa spake:
“Long is the way, long must thou wander, But long is love as well; Thou mayst find, perchance, what thou fain wouldst have, If the fates their favor will give.”
lines: “Long is the way, long must thou wander,
But long is love as well;
Thou mayst find, perchance, what thou fain wouldst have,
If the fates their favor will give.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Charms full good then chant to me, mother, And seek thy son to guard; For death do I fear on the way I shall fare, And in years am I young, methinks.”
lines: “Charms full good then chant to me, mother,
And seek thy son to guard;
For death do I fear on the way I shall fare,
And in years am I young, methinks.”

items.text: Groa spake:
“Then first I will chant thee the charm oft-tried, That Rani taught to Rind; From the shoulder whate’er mislikes thee shake, For helper thyself shalt thou have.
lines: “Then first I will chant thee the charm oft-tried,
That Rani taught to Rind;
From the shoulder whate’er mislikes thee shake,
For helper thyself shalt thou have.

items.text: “Then next I will chant thee, if needs thou must travel, And wander a purposeless way: The bolts of Urth shall on every side Be thy guards on the road thou goest.
lines: “Then next I will chant thee, if needs thou must travel,
And wander a purposeless way:
The bolts of Urth shall on every side
Be thy guards on the road thou goest.

items.text: “Then third I will chant thee, if threatening streams The danger of death shall bring: Yet to Hel shall turn both Horn and Ruth, And before thee the waters shall fail.
lines: “Then third I will chant thee, if threatening streams
The danger of death shall bring:
Yet to Hel shall turn both Horn and Ruth,
And before thee the waters shall fail.

items.text: “Then fourth I will chant thee, if come thy foes On the gallows-way against thee: Into thine hands shall their hearts be given, And peace shall the warriors wish.
lines: “Then fourth I will chant thee, if come thy foes
On the gallows-way against thee:
Into thine hands shall their hearts be given,
And peace shall the warriors wish.

items.text: “Then fifth I will chant thee, if fetters perchance Shall bind thy bending limbs: O’er thy thighs do I chant a loosening-charm, And the lock is burst from the limbs, And the fetters fall from the feet.
lines: “Then fifth I will chant thee, if fetters perchance
Shall bind thy bending limbs:
O’er thy thighs do I chant a loosening-charm,
And the lock is burst from the limbs,
And the fetters fall from the feet.

items.text: “Then sixth I will chant thee, if storms on the sea Have might unknown to man: Yet never shall wind or wave do harm, And calm is the course of thy boat.
lines: “Then sixth I will chant thee, if storms on the sea
Have might unknown to man:
Yet never shall wind or wave do harm,
And calm is the course of thy boat.

items.text: “Then seventh I chant thee, if frost shall seek To kill thee on lofty crags: The fatal cold shall not grip thy flesh, And whole thy body shall be.
lines: “Then seventh I chant thee, if frost shall seek
To kill thee on lofty crags:
The fatal cold shall not grip thy flesh,
And whole thy body shall be.

items.text: “Then eighth will I chant thee, if ever by night Thou shalt wander on murky ways: Yet never the curse of a Christian woman From the dead shall do thee harm.
lines: “Then eighth will I chant thee, if ever by night
Thou shalt wander on murky ways:
Yet never the curse of a Christian woman
From the dead shall do thee harm.

items.text: “Then ninth will I chant thee, if needs thou must strive With a warlike giant in words: Thy heart good store of wit shall have, And thy mouth of words full wise.
lines: “Then ninth will I chant thee, if needs thou must strive
With a warlike giant in words:
Thy heart good store of wit shall have,
And thy mouth of words full wise.

items.text: “Now fare on the way where danger waits, Let evils not lessen thy love! I have stood at the door of the earth-fixed stones, The while I chanted thee charms.
lines: “Now fare on the way where danger waits,
Let evils not lessen thy love!
I have stood at the door of the earth-fixed stones,
The while I chanted thee charms.

items.text: “Bear hence, my son, what thy mother hath said, And let it live in thy breast; Thine ever shall be the best of fortune, So long as my words shall last.”
lines: “Bear hence, my son, what thy mother hath said,
And let it live in thy breast;
Thine ever shall be the best of fortune,
So long as my words shall last.”

items.text: II. FJOLSVINNSMOL
THE LAY OF FJOLSVITH
Before the house he beheld one coming To the home of the giants high.
lines: Before the house he beheld one coming
To the home of the giants high.

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“What giant is here, in front of the house, And around him fires are flaming?”
lines: “What giant is here, in front of the house,
And around him fires are flaming?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“What seekest thou here? for what is thy search? What, friendless one, fain wouldst thou know? By the ways so wet must thou wander hence, For, weakling, no home hast thou here.”
lines: “What seekest thou here? for what is thy search?
What, friendless one, fain wouldst thou know?
By the ways so wet must thou wander hence,
For, weakling, no home hast thou here.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“What giant is here, in front of the house, To the wayfarer welcome denying?”
lines: “What giant is here, in front of the house,
To the wayfarer welcome denying?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Greeting full fair thou never shalt find, So hence shalt thou get thee home.
lines: “Greeting full fair thou never shalt find,
So hence shalt thou get thee home.

items.text: “Fjolsvith am I, and wise am I found, But miserly am I with meat; Thou never shalt enter within the house,— Go forth like a wolf on thy way!”
lines: “Fjolsvith am I, and wise am I found,
But miserly am I with meat;
Thou never shalt enter within the house,—
Go forth like a wolf on thy way!”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Few from the joy of their eyes will go forth, When the sight of their loves they seek; Full bright are the gates of the golden hall, And a home shall I here enjoy.”
lines: “Few from the joy of their eyes will go forth,
When the sight of their loves they seek;
Full bright are the gates of the golden hall,
And a home shall I here enjoy.”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Tell me now, fellow, what father thou hast, And the kindred of whom thou camst.”
lines: “Tell me now, fellow, what father thou hast,
And the kindred of whom thou camst.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Vindkald am I, and Varkald’s son, And Fjolkald his father was.
lines: “Vindkald am I, and Varkald’s son,
And Fjolkald his father was.

items.text: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: Who is it that holds and has for his own The rule of the hall so rich?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
Who is it that holds and has for his own
The rule of the hall so rich?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Mengloth is she, her mother bore her To the son of Svafrthorin; She is it that holds and has for her own The rule of the hall so rich.”
lines: “Mengloth is she, her mother bore her
To the son of Svafrthorin;
She is it that holds and has for her own
The rule of the hall so rich.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: What call they the gate? for among the gods Ne’er saw man so grim a sight.”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
What call they the gate? for among the gods
Ne’er saw man so grim a sight.”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Thrymgjol they call it; ’twas made by the three, The sons of Solblindi; And fast as a fetter the farer it holds, Whoever shall lift the latch.”
lines: “Thrymgjol they call it; ’twas made by the three,
The sons of Solblindi;
And fast as a fetter the farer it holds,
Whoever shall lift the latch.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: What call they the house? for no man beheld ‘Mongst the gods so grim a sight.”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
What call they the house? for no man beheld
‘Mongst the gods so grim a sight.”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Gastropnir is it, of old I made it From the limbs of Leirbrimir; I braced it so strongly that fast it shall stand So long as the world shall last.”
lines: “Gastropnir is it, of old I made it
From the limbs of Leirbrimir;
I braced it so strongly that fast it shall stand
So long as the world shall last.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: What call they the tree that casts abroad Its limbs o’er every land?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
What call they the tree that casts abroad
Its limbs o’er every land?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Mimameith its name, and no man knows What root beneath it runs; And few can guess what shall fell the tree, For fire nor iron shall fell it.”
lines: “Mimameith its name, and no man knows
What root beneath it runs;
And few can guess what shall fell the tree,
For fire nor iron shall fell it.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: What grows from the seed of the tree so great, That fire nor iron shall fell?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
What grows from the seed of the tree so great,
That fire nor iron shall fell?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Women, sick with child, shall seek Its fruit to the flames to bear; Then out shall come what within was hid, And so is it mighty with men.”
lines: “Women, sick with child, shall seek
Its fruit to the flames to bear;
Then out shall come what within was hid,
And so is it mighty with men.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: What cock is he on the highest bough, That glitters all with gold?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
What cock is he on the highest bough,
That glitters all with gold?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Vithofnir his name, and now he shines Like lightning on Mimameith’s limbs; And great is the trouble with which he grieves Both Surt and Sinmora.”
lines: “Vithofnir his name, and now he shines
Like lightning on Mimameith’s limbs;
And great is the trouble with which he grieves
Both Surt and Sinmora.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: What call they the hounds, that before the house So fierce and angry are?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
What call they the hounds, that before the house
So fierce and angry are?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Gif call they one, and Geri the other, If now the truth thou wouldst know; Great they are, and their might will grow, Till the gods to death are doomed.”
lines: “Gif call they one, and Geri the other,
If now the truth thou wouldst know;
Great they are, and their might will grow,
Till the gods to death are doomed.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: May no man hope the house to enter, While the hungry hounds are sleeping?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
May no man hope the house to enter,
While the hungry hounds are sleeping?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Together they sleep not, for so was it fixed When the guard to them was given; One sleeps by night, the next by day, So no man may enter ever.”
lines: “Together they sleep not, for so was it fixed
When the guard to them was given;
One sleeps by night, the next by day,
So no man may enter ever.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: Is there no meat that men may give them, And leap within while they eat?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
Is there no meat that men may give them,
And leap within while they eat?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Two wing-joints there be in Vithofnir’s body, If now the truth thou wouldst know; That alone is the meat that men may give them, And leap within while they eat.”
lines: “Two wing-joints there be in Vithofnir’s body,
If now the truth thou wouldst know;
That alone is the meat that men may give them,
And leap within while they eat.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: What weapon can send Vithofnir to seek The house of Hel below?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
What weapon can send Vithofnir to seek
The house of Hel below?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Lævatein is there, that Lopt with runes Once made by the doors of death; In Lægjarn’s chest by Sinmora lies it, And nine locks fasten it firm.”
lines: “Lævatein is there, that Lopt with runes
Once made by the doors of death;
In Lægjarn’s chest by Sinmora lies it,
And nine locks fasten it firm.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: May a man come thence who thither goes, And tries the sword to take?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
May a man come thence who thither goes,
And tries the sword to take?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Thence may he come who thither goes, And tries the sword to take, If with him he carries what few can win, To give to the goddess of gold.”
lines: “Thence may he come who thither goes,
And tries the sword to take,
If with him he carries what few can win,
To give to the goddess of gold.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: What treasure is there that men may take To rejoice the giantess pale?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
What treasure is there that men may take
To rejoice the giantess pale?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“The sickle bright in thy wallet bear, Mid Vithofnir’s feathers found; To Sinmora give it, and then shall she grant That the weapon by thee be won.”
lines: “The sickle bright in thy wallet bear,
Mid Vithofnir’s feathers found;
To Sinmora give it, and then shall she grant
That the weapon by thee be won.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: What call they the hall, encompassed here With flickering magic flames?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
What call they the hall, encompassed here
With flickering magic flames?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Lyr is it called, and long it shall On the tip of a spear-point tremble; Of the noble house mankind has heard, But more has it never known.”
lines: “Lyr is it called, and long it shall
On the tip of a spear-point tremble;
Of the noble house mankind has heard,
But more has it never known.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: What one of the gods has made so great The hall I behold within?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
What one of the gods has made so great
The hall I behold within?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Uni and Iri, Bari and Jari, Var and Vegdrasil, Dori and Ori, Delling, and there Was Loki, the fear of the folk.”
lines: “Uni and Iri, Bari and Jari,
Var and Vegdrasil,
Dori and Ori, Delling, and there
Was Loki, the fear of the folk.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: What call they the mountain on which the maid Is lying so lovely to see?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
What call they the mountain on which the maid
Is lying so lovely to see?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Lyfjaberg is it, and long shall it be A joy to the sick and the sore; For well shall grow each woman who climbs it, Though sick full long she has lain.”
lines: “Lyfjaberg is it, and long shall it be
A joy to the sick and the sore;
For well shall grow each woman who climbs it,
Though sick full long she has lain.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: What maidens are they that at Mengloth’s knees Are sitting so gladly together?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
What maidens are they that at Mengloth’s knees
Are sitting so gladly together?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Hlif is one named, Hlifthrasa another, Thjothvara call they the third; Bjort and Bleik, Blith and Frith, Eir and Aurbotha.”
lines: “Hlif is one named, Hlifthrasa another,
Thjothvara call they the third;
Bjort and Bleik, Blith and Frith,
Eir and Aurbotha.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: Aid bring they to all who offerings give, If need be found therefor?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
Aid bring they to all who offerings give,
If need be found therefor?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Soon aid they all who offerings give On the holy altars high; And if danger they see for the sons of men, Then each from ill do they guard.”
lines: “Soon aid they all who offerings give
On the holy altars high;
And if danger they see for the sons of men,
Then each from ill do they guard.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask, For now the truth would I know: Lives there the man who in Mengloth’s arms So fair may seek to sleep?”
lines: “Now answer me, Fjolsvith, the question I ask,
For now the truth would I know:
Lives there the man who in Mengloth’s arms
So fair may seek to sleep?”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“No man there is who in Mengloth’s arms So fair may seek to sleep, Save Svipdag alone, for the sun-bright maid Is destined his bride to be.”
lines: “No man there is who in Mengloth’s arms
So fair may seek to sleep,
Save Svipdag alone, for the sun-bright maid
Is destined his bride to be.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Fling back the gates! make the gateway wide! Here mayst thou Svipdag see! Hence get thee to find if gladness soon Mengloth to me will give.”
lines: “Fling back the gates! make the gateway wide!
Here mayst thou Svipdag see!
Hence get thee to find if gladness soon
Mengloth to me will give.”

items.text: Fjolsvith spake:
“Hearken, Mengloth, a man is come; Go thou the guest to see! The hounds are fawning, the house bursts open,— Svipdag, methinks, is there.”
lines: “Hearken, Mengloth, a man is come;
Go thou the guest to see!
The hounds are fawning, the house bursts open,—
Svipdag, methinks, is there.”

items.text: Mengloth spake:
“On the gallows high shall hungry ravens Soon thine eyes pluck out, If thou liest in saying that here at last The hero is come to my hall.
lines: “On the gallows high shall hungry ravens
Soon thine eyes pluck out,
If thou liest in saying that here at last
The hero is come to my hall.

items.text: “Whence camest thou hither? how camest thou here? What name do thy kinsmen call thee? Thy race and thy name as a sign must I know, That thy bride I am destined to be.”
lines: “Whence camest thou hither? how camest thou here?
What name do thy kinsmen call thee?
Thy race and thy name as a sign must I know,
That thy bride I am destined to be.”

items.text: Svipdag spake:
“Svipdag am I, and Solbjart’s son; Thence came I by wind-cold ways; With the words of Urth shall no man war, Though unearned her gifts be given.”
lines: “Svipdag am I, and Solbjart’s son;
Thence came I by wind-cold ways;
With the words of Urth shall no man war,
Though unearned her gifts be given.”

items.text: Mengloth spake:
“Welcome thou art, for long have I waited; The welcoming kiss shalt thou win! For two who love is the longed-for meeting The greatest gladness of all.
lines: “Welcome thou art, for long have I waited;
The welcoming kiss shalt thou win!
For two who love is the longed-for meeting
The greatest gladness of all.

items.text: “Long have I sat on Lyfjaberg here, Awaiting thee day by day; And now I have what I ever hoped, For here thou art come to my hall.
lines: “Long have I sat on Lyfjaberg here,
Awaiting thee day by day;
And now I have what I ever hoped,
For here thou art come to my hall.

items.text: “Alike we yearned; I longed for thee, And thou for my love hast longed; But now henceforth together we know Our lives to the end we shall live.”
lines: “Alike we yearned; I longed for thee,
And thou for my love hast longed;
But now henceforth together we know
Our lives to the end we shall live.”

items.text: There was a king in Sweden named Nithuth. He had two sons and one daughter; her name was Bothvild. There were three brothers, sons of a king of the Finns: one was called Slagfith, another Egil, the third Völund. They went on snowshoes and hunted wild beasts. They came into Ulfdalir and there they built themselves a house; there was a lake there which is called Ulfsjar. Early one morning they found on the shore of the lake three women, who were spinning flax. Near them were their swan-garments, for they were Valkyries. Two of them were daughters of King Hlothver, Hlathguth the Swan-White and Hervor the All-Wise, and the third was Olrun, daughter of Kjar from Valland. These did they bring home to their hall with them. Egil took Olrun, and Slagfith Swan-White, and Völund All-Wise. There they dwelt seven winters; but then they flew away to find battles, and came back no more. Then Egil set forth on his snowshoes to follow Olrun, and Slagfith followed Swan-White, but Völund stayed in Ulfdalir. He was a most skillful man, as men know from old tales. King Nithuth had him taken by force, as the poem here tells.
Maids from the south through Myrkwood flew, Fair and young, their fate to follow; On the shore of the sea to rest them they sat, The maids of the south, and flax they spun.
lines: Maids from the south through Myrkwood flew,
Fair and young, their fate to follow;
On the shore of the sea to rest them they sat,
The maids of the south, and flax they spun.

items.text: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Hlathguth and Hervor, Hlothver’s children, And Olrun the Wise Kjar’s daughter was.
lines: Hlathguth and Hervor, Hlothver’s children,
And Olrun the Wise Kjar’s daughter was.

items.text: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . One in her arms took Egil then To her bosom white, the woman fair.
lines: One in her arms took Egil then
To her bosom white, the woman fair.

items.text: Swan-White second,— swan-feathers she wore, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . And her arms the third of the sisters threw Next round Völund’s neck so white.
lines: Swan-White second,— swan-feathers she wore,
And her arms the third of the sisters threw
Next round Völund’s neck so white.

items.text: There did they sit for seven winters, In the eighth at last came their longing again, (And in the ninth did need divide them). The maidens yearned for the murky wood, The fair young maids, their fate to follow.
lines: There did they sit for seven winters,
In the eighth at last came their longing again,
(And in the ninth did need divide them).
The maidens yearned for the murky wood,
The fair young maids, their fate to follow.

items.text: Völund home from his hunting came, From a weary way, the weather-wise bowman, Slagfith and Egil the hall found empty, Out and in went they, everywhere seeking.
lines: Völund home from his hunting came,
From a weary way, the weather-wise bowman,
Slagfith and Egil the hall found empty,
Out and in went they, everywhere seeking.

items.text: East fared Egil after Olrun, And Slagfith south to seek for Swan-White; Völund alone in Ulfdalir lay, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: East fared Egil after Olrun,
And Slagfith south to seek for Swan-White;
Völund alone in Ulfdalir lay,

items.text: Red gold he fashioned with fairest gems, And rings he strung on ropes of bast; So for his wife he waited long, If the fair one home might come to him.
lines: Red gold he fashioned with fairest gems,
And rings he strung on ropes of bast;
So for his wife he waited long,
If the fair one home might come to him.

items.text: This Nithuth learned, the lord of the Njars, That Völund alone in Ulfdalir lay; By night went his men, their mail-coats were studded, Their shields in the waning moonlight shone.
lines: This Nithuth learned, the lord of the Njars,
That Völund alone in Ulfdalir lay;
By night went his men, their mail-coats were studded,
Their shields in the waning moonlight shone.

items.text: From their saddles the gable wall they sought, And in they went at the end of the hall; Rings they saw there on ropes of bast, Seven hundred the hero had.
lines: From their saddles the gable wall they sought,
And in they went at the end of the hall;
Rings they saw there on ropes of bast,
Seven hundred the hero had.

items.text: Off they took them, but all they left Save one alone which they bore away. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: Off they took them, but all they left
Save one alone which they bore away.

items.text: Völund home from his hunting came, From a weary way, the weather-wise bowman; A brown bear’s flesh would he roast with fire; Soon the wood so dry was burning well, (The wind-dried wood that Völund’s was).
lines: Völund home from his hunting came,
From a weary way, the weather-wise bowman;
A brown bear’s flesh would he roast with fire;
Soon the wood so dry was burning well,
(The wind-dried wood that Völund’s was).

items.text: On the bearskin he rested, and counted the rings, The master of elves, but one he missed; That Hlothver’s daughter had it he thought, And the all-wise maid had come once more.
lines: On the bearskin he rested, and counted the rings,
The master of elves, but one he missed;
That Hlothver’s daughter had it he thought,
And the all-wise maid had come once more.

items.text: So long he sat that he fell asleep, His waking empty of gladness was; Heavy chains he saw on his hands, And fetters bound his feet together.
lines: So long he sat that he fell asleep,
His waking empty of gladness was;
Heavy chains he saw on his hands,
And fetters bound his feet together.

items.text: Völund spake:
“What men are they who thus have laid Ropes of bast to bind me now?”
lines: “What men are they who thus have laid
Ropes of bast to bind me now?”

items.text: Then Nithuth called, the lord of the Njars: “How gottest thou, Völund, greatest of elves, These treasures of ours in Ulfdalir?”
lines: Then Nithuth called, the lord of the Njars:
“How gottest thou, Völund, greatest of elves,
These treasures of ours in Ulfdalir?”

items.text: Völund spake:
“The gold was not on Grani’s way, Far, methinks, is our realm from the hills of the Rhine; I mind me that treasures more we had When happy together at home we were.”
lines: “The gold was not on Grani’s way,
Far, methinks, is our realm from the hills of the Rhine;
I mind me that treasures more we had
When happy together at home we were.”

items.text: Without stood the wife of Nithuth wise, And in she came from the end of the hall; On the floor she stood, and softly spoke: “Not kind does he look who comes from the wood.”
lines: Without stood the wife of Nithuth wise,
And in she came from the end of the hall;
On the floor she stood, and softly spoke:
“Not kind does he look who comes from the wood.”

items.text: King Nithuth gave to his daughter Bothvild the gold ring that he had taken from the bast rope in Völund’s house, and he himself wore the sword that Völund had had. The queen spake:

“The glow of his eyes is like gleaming snakes, His teeth he gnashes if now is shown The sword, or Bothvild’s ring he sees; Let them straightway cut his sinews of strength, And set him then in Sævarstath.”
lines: “The glow of his eyes is like gleaming snakes,
His teeth he gnashes if now is shown
The sword, or Bothvild’s ring he sees;
Let them straightway cut his sinews of strength,
And set him then in Sævarstath.”

items.text: So was it done: the sinews in his knee-joints were cut, and he was set in an island which was near the mainland, and was called Sævarstath. There he smithied for the king all kinds of precious things. No man dared to go to him, save only the king himself. Völund spake:

“At Nithuth’s girdle gleams the sword That I sharpened keen with cunningest craft, (And hardened the steel with highest skill;) The bright blade far forever is borne, (Nor back shall I see it borne to my smithy;) Now Bothvild gets the golden ring (That was once my bride’s,— ne’er well shall it be.)”
lines: “At Nithuth’s girdle gleams the sword
That I sharpened keen with cunningest craft,
(And hardened the steel with highest skill;)
The bright blade far forever is borne,
(Nor back shall I see it borne to my smithy;)
Now Bothvild gets the golden ring
(That was once my bride’s,— ne’er well shall it be.)”

items.text: He sat, nor slept, and smote with his hammer, Fast for Nithuth wonders he fashioned; Two boys did go in his door to gaze, Nithuth’s sons, into Sævarstath.
lines: He sat, nor slept, and smote with his hammer,
Fast for Nithuth wonders he fashioned;
Two boys did go in his door to gaze,
Nithuth’s sons, into Sævarstath.

items.text: They came to the chest, and they craved the keys, The evil was open when in they looked; To the boys it seemed that gems they saw, Gold in plenty and precious stones.
lines: They came to the chest, and they craved the keys,
The evil was open when in they looked;
To the boys it seemed that gems they saw,
Gold in plenty and precious stones.

items.text: Völund spake:
“Come ye alone, the next day come, Gold to you both shall then be given; Tell not the maids or the men of the hall, To no one say that me you have sought.”
lines: “Come ye alone, the next day come,
Gold to you both shall then be given;
Tell not the maids or the men of the hall,
To no one say that me you have sought.”

items.text: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Early did brother to brother call: “Swift let us go the rings to see.”
lines: Early did brother to brother call:
“Swift let us go the rings to see.”

items.text: They came to the chest, and they craved the keys, The evil was open when in they looked; He smote off their heads, and their feet he hid Under the sooty straps of the bellows.
lines: They came to the chest, and they craved the keys,
The evil was open when in they looked;
He smote off their heads, and their feet he hid
Under the sooty straps of the bellows.

items.text: Their skulls, once hid by their hair, he took, Set them in silver and sent them to Nithuth; Gems full fair from their eyes he fashioned, To Nithuth’s wife so wise he gave them.
lines: Their skulls, once hid by their hair, he took,
Set them in silver and sent them to Nithuth;
Gems full fair from their eyes he fashioned,
To Nithuth’s wife so wise he gave them.

items.text: And from the teeth of the twain he wrought A brooch for the breast, to Bothvild he sent it; . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: And from the teeth of the twain he wrought
A brooch for the breast, to Bothvild he sent it;

items.text: Bothvild then of her ring did boast, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . “The ring I have broken, I dare not say it save to thee.”
lines: Bothvild then of her ring did boast,
. . . . . . . . “The ring I have broken,
I dare not say it save to thee.”

items.text: Völund spake:
“I shall weld the break in the gold so well That fairer than ever thy father shall find it, And better much thy mother shall think it, And thou no worse than ever it was.”
lines: “I shall weld the break in the gold so well
That fairer than ever thy father shall find it,
And better much thy mother shall think it,
And thou no worse than ever it was.”

items.text: Beer he brought, he was better in cunning, Until in her seat full soon she slept.
lines: Beer he brought, he was better in cunning,
Until in her seat full soon she slept.

items.text: Völund spake:
“Now vengeance I have for all my hurts, Save one alone, on the evil woman.”
lines: “Now vengeance I have for all my hurts,
Save one alone, on the evil woman.”

items.text: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Quoth Völund: “Would that well were the sinews Maimed in my feet by Nithuth’s men.”
lines: Quoth Völund: “Would that well were the sinews
Maimed in my feet by Nithuth’s men.”

items.text: Laughing Völund rose aloft, Weeping Bothvild went from the isle, For her lover’s flight and her father’s wrath.
lines: Laughing Völund rose aloft,
Weeping Bothvild went from the isle,
For her lover’s flight and her father’s wrath.

items.text: Without stood the wife of Nithuth wise, And in she came from the end of the hall; But he by the wall in weariness sat: “Wakest thou, Nithuth, lord of the Njars?”
lines: Without stood the wife of Nithuth wise,
And in she came from the end of the hall;
But he by the wall in weariness sat:
“Wakest thou, Nithuth, lord of the Njars?”

items.text: Nithuth spake:
“Always I wake, and ever joyless, Little I sleep since my sons were slain; Cold is my head, cold was thy counsel, One thing, with Völund to speak, I wish.
lines: “Always I wake, and ever joyless,
Little I sleep since my sons were slain;
Cold is my head, cold was thy counsel,
One thing, with Völund to speak, I wish.

items.text: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . “Answer me, Völund, greatest of elves, What happed with my boys that hale once were?”
lines: “Answer me, Völund, greatest of elves,
What happed with my boys that hale once were?”

items.text: Völund spake:

“First shalt thou all the oaths now swear, By the rail of ship, and the rim of shield, By the shoulder of steed, and the edge of sword, That to Völund’s wife thou wilt work no ill, Nor yet my bride to her death wilt bring, Though a wife I should have that well thou knowest, And a child I should have within thy hall.
lines: “First shalt thou all the oaths now swear,
By the rail of ship, and the rim of shield,
By the shoulder of steed, and the edge of sword,
That to Völund’s wife thou wilt work no ill,
Nor yet my bride to her death wilt bring,
Though a wife I should have that well thou knowest,
And a child I should have within thy hall.

items.text: “Seek the smithy that thou didst set, Thou shalt find the bellows sprinkled with blood; I smote off the heads of both thy sons, And their feet ’neath the sooty straps I hid.
lines: “Seek the smithy that thou didst set,
Thou shalt find the bellows sprinkled with blood;
I smote off the heads of both thy sons,
And their feet ’neath the sooty straps I hid.

items.text: “Their skulls, once hid by their hair, I took, Set them in silver and sent them to Nithuth; Gems full fair from their eyes I fashioned, To Nithuth’s wife so wise I gave them.
lines: “Their skulls, once hid by their hair, I took,
Set them in silver and sent them to Nithuth;
Gems full fair from their eyes I fashioned,
To Nithuth’s wife so wise I gave them.

items.text: “And from the teeth of the twain I wrought A brooch for the breast, to Bothvild I gave it; Now big with child does Bothvild go, The only daughter ye two had ever.”
lines: “And from the teeth of the twain I wrought
A brooch for the breast, to Bothvild I gave it;
Now big with child does Bothvild go,
The only daughter ye two had ever.”

items.text: Nithuth spake:

“Never spakest thou word that worse could hurt me, Nor that made me, Völund, more bitter for vengeance; There is no man so high from thy horse to take thee, Or so doughty an archer as down to shoot thee, While high in the clouds thy course thou takest.”
lines: “Never spakest thou word that worse could hurt me,
Nor that made me, Völund, more bitter for vengeance;
There is no man so high from thy horse to take thee,
Or so doughty an archer as down to shoot thee,
While high in the clouds thy course thou takest.”

items.text: Laughing Völund rose aloft, But left in sadness Nithuth sat. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: Laughing Völund rose aloft,
But left in sadness Nithuth sat.

items.text: Then spake Nithuth, lord of the Njars: “Rise up, Thakkrath, best of my thralls, Bid Bothvild come, the bright-browed maid, Bedecked so fair, with her father to speak.”
lines: Then spake Nithuth, lord of the Njars:
“Rise up, Thakkrath, best of my thralls,
Bid Bothvild come, the bright-browed maid,
Bedecked so fair, with her father to speak.”

items.text: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . “Is it true, Bothvild, that which was told me; Once in the isle with Völund wert thou?”
lines: “Is it true, Bothvild, that which was told me;
Once in the isle with Völund wert thou?”

items.text: Bothvild spake:

“True is it, Nithuth, that which was told thee, Once in the isle with Völund was I, An hour of lust, alas it should be! Nought was my might with such a man, Nor from his strength could I save myself.”
lines: “True is it, Nithuth, that which was told thee,
Once in the isle with Völund was I,
An hour of lust, alas it should be!
Nought was my might with such a man,
Nor from his strength could I save myself.”

items.text: OF HJORVARTH AND SIGRLIN

Hjorvarth was the name of a king, who had four wives: one was called Alfhild, and their son was named Hethin; the second was called Særeith, and their son was named Humlung; the third was called Sinrjoth, and their son was named Hymling. King Hjorvarth had made a great vow to have as wife whatsoever woman he knew was fairest. He learned that King Svafnir had a daughter fairer than all others, whose name was Sigrlin. Ithmund was the name of one of his jarls; he had a son called Atli, who went to woo Sigrlin on behalf of the king. He dwelt the winter long with King Svafnir. There was a jarl called Franmar, Sigrlin’s foster-father; his daughter was named Alof. The jarl told him that the maiden’s hand was denied, and Atli went home. Atli, the jarl’s son, stood one day in a certain wood; a bird sat in the branches up over him, and it had heard that his men called Hjorvarth’s wives the fairest of women. The bird twittered, and Atli hearkened to what it spoke. It said:
“Sawest thou Sigrlin, Svafnir’s daughter, The fairest maid in her home-land found? Though Hjorvarth’s wives by men are held Goodly to see in Glasir’s wood.”
lines: “Sawest thou Sigrlin, Svafnir’s daughter,
The fairest maid in her home-land found?
Though Hjorvarth’s wives by men are held
Goodly to see in Glasir’s wood.”

items.text: Atli spake:
“Now with Atli, Ithmund’s son, Wilt thou say more, thou bird so wise?”
lines: “Now with Atli, Ithmund’s son,
Wilt thou say more, thou bird so wise?”

items.text: The bird spake:
“I may if the prince an offering makes, And I have what I will from the house of the king.”
lines: “I may if the prince an offering makes,
And I have what I will from the house of the king.”

items.text: Atli spake:
“Choose not Hjorvarth, nor sons of his, Nor the wives so fair of the famous chief; Ask not the brides that the prince’s are; Fair let us deal in friendly wise.”
lines: “Choose not Hjorvarth, nor sons of his,
Nor the wives so fair of the famous chief;
Ask not the brides that the prince’s are;
Fair let us deal in friendly wise.”

items.text: The bird spake:
“A fane will I ask, and altars many, Gold-horned cattle the prince shall give me, If Sigrlin yet shall sleep in his arms, Or free of will the hero shall follow.”
lines: “A fane will I ask, and altars many,
Gold-horned cattle the prince shall give me,
If Sigrlin yet shall sleep in his arms,
Or free of will the hero shall follow.”

items.text: This was before Atli went on his journey; but when he came home, and the king asked his tidings, he said:
“Trouble we had, but tidings none, Our horses failed in the mountains high, The waters of Sæmorn we needs must wade; Svafnir’s daughter, with rings bedecked, She whom we sought, was still denied us.”
lines: “Trouble we had, but tidings none,
Our horses failed in the mountains high,
The waters of Sæmorn we needs must wade;
Svafnir’s daughter, with rings bedecked,
She whom we sought, was still denied us.”

items.text: The king bade that they should go another time, and he went with them himself. But when they came up on the mountain, they saw Svavaland burning and mighty dust-clouds from many steeds. The king rode from the mountain forward into the land, and made a night’s stay hard by a stream. Atli kept watch and went over the stream; he found there a house. A great bird sat on the housetop to guard it, but he was asleep. Atli hurled his spear at the bird and slew it, and in the house he found Sigrlin the king’s daughter and Alof the jarl’s daughter, and he brought them both thence with him. Jarl Franmar had changed himself into the likeness of an eagle, and guarded them from the enemy host by magic. Hrothmar was the name of a king, a wooer of Sigrlin; he slew the king of Svavaland and had plundered and burned his land. King Hjorvarth took Sigrlin, and Atli took Alof.
(II)

Hjorvarth and Sigrlin had a son, mighty and of noble stature; he was a silent man, and no name stuck fast to him. He sat on a hill, and saw nine Valkyries riding; one of them was the fairest of all. She spake:
“Late wilt thou, Helgi, have hoard of rings, Thou battle-tree fierce, or of shining fields,— The eagle screams soon,— if never thou speakest, Though, hero, hard thy heart may cry.”
lines: “Late wilt thou, Helgi, have hoard of rings,
Thou battle-tree fierce, or of shining fields,—
The eagle screams soon,— if never thou speakest,
Though, hero, hard thy heart may cry.”

items.text: Helgi spake:
“What gift shall I have with Helgi’s name, Glorious maid, for the giving is thine? All thy words shall I think on well, But I want them not if I win not thee.”
lines: “What gift shall I have with Helgi’s name,
Glorious maid, for the giving is thine?
All thy words shall I think on well,
But I want them not if I win not thee.”

items.text: The Valkyrie spake:
“Swords I know lying in Sigarsholm, Fifty there are save only four; One there is that is best of all, The shield-destroyer, with gold it shines.
lines: “Swords I know lying in Sigarsholm,
Fifty there are save only four;
One there is that is best of all,
The shield-destroyer, with gold it shines.

items.text: “In the hilt is fame, in the haft is courage, In the point is fear, for its owner’s foes; On the blade there lies a blood-flecked snake, And a serpent’s tail round the flat is twisted.”
lines: “In the hilt is fame, in the haft is courage,
In the point is fear, for its owner’s foes;
On the blade there lies a blood-flecked snake,
And a serpent’s tail round the flat is twisted.”

items.text: Eylimi was the name of a king, whose daughter was Svava; she was a Valkyrie, and rode air and sea. She gave Helgi this name, and shielded him oft thereafter in battle. Helgi spake:
“Hjorvarth, king, unwholesome thy counsels, Though famed thou art in leading the folk, Letting fire the homes of heroes eat, Who evil deed had never done thee.
lines: “Hjorvarth, king, unwholesome thy counsels,
Though famed thou art in leading the folk,
Letting fire the homes of heroes eat,
Who evil deed had never done thee.

items.text: “Yet Hrothmar still the hoard doth hold, The wealth that once our kinsmen wielded; Full seldom care the king disturbs, Heir to dead men he deems himself.”
lines: “Yet Hrothmar still the hoard doth hold,
The wealth that once our kinsmen wielded;
Full seldom care the king disturbs,
Heir to dead men he deems himself.”

items.text: Hjorvarth answered that he would give Helgi a following if he fain would avenge his mother’s father. Then Helgi got the sword that Svava had told him of. So he went, and Atli with him, and they slew Hrothmar, and they did many great deeds.
(III)

He slew the giant Hati, whom he found sitting on a certain mountain. Helgi and Atli lay with their ships in Hatafjord. Atli kept watch during the first part of the night. Hrimgerth, Hati’s daughter, spake:
“Who are the heroes in Hatafjord? The ships are covered with shields; Bravely ye look, and little ye fear, The name of the king would I know.”
lines: “Who are the heroes in Hatafjord?
The ships are covered with shields;
Bravely ye look, and little ye fear,
The name of the king would I know.”

items.text: Atli spake:
“Helgi his name, and never thou mayst Harm to the hero bring; With iron is fitted the prince’s fleet, Nor can witches work us ill.”
lines: “Helgi his name, and never thou mayst
Harm to the hero bring;
With iron is fitted the prince’s fleet,
Nor can witches work us ill.”

items.text: Hrimgerth spake:
“Who now, thou mighty man, art thou? By what name art thou known to men? He trusts thee well, the prince who wills That thou stand at the stem of his ship.”
lines: “Who now, thou mighty man, art thou?
By what name art thou known to men?
He trusts thee well, the prince who wills
That thou stand at the stem of his ship.”

items.text: Atli spake:
“Atli am I, and ill shalt thou find me, Great hate for witches I have; Oft have I been in the dripping bows, And to dusk-riders death have brought.
lines: “Atli am I, and ill shalt thou find me,
Great hate for witches I have;
Oft have I been in the dripping bows,
And to dusk-riders death have brought.

items.text: “Corpse-hungry giantess, how art thou called? Say, witch, who thy father was! Nine miles deeper down mayst thou sink, And a tree grow tall on thy bosom.”
lines: “Corpse-hungry giantess, how art thou called?
Say, witch, who thy father was!
Nine miles deeper down mayst thou sink,
And a tree grow tall on thy bosom.”

items.text: Hrimgerth spake:
“Hrimgerth am I, my father was Hati, Of giants the most in might; Many a woman he won from her home, Ere Helgi hewed him down.”
lines: “Hrimgerth am I, my father was Hati,
Of giants the most in might;
Many a woman he won from her home,
Ere Helgi hewed him down.”

items.text: Atli spake:
“Witch, in front of the ship thou wast, And lay before the fjord; To Ron wouldst have given the ruler’s men, If a spear had not stuck in thy flesh.”
lines: “Witch, in front of the ship thou wast,
And lay before the fjord;
To Ron wouldst have given the ruler’s men,
If a spear had not stuck in thy flesh.”

items.text: Hrimgerth spake:
“Dull art thou, Atli, thou dreamest, methinks, The lids lie over thine eyes; By the leader’s ships my mother lay, Hlothvarth’s sons on the sea I slew.
lines: “Dull art thou, Atli, thou dreamest, methinks,
The lids lie over thine eyes;
By the leader’s ships my mother lay,
Hlothvarth’s sons on the sea I slew.

items.text: “Thou wouldst neigh, Atli, but gelded thou art, See, Hrimgerth hoists her tail; In thy hinder end is thy heart, methinks, Though thy speech is a stallion’s cry.”
lines: “Thou wouldst neigh, Atli, but gelded thou art,
See, Hrimgerth hoists her tail;
In thy hinder end is thy heart, methinks,
Though thy speech is a stallion’s cry.”

items.text: Atli spake:
“A stallion I seem if thou seekest to try me, And I leap to land from the sea; I shall smite thee to bits, if so I will, And heavy sinks Hrimgerth’s tail.”
lines: “A stallion I seem if thou seekest to try me,
And I leap to land from the sea;
I shall smite thee to bits, if so I will,
And heavy sinks Hrimgerth’s tail.”

items.text: Hrimgerth spake:
“Go ashore then, Atli, if sure of thy might, Let us come to Varin’s cove; Straight shall thy rounded ribs be made If thou comest within my claws.”
lines: “Go ashore then, Atli, if sure of thy might,
Let us come to Varin’s cove;
Straight shall thy rounded ribs be made
If thou comest within my claws.”

items.text: Atli spake:
“I will not go till the warriors wake, Again their chief to guard; I should wonder not, foul witch, if up From beneath our keel thou shouldst come.”
lines: “I will not go till the warriors wake,
Again their chief to guard;
I should wonder not, foul witch, if up
From beneath our keel thou shouldst come.”

items.text: Hrimgerth spake:
“Awake now, Helgi, and Hrimgerth requite, That Hati to death thou didst hew; If a single night she can sleep by the prince, Then requited are all her ills.”
lines: “Awake now, Helgi, and Hrimgerth requite,
That Hati to death thou didst hew;
If a single night she can sleep by the prince,
Then requited are all her ills.”

items.text: Helgi spake:
“’Tis Lothin shall have thee,— thou’rt loathsome to men,— His home in Tholley he has; Of the wild-dwellers worst is the giant wise, He is meet as a mate for thee.”
lines: “’Tis Lothin shall have thee,— thou’rt loathsome to men,—
His home in Tholley he has;
Of the wild-dwellers worst is the giant wise,
He is meet as a mate for thee.”

items.text: Hrimgerth spake:

“More thou lovest her who scanned the harbor, Last night among the men; (The gold-decked maid bore magic, methinks, When the land from the sea she sought, And fast she kept your fleet;) She alone is to blame that I may not bring Death to the monarch’s men.”
lines: “More thou lovest her who scanned the harbor,
Last night among the men;
(The gold-decked maid bore magic, methinks,
When the land from the sea she sought,
And fast she kept your fleet;)
She alone is to blame that I may not bring
Death to the monarch’s men.”

items.text: Helgi spake:
“Hrimgerth, mark, if thy hurts I requite, Tell now the truth to the king; Was there one who the ships of the warrior warded, Or did many together go?”
lines: “Hrimgerth, mark, if thy hurts I requite,
Tell now the truth to the king;
Was there one who the ships of the warrior warded,
Or did many together go?”

items.text: Hrimgerth spake:

“Thrice nine there were, but one rode first, A helmed maid white of hue; Their horses quivered, there came from their manes Dew in the dales so deep, (Hail on the woods so high, Thence men their harvest have, But ill was the sight I saw.)”
lines: “Thrice nine there were, but one rode first,
A helmed maid white of hue;
Their horses quivered, there came from their manes
Dew in the dales so deep,
(Hail on the woods so high,
Thence men their harvest have,
But ill was the sight I saw.)”

items.text: Atli spake:
“Look eastward, Hrimgerth, for Helgi has struck thee Down with the runes of death; Safe in harbor floats the prince’s fleet, And safe are the monarch’s men.”
lines: “Look eastward, Hrimgerth, for Helgi has struck thee
Down with the runes of death;
Safe in harbor floats the prince’s fleet,
And safe are the monarch’s men.”

items.text: Helgi spake:
“It is day, Hrimgerth, for Atli held thee Till now thy life thou must lose; As a harbor mark men shall mock at thee, Where in stone thou shalt ever stand.”
lines: “It is day, Hrimgerth, for Atli held thee
Till now thy life thou must lose;
As a harbor mark men shall mock at thee,
Where in stone thou shalt ever stand.”

items.text: (IV)

King Helgi was a mighty warrior. He came to King Eylimi and sought the hand of his daughter, Svava. Then Helgi and Svava exchanged vows, and greatly they loved each other. Svava was at home with her father, while Helgi was in the field; Svava was still a Valkyrie as before.

Hethin was at home with his father, King Hjorvarth, in Norway. Hethin was coming home alone from the forest one Yule-eve, and found a troll-woman; she rode on a wolf, and had snakes in place of a bridle. She asked Hethin for his company. “Nay,” said he. She said, “Thou shalt pay for this at the king’s toast.” That evening the great vows were taken; the sacred boar was brought in, the men laid their hands thereon, and took their vows at the king’s toast. Hethin vowed that he would have Svava, Eylimi’s daughter, the beloved of his brother Helgi; then such great grief seized him that he went forth on wild paths southward over the land, and found Helgi, his brother. Helgi said:
“Welcome, Hethin! what hast thou to tell Of tidings new that from Norway come? Wherefore didst leave thy land, O prince, And fared alone to find us here?”
lines: “Welcome, Hethin! what hast thou to tell
Of tidings new that from Norway come?
Wherefore didst leave thy land, O prince,
And fared alone to find us here?”

items.text: Hethin spake:
“A deed more evil I have done Than, brother mine, thou e’er canst mend; For I have chosen the child of the king, Thy bride, for mine at the monarch’s toast.”
lines: “A deed more evil I have done
Than, brother mine, thou e’er canst mend;
For I have chosen the child of the king,
Thy bride, for mine at the monarch’s toast.”

items.text: Helgi spake:

“Grieve not, Hethin, for true shall hold The words we both by the beer have sworn; To the isle a warrior wills that I go, (There shall I come the third night hence;) And doubtful must be my coming back, (So may all be well, if fate so wills.)”
lines: “Grieve not, Hethin, for true shall hold
The words we both by the beer have sworn;
To the isle a warrior wills that I go,
(There shall I come the third night hence;)
And doubtful must be my coming back,
(So may all be well, if fate so wills.)”

items.text: Hethin spake:
“Thou saidst once, Helgi, that Hethin was A friend full good, and gifts didst give him; More seemly it were thy sword to redden, Than friendship thus to thy foe to give.”
lines: “Thou saidst once, Helgi, that Hethin was
A friend full good, and gifts didst give him;
More seemly it were thy sword to redden,
Than friendship thus to thy foe to give.”

items.text: Helgi spoke thus because he foresaw his death, for his following-spirits had met Hethin when he saw the woman riding on the wolf. Alf was the name of a king, the son of Hrothmar, who had marked out a battle-place with Helgi at Sigarsvoll after a stay of three nights. Then Helgi spake:
“On a wolf there rode, when dusk it was, A woman who fain would have him follow; Well she knew that now would fall Sigrlin’s son at Sigarsvoll.”
lines: “On a wolf there rode, when dusk it was,
A woman who fain would have him follow;
Well she knew that now would fall
Sigrlin’s son at Sigarsvoll.”

items.text: There was a great battle, and there Helgi got a mortal wound.
Sigar riding did Helgi send To seek out Eylimi’s only daughter: “Bid her swiftly ready to be, If her lover alive she would find.”
lines: Sigar riding did Helgi send
To seek out Eylimi’s only daughter:
“Bid her swiftly ready to be,
If her lover alive she would find.”

items.text: Sigar spake:
“Hither now has Helgi sent me, With thee, Svava, thyself to speak; The hero said he fain would see thee Ere life the nobly born should leave.”
lines: “Hither now has Helgi sent me,
With thee, Svava, thyself to speak;
The hero said he fain would see thee
Ere life the nobly born should leave.”

items.text: Svava spake:
“What chanced with Helgi, Hjorvarth’s son? Hard to me is harm now come; If the sea smote him, or sword bit him, Ill shall I bring to all his foes.”
lines: “What chanced with Helgi, Hjorvarth’s son?
Hard to me is harm now come;
If the sea smote him, or sword bit him,
Ill shall I bring to all his foes.”

items.text: Sigar spake:
“In the morn he fell at Frekastein, The king who was noblest beneath the sun; Alf has the joy of victory all, Though need therefor is never his.”
lines: “In the morn he fell at Frekastein,
The king who was noblest beneath the sun;
Alf has the joy of victory all,
Though need therefor is never his.”

items.text: Helgi spake:
“Hail to thee, Svava! thy sorrow rule, Our meeting last in life is this; Hard the wounds of the hero bleed, And close to my heart the sword has come.
lines: “Hail to thee, Svava! thy sorrow rule,
Our meeting last in life is this;
Hard the wounds of the hero bleed,
And close to my heart the sword has come.

items.text: “I bid thee, Svava,— weep not, bride,— If thou wilt hearken to these my words, The bed for Hethin have thou ready, And yield thy love to the hero young.”
lines: “I bid thee, Svava,— weep not, bride,—
If thou wilt hearken to these my words,
The bed for Hethin have thou ready,
And yield thy love to the hero young.”

items.text: Svava spake:
“A vow I had in my dear-loved home, When Helgi sought with rings to have me, That not of my will, if the warrior died, Would I fold in my arms a man unfamed.”
lines: “A vow I had in my dear-loved home,
When Helgi sought with rings to have me,
That not of my will, if the warrior died,
Would I fold in my arms a man unfamed.”

items.text: Hethin spake:
“Kiss me, Svava, I come not back, Rogheim to see, or Rothulsfjoll, Till vengeance I have for the son of Hjorvarth, The king who was noblest beneath the sun.”
lines: “Kiss me, Svava, I come not back,
Rogheim to see, or Rothulsfjoll,
Till vengeance I have for the son of Hjorvarth,
The king who was noblest beneath the sun.”

items.text: Of Helgi and Svava it is said that they were born again.
In olden days, when eagles screamed, And holy streams from heaven’s crags fell, Was Helgi then, the hero-hearted, Borghild’s son, in Bralund born.
lines: In olden days, when eagles screamed,
And holy streams from heaven’s crags fell,
Was Helgi then, the hero-hearted,
Borghild’s son, in Bralund born.

items.text: ’Twas night in the dwelling, and Norns there came, Who shaped the life of the lofty one; They bade him most famed of fighters all And best of princes ever to be.
lines: ’Twas night in the dwelling, and Norns there came,
Who shaped the life of the lofty one;
They bade him most famed of fighters all
And best of princes ever to be.

items.text: Mightily wove they the web of fate, While Bralund’s towns were trembling all; And there the golden threads they wove, And in the moon’s hall fast they made them.
lines: Mightily wove they the web of fate,
While Bralund’s towns were trembling all;
And there the golden threads they wove,
And in the moon’s hall fast they made them.

items.text: East and west the ends they hid, In the middle the hero should have his land; And Neri’s kinswoman northward cast A chain, and bade it firm ever to be.
lines: East and west the ends they hid,
In the middle the hero should have his land;
And Neri’s kinswoman northward cast
A chain, and bade it firm ever to be.

items.text: Once sorrow had the Ylfings’ son, And grief the bride who the loved one had borne. * * * * * * Quoth raven to raven, on treetop resting, Seeking for food, “There is something I know.
lines: Once sorrow had the Ylfings’ son,
And grief the bride who the loved one had borne.
Quoth raven to raven, on treetop resting,
Seeking for food, “There is something I know.

items.text: “In mail-coat stands the son of Sigmund, A half-day old; now day is here; His eyes flash sharp as the heroes’ are, He is friend of the wolves; full glad are we.”
lines: “In mail-coat stands the son of Sigmund,
A half-day old; now day is here;
His eyes flash sharp as the heroes’ are,
He is friend of the wolves; full glad are we.”

items.text: The warrior throng a ruler thought him, Good times, they said, mankind should see; The king himself from battle-press came, To give the prince a leek full proud.
lines: The warrior throng a ruler thought him,
Good times, they said, mankind should see;
The king himself from battle-press came,
To give the prince a leek full proud.

items.text: Helgi he named him, and Hringstathir gave him, Solfjoll, Snæfjoll, and Sigarsvoll, Hringstoth, Hotun, and Himinvangar, And a blood-snake bedecked to Sinfjotli’s brother.
lines: Helgi he named him, and Hringstathir gave him,
Solfjoll, Snæfjoll, and Sigarsvoll,
Hringstoth, Hotun, and Himinvangar,
And a blood-snake bedecked to Sinfjotli’s brother.

items.text: Mighty he grew in the midst of his friends, The fair-born elm, in fortune’s glow; To his comrades gold he gladly gave, The hero spared not the blood-flecked hoard.
lines: Mighty he grew in the midst of his friends,
The fair-born elm, in fortune’s glow;
To his comrades gold he gladly gave,
The hero spared not the blood-flecked hoard.

items.text: Short time for war the chieftain waited, When fifteen winters old he was; Hunding he slew, the hardy wight Who long had ruled o’er lands and men.
lines: Short time for war the chieftain waited,
When fifteen winters old he was;
Hunding he slew, the hardy wight
Who long had ruled o’er lands and men.

items.text: Of Sigmund’s son then next they sought Hoard and rings, the sons of Hunding; They bade the prince requital pay For booty stolen and father slain.
lines: Of Sigmund’s son then next they sought
Hoard and rings, the sons of Hunding;
They bade the prince requital pay
For booty stolen and father slain.

items.text: The prince let not their prayers avail, Nor gold for their dead did the kinsmen get; Waiting, he said, was a mighty storm Of lances gray and Othin’s grimness.
lines: The prince let not their prayers avail,
Nor gold for their dead did the kinsmen get;
Waiting, he said, was a mighty storm
Of lances gray and Othin’s grimness.

items.text: The warriors forth to the battle went, The field they chose at Logafjoll; Frothi’s peace midst foes they broke, Through the isle went hungrily Vithrir’s hounds.
lines: The warriors forth to the battle went,
The field they chose at Logafjoll;
Frothi’s peace midst foes they broke,
Through the isle went hungrily Vithrir’s hounds.

items.text: The king then sat, when he had slain Eyjolf and Alf, ’neath the eagle-stone; Hjorvarth and Hovarth, Hunding’s sons, The kin of the spear-wielder, all had he killed.
lines: The king then sat, when he had slain
Eyjolf and Alf, ’neath the eagle-stone;
Hjorvarth and Hovarth, Hunding’s sons,
The kin of the spear-wielder, all had he killed.

items.text: Then glittered light from Logafjoll, And from the light the flashes leaped; . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: Then glittered light from Logafjoll,
And from the light the flashes leaped;

items.text: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . High under helms on heaven’s field; Their byrnies all with blood were red, And from their spears the sparks flew forth.
lines: High under helms on heaven’s field;
Their byrnies all with blood were red,
And from their spears the sparks flew forth.

items.text: Early then in wolf-wood asked The mighty king of the southern maid, If with the hero home would she Come that night; the weapons clashed.
lines: Early then in wolf-wood asked
The mighty king of the southern maid,
If with the hero home would she
Come that night; the weapons clashed.

items.text: Down from her horse sprang Hogni’s daughter,— The shields were still,— and spake to the hero: “Other tasks are ours, methinks, Than drinking beer with the breaker of rings.
lines: Down from her horse sprang Hogni’s daughter,—
The shields were still,— and spake to the hero:
“Other tasks are ours, methinks,
Than drinking beer with the breaker of rings.

items.text: “My father has pledged his daughter fair As bride to Granmar’s son so grim; But, Helgi, I once Hothbrodd called As fine a king as the son of a cat.
lines: “My father has pledged his daughter fair
As bride to Granmar’s son so grim;
But, Helgi, I once Hothbrodd called
As fine a king as the son of a cat.

items.text: “Yet the hero will come a few nights hence, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Unless thou dost bid him the battle-ground seek, Or takest the maid from the warrior mighty.”
lines: “Yet the hero will come a few nights hence,
Unless thou dost bid him the battle-ground seek,
Or takest the maid from the warrior mighty.”

items.text: Helgi spake:
“Fear him not, though Isung he felled, First must our courage keen be tried, Before unwilling thou fare with the knave; Weapons will clash, if to death I come not.”
lines: “Fear him not, though Isung he felled,
First must our courage keen be tried,
Before unwilling thou fare with the knave;
Weapons will clash, if to death I come not.”

items.text: Messengers sent the mighty one then, By land and by sea, a host to seek, Store of wealth of the water’s gleam, And men to summon, and sons of men.
lines: Messengers sent the mighty one then,
By land and by sea, a host to seek,
Store of wealth of the water’s gleam,
And men to summon, and sons of men.

items.text: “Bid them straightway seek the ships, And off Brandey ready to be!” There the chief waited till thither were come Men by hundreds from Hethinsey.
lines: “Bid them straightway seek the ships,
And off Brandey ready to be!”
There the chief waited till thither were come
Men by hundreds from Hethinsey.

items.text: Soon off Stafnsnes stood the ships, Fair they glided and gay with gold; Then Helgi spake to Hjorleif asking: “Hast thou counted the gallant host?”
lines: Soon off Stafnsnes stood the ships,
Fair they glided and gay with gold;
Then Helgi spake to Hjorleif asking:
“Hast thou counted the gallant host?”

items.text: The young king answered the other then: “Long were it to tell from Tronueyr The long-stemmed ships with warriors laden That come from without into Orvasund.
lines: The young king answered the other then:
“Long were it to tell from Tronueyr
The long-stemmed ships with warriors laden
That come from without into Orvasund.

items.text: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . “There are hundreds twelve of trusty men, But in Hotun lies the host of the king, Greater by half; I have hope of battle.”
lines: “There are hundreds twelve of trusty men,
But in Hotun lies the host of the king,
Greater by half; I have hope of battle.”

items.text: The ship’s-tents soon the chieftain struck, And waked the throng of warriors all; (The heroes the red of dawn beheld;) And on the masts the gallant men Made fast the sails in Varinsfjord.
lines: The ship’s-tents soon the chieftain struck,
And waked the throng of warriors all;
(The heroes the red of dawn beheld;)
And on the masts the gallant men
Made fast the sails in Varinsfjord.

items.text: There was beat of oars and clash of iron, Shield smote shield as the ships’-folk rowed; Swiftly went the warrior-laden Fleet of the ruler forth from the land.
lines: There was beat of oars and clash of iron,
Shield smote shield as the ships’-folk rowed;
Swiftly went the warrior-laden
Fleet of the ruler forth from the land.

items.text: So did it sound, when together the sisters Of Kolga struck with the keels full long, As if cliffs were broken with beating surf, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: So did it sound, when together the sisters
Of Kolga struck with the keels full long,
As if cliffs were broken with beating surf,

items.text: Helgi bade higher hoist the sails, Nor did the ships’-folk shun the waves, Though dreadfully did Ægir’s daughters Seek the steeds of the sea to sink.
lines: Helgi bade higher hoist the sails,
Nor did the ships’-folk shun the waves,
Though dreadfully did Ægir’s daughters
Seek the steeds of the sea to sink.

items.text: But from above did Sigrun brave Aid the men and all their faring; Mightily came from the claws of Ron The leader’s sea-beast off Gnipalund.
lines: But from above did Sigrun brave
Aid the men and all their faring;
Mightily came from the claws of Ron
The leader’s sea-beast off Gnipalund.

items.text: At evening there in Unavagar Floated the fleet bedecked full fair; But they who saw from Svarin’s hill, Bitter at heart the host beheld.
lines: At evening there in Unavagar
Floated the fleet bedecked full fair;
But they who saw from Svarin’s hill,
Bitter at heart the host beheld.

items.text: Then Gothmund asked, goodly of birth, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . “Who is the monarch who guides the host, And to the land the warriors leads?”
lines: Then Gothmund asked, goodly of birth,
“Who is the monarch who guides the host,
And to the land the warriors leads?”

items.text: Sinfjotli answered, and up on an oar Raised a shield all red with golden rim; A sea-sentry was he, skilled to speak, And in words with princes well to strive.
lines: Sinfjotli answered, and up on an oar
Raised a shield all red with golden rim;
A sea-sentry was he, skilled to speak,
And in words with princes well to strive.

items.text: “Say tonight when you feed the swine, And send your bitches to seek their swill, That out of the East have the Ylfings come, Greedy for battle, to Gnipalund.
lines: “Say tonight when you feed the swine,
And send your bitches to seek their swill,
That out of the East have the Ylfings come,
Greedy for battle, to Gnipalund.

items.text: “There will Hothbrodd Helgi find, In the midst of the fleet, and flight he scorns; Often has he the eagles gorged, Whilst thou at the quern wert slave-girls kissing.”
lines: “There will Hothbrodd Helgi find,
In the midst of the fleet, and flight he scorns;
Often has he the eagles gorged,
Whilst thou at the quern wert slave-girls kissing.”

items.text: Gothmund spake:
“Hero, the ancient sayings heed, And bring not lies to the nobly born. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: “Hero, the ancient sayings heed,
And bring not lies to the nobly born.

items.text: “Thou hast eaten the entrails of wolves, And of thy brothers the slayer been; Oft wounds to suck thy cold mouth sought, And loathed in rocky dens didst lurk.”
lines: “Thou hast eaten the entrails of wolves,
And of thy brothers the slayer been;
Oft wounds to suck thy cold mouth sought,
And loathed in rocky dens didst lurk.”

items.text: Sinfjotli spake:
“A witch in Varin’s isle thou wast, A woman false, and lies didst fashion; Of the mail-clad heroes thou wouldst have No other, thou saidst, save Sinfjotli only.
lines: “A witch in Varin’s isle thou wast,
A woman false, and lies didst fashion;
Of the mail-clad heroes thou wouldst have
No other, thou saidst, save Sinfjotli only.
