And his fate the way to the wanderer shows;
The doughty king a daughter has,
That thou as a bride mayst, Sigurth, buy.”

items.text: Another spake:
“A hall stands high on Hindarfjoll, All with flame is it ringed without; Warriors wise did make it once Out of the flaming light of the flood.
lines: “A hall stands high on Hindarfjoll,
All with flame is it ringed without;
Warriors wise did make it once
Out of the flaming light of the flood.

items.text: “On the mountain sleeps a battle-maid, And about her plays the bane of the wood; Ygg with the thorn hath smitten her thus, For she felled the fighter he fain would save.
lines: “On the mountain sleeps a battle-maid,
And about her plays the bane of the wood;
Ygg with the thorn hath smitten her thus,
For she felled the fighter he fain would save.

items.text: “There mayst thou behold the maiden helmed, Who forth on Vingskornir rode from the fight; The victory-bringer her sleep shall break not, Thou heroes’ son, so the Norns have set.”
lines: “There mayst thou behold the maiden helmed,
Who forth on Vingskornir rode from the fight;
The victory-bringer her sleep shall break not,
Thou heroes’ son, so the Norns have set.”

items.text: Sigurth rode along Fafnir’s trail to his lair, and found it open. The gate-posts were of iron, and the gates; of iron, too, were all the beams in the house, which was dug down into the earth. There Sigurth found a mighty store of gold, and he filled two chests full thereof; he took the fear-helm and a golden mail-coat and the sword Hrotti, and many other precious things, and loaded Grani with them, but the horse would not go forward until Sigurth mounted on his back.

Sigurth rode up on Hindarfjoll and turned southward toward the land of the Franks. On the mountain he saw a great light, as if fire were burning, and the glow reached up to heaven. And when he came thither, there stood a tower of shields, and above it was a banner. Sigurth went into the shield-tower, and saw that a man lay there sleeping with all his war-weapons. First he took the helm from his head, and then he saw that it was a woman. The mail-coat was as fast as if it had grown to the flesh. Then he cut the mail-coat from the head-opening downward, and out to both the arm-holes. Then he took the mail-coat from her, and she awoke, and sat up and saw Sigurth, and said:
“What bit through the byrnie? how was broken my sleep? Who made me free of the fetters pale?”
lines: “What bit through the byrnie? how was broken my sleep?
Who made me free of the fetters pale?”

items.text: He answered:
“Sigmund’s son, with Sigurth’s sword, That late with flesh hath fed the ravens.”
lines: “Sigmund’s son, with Sigurth’s sword,
That late with flesh hath fed the ravens.”

items.text: Sigurth sat beside her and asked her name. She took a horn full of mead and gave him a memory-draught.
“Hail, day! Hail, sons of day! And night and her daughter now! Look on us here with loving eyes, That waiting we victory win.
lines: “Hail, day! Hail, sons of day!
And night and her daughter now!
Look on us here with loving eyes,
That waiting we victory win.

items.text: “Hail to the gods! Ye goddesses, hail, And all the generous earth! Give to us wisdom and goodly speech, And healing hands, life-long.
lines: “Hail to the gods! Ye goddesses, hail,
And all the generous earth!
Give to us wisdom and goodly speech,
And healing hands, life-long.

items.text: “Long did I sleep, my slumber was long, And long are the griefs of life; Othin decreed that I could not break The heavy spells of sleep.”
lines: “Long did I sleep, my slumber was long,
And long are the griefs of life;
Othin decreed that I could not break
The heavy spells of sleep.”

items.text: Her name was Sigrdrifa, and she was a Valkyrie. She said that two kings fought in battle; one was called Hjalmgunnar, an old man but a mighty warrior, and Othin had promised him the victory, and
The other was Agnar, brother of Autha, None he found who fain would shield him.
lines: The other was Agnar, brother of Autha,
None he found who fain would shield him.

items.text: Sigrdrifa slew Hjalmgunnar in the battle, and Othin pricked her with the sleep-thorn in punishment for this, and said that she should never thereafter win victory in battle, but that she should be wedded. “And I said to him that I had made a vow in my turn, that I would never marry a man who knew the meaning of fear.” Sigurth answered and asked her to teach him wisdom, if she knew of what took place in all the worlds. Sigrdrifa said:
“Beer I bring thee, tree of battle, Mingled of strength and mighty fame; Charms it holds and healing signs, Spells full good, and gladness-runes.”
lines: “Beer I bring thee, tree of battle,
Mingled of strength and mighty fame;
Charms it holds and healing signs,
Spells full good, and gladness-runes.”

items.text: Winning-runes learn, if thou longest to win, And the runes on thy sword-hilt write; Some on the furrow, and some on the flat, And twice shalt thou call on Tyr.
lines: Winning-runes learn, if thou longest to win,
And the runes on thy sword-hilt write;
Some on the furrow, and some on the flat,
And twice shalt thou call on Tyr.

items.text: Ale-runes learn, that with lies the wife Of another betray not thy trust; On the horn thou shalt write, and the backs of thy hands, And Need shalt mark on thy nails. Thou shalt bless the draught, and danger escape, And cast a leek in the cup; (For so I know thou never shalt see Thy mead with evil mixed.)
lines: Ale-runes learn, that with lies the wife
Of another betray not thy trust;
On the horn thou shalt write, and the backs of thy hands,
And Need shalt mark on thy nails.
Thou shalt bless the draught, and danger escape,
And cast a leek in the cup;
(For so I know thou never shalt see
Thy mead with evil mixed.)

items.text: Birth-runes learn, if help thou wilt lend, The babe from the mother to bring; On thy palms shalt write them, and round thy joints, And ask the fates to aid.
lines: Birth-runes learn, if help thou wilt lend,
The babe from the mother to bring;
On thy palms shalt write them, and round thy joints,
And ask the fates to aid.

items.text: Wave-runes learn, if well thou wouldst shelter The sail-steeds out on the sea; On the stem shalt thou write, and the steering-blade, And burn them into the oars; Though high be the breakers, and black the waves, Thou shalt safe the harbor seek.
lines: Wave-runes learn, if well thou wouldst shelter
The sail-steeds out on the sea;
On the stem shalt thou write, and the steering-blade,
And burn them into the oars;
Though high be the breakers, and black the waves,
Thou shalt safe the harbor seek.

items.text: Branch-runes learn, if a healer wouldst be, And cure for wounds wouldst work; On the bark shalt thou write, and on trees that be With boughs to the eastward bent.
lines: Branch-runes learn, if a healer wouldst be,
And cure for wounds wouldst work;
On the bark shalt thou write, and on trees that be
With boughs to the eastward bent.

items.text: Speech-runes learn, that none may seek To answer harm with hate; Well he winds and weaves them all, And sets them side by side, At the judgment-place, when justice there The folk shall fairly win.
lines: Speech-runes learn, that none may seek
To answer harm with hate;
Well he winds and weaves them all,
And sets them side by side,
At the judgment-place, when justice there
The folk shall fairly win.

items.text: Thought-runes learn, if all shall think Thou art keenest minded of men.
lines: Thought-runes learn, if all shall think
Thou art keenest minded of men.

items.text: Them Hropt arranged, and them he wrote, And them in thought he made, Out of the draught that down had dropped From the head of Heithdraupnir, And the horn of Hoddrofnir.
lines: Them Hropt arranged, and them he wrote,
And them in thought he made,
Out of the draught that down had dropped
From the head of Heithdraupnir,
And the horn of Hoddrofnir.

items.text: On the mountain he stood with Brimir’s sword, On his head the helm he bore; Then first the head of Mim spoke forth, And words of truth it told.
lines: On the mountain he stood with Brimir’s sword,
On his head the helm he bore;
Then first the head of Mim spoke forth,
And words of truth it told.

items.text: He bade write on the shield before the shining goddess, On Arvak’s ear, and on Alsvith’s hoof, On the wheel of the car of Hrungnir’s killer, On Sleipnir’s teeth, and the straps of the sledge.
lines: He bade write on the shield before the shining goddess,
On Arvak’s ear, and on Alsvith’s hoof,
On the wheel of the car of Hrungnir’s killer,
On Sleipnir’s teeth, and the straps of the sledge.

items.text: On the paws of the bear, and on Bragi’s tongue, On the wolf’s claws bared, and the eagle’s beak, On bloody wings, and bridge’s end, On freeing hands and helping foot-prints.
lines: On the paws of the bear, and on Bragi’s tongue,
On the wolf’s claws bared, and the eagle’s beak,
On bloody wings, and bridge’s end,
On freeing hands and helping foot-prints.

items.text: On glass and on gold, and on goodly charms, In wine and in beer, and on well-loved seats, On Gungnir’s point, and on Grani’s breast, On the nails of Norns, and the night-owl’s beak.
lines: On glass and on gold, and on goodly charms,
In wine and in beer, and on well-loved seats,
On Gungnir’s point, and on Grani’s breast,
On the nails of Norns, and the night-owl’s beak.

items.text: Shaved off were the runes that of old were written, And mixed with the holy mead, And sent on ways so wide; So the gods had them, so the elves got them, And some for the Wanes so wise, And some for mortal men.
lines: Shaved off were the runes that of old were written,
And mixed with the holy mead,
And sent on ways so wide;
So the gods had them, so the elves got them,
And some for the Wanes so wise,
And some for mortal men.

items.text: Beech-runes are there, birth-runes are there, And all the runes of ale, And the magic runes of might; Who knows them rightly and reads them true, Has them himself to help; Ever they aid, Till the gods are gone.
lines: Beech-runes are there, birth-runes are there,
And all the runes of ale,
And the magic runes of might;
Who knows them rightly and reads them true,
Has them himself to help;
Ever they aid,
Till the gods are gone.

items.text: Brynhild spake:
“Now shalt thou choose, for the choice is given, Thou tree of the biting blade; Speech or silence, ’tis thine to say, Our evil is destined all.”
lines: “Now shalt thou choose, for the choice is given,
Thou tree of the biting blade;
Speech or silence, ’tis thine to say,
Our evil is destined all.”

items.text: Sigurth spake:
“I shall not flee, though my fate be near, I was born not a coward to be; Thy loving word for mine will I win, As long as I shall live.”
lines: “I shall not flee, though my fate be near,
I was born not a coward to be;
Thy loving word for mine will I win,
As long as I shall live.”

items.text: Then first I rede thee, that free of guilt Toward kinsmen ever thou art; No vengeance have, though they work thee harm, Reward after death thou shalt win.
lines: Then first I rede thee, that free of guilt
Toward kinsmen ever thou art;
No vengeance have, though they work thee harm,
Reward after death thou shalt win.

items.text: Then second I rede thee, to swear no oath If true thou knowest it not; Bitter the fate of the breaker of troth, And poor is the wolf of his word.
lines: Then second I rede thee, to swear no oath
If true thou knowest it not;
Bitter the fate of the breaker of troth,
And poor is the wolf of his word.

items.text: Then third I rede thee, that thou at the Thing Shalt fight not in words with fools; For the man unwise a worser word Than he thinks doth utter oft.
lines: Then third I rede thee, that thou at the Thing
Shalt fight not in words with fools;
For the man unwise a worser word
Than he thinks doth utter oft.

items.text: Ill it is if silent thou art, A coward born men call thee, And truth mayhap they tell; Seldom safe is fame, Unless wide renown be won; On the day thereafter send him to death, Let him pay the price of his lies.
lines: Ill it is if silent thou art,
A coward born men call thee,
And truth mayhap they tell;
Seldom safe is fame,
Unless wide renown be won;
On the day thereafter send him to death,
Let him pay the price of his lies.

items.text: Then fourth I rede thee, if thou shalt find A wily witch on thy road, It is better to go than her guest to be, Though night enfold thee fast.
lines: Then fourth I rede thee, if thou shalt find
A wily witch on thy road,
It is better to go than her guest to be,
Though night enfold thee fast.

items.text: Eyes that see need the sons of men Who fight in battle fierce; Oft witches evil sit by the way, Who blade and courage blunt.
lines: Eyes that see need the sons of men
Who fight in battle fierce;
Oft witches evil sit by the way,
Who blade and courage blunt.

items.text: Then fifth I rede thee, though maidens fair Thou seest on benches sitting, Let the silver of kinship not rob thee of sleep, And the kissing of women beware.
lines: Then fifth I rede thee, though maidens fair
Thou seest on benches sitting,
Let the silver of kinship not rob thee of sleep,
And the kissing of women beware.

items.text: Then sixth I rede thee, if men shall wrangle, And ale-talk rise to wrath, No words with a drunken warrior have, For wine steals many men’s wits.
lines: Then sixth I rede thee, if men shall wrangle,
And ale-talk rise to wrath,
No words with a drunken warrior have,
For wine steals many men’s wits.

items.text: Brawls and ale full oft have been An ill to many a man, Death for some, and sorrow for some; Full many the woes of men.
lines: Brawls and ale full oft have been
An ill to many a man,
Death for some, and sorrow for some;
Full many the woes of men.

items.text: Then seventh I rede thee, if battle thou seekest With a foe that is full of might; It is better to fight than to burn alive In the hall of the hero rich.
lines: Then seventh I rede thee, if battle thou seekest
With a foe that is full of might;
It is better to fight than to burn alive
In the hall of the hero rich.

items.text: Then eighth I rede thee, that evil thou shun, And beware of lying words; Take not a maid, nor the wife of a man, Nor lure them on to lust.
lines: Then eighth I rede thee, that evil thou shun,
And beware of lying words;
Take not a maid, nor the wife of a man,
Nor lure them on to lust.

items.text: Then ninth I rede thee: burial render If thou findest a fallen corpse, Of sickness dead, or dead in the sea, Or dead of weapons’ wounds.
lines: Then ninth I rede thee: burial render
If thou findest a fallen corpse,
Of sickness dead, or dead in the sea,
Or dead of weapons’ wounds.

items.text: A bath shalt thou give them who corpses be, And hands and head shalt wash; Wipe them and comb, ere they go in the coffin, And pray that they sleep in peace.
lines: A bath shalt thou give them who corpses be,
And hands and head shalt wash;
Wipe them and comb, ere they go in the coffin,
And pray that they sleep in peace.

items.text: Then tenth I rede thee, that never thou trust The word of the race of wolves, (If his brother thou broughtest to death, Or his father thou didst fell;) Often a wolf in a son there is, Though gold he gladly takes.
lines: Then tenth I rede thee, that never thou trust
The word of the race of wolves,
(If his brother thou broughtest to death,
Or his father thou didst fell;)
Often a wolf in a son there is,
Though gold he gladly takes.

items.text: Battle and hate and harm, methinks, Full seldom fall asleep; Wits and weapons the warrior needs If boldest of men he would be.
lines: Battle and hate and harm, methinks,
Full seldom fall asleep;
Wits and weapons the warrior needs
If boldest of men he would be.

items.text: Then eleventh I rede thee, that wrath thou shun, And treachery false with thy friends; Not long the leader’s life shall be, For great are the foes he faces.
lines: Then eleventh I rede thee, that wrath thou shun,
And treachery false with thy friends;
Not long the leader’s life shall be,
For great are the foes he faces.

items.text: Hogni spake:
“(What evil deed has Sigurth) done, That the hero’s life thou fain wouldst have?”
lines: “(What evil deed has Sigurth) done,
That the hero’s life thou fain wouldst have?”

items.text: Gunnar spake:
“Sigurth oaths to me hath sworn, Oaths hath sworn, and all hath broken; He betrayed me there where truest all His oaths, methinks, he ought to have kept.”
lines: “Sigurth oaths to me hath sworn,
Oaths hath sworn, and all hath broken;
He betrayed me there where truest all
His oaths, methinks, he ought to have kept.”

items.text: Hogni spake:
“Thy heart hath Brynhild whetted to hate, Evil to work and harm to win; She grudges the honor that Guthrun has, And that joy of herself thou still dost have.”
lines: “Thy heart hath Brynhild whetted to hate,
Evil to work and harm to win;
She grudges the honor that Guthrun has,
And that joy of herself thou still dost have.”

items.text: They cooked a wolf, they cut up a snake, They gave to Gotthorm the greedy one’s flesh, Before the men, to murder minded, Laid their hands on the hero bold.
lines: They cooked a wolf, they cut up a snake,
They gave to Gotthorm the greedy one’s flesh,
Before the men, to murder minded,
Laid their hands on the hero bold.

items.text: Slain was Sigurth south of the Rhine; From a limb a raven called full loud: “Your blood shall redden Atli’s blade, And your oaths shall bind you both in chains.”
lines: Slain was Sigurth south of the Rhine;
From a limb a raven called full loud:
“Your blood shall redden Atli’s blade,
And your oaths shall bind you both in chains.”

items.text: Without stood Guthrun, Gjuki’s daughter, Hear now the speech that first she spake: “Where is Sigurth now, the noble king, That my kinsmen riding before him come?”
lines: Without stood Guthrun, Gjuki’s daughter,
Hear now the speech that first she spake:
“Where is Sigurth now, the noble king,
That my kinsmen riding before him come?”

items.text: Only this did Hogni answer: “Sigurth we with our swords have slain; The gray horse mourns by his master dead.”
lines: Only this did Hogni answer:
“Sigurth we with our swords have slain;
The gray horse mourns by his master dead.”

items.text: Then Brynhild spake, the daughter of Buthli: “Well shall ye joy in weapons and lands; Sigurth alone of all had been lord, If a little longer his life had been.
lines: Then Brynhild spake, the daughter of Buthli:
“Well shall ye joy in weapons and lands;
Sigurth alone of all had been lord,
If a little longer his life had been.

items.text: “Right were it not that so he should rule O’er Gjuki’s wealth and the race of the Goths; Five are the sons for ruling the folk, And greedy of fight, that he hath fathered.”
lines: “Right were it not that so he should rule
O’er Gjuki’s wealth and the race of the Goths;
Five are the sons for ruling the folk,
And greedy of fight, that he hath fathered.”

items.text: Then Brynhild laughed— and the building echoed— Only once, with all her heart; “Long shall ye joy in lands and men, Now ye have slain the hero noble.”
lines: Then Brynhild laughed— and the building echoed—
Only once, with all her heart;
“Long shall ye joy in lands and men,
Now ye have slain the hero noble.”

items.text: Then Guthrun spake, the daughter of Gjuki: “Much thou speakest in evil speech; Accursed be Gunnar, Sigurth’s killer, Vengeance shall come for his cruel heart.”
lines: Then Guthrun spake, the daughter of Gjuki:
“Much thou speakest in evil speech;
Accursed be Gunnar, Sigurth’s killer,
Vengeance shall come for his cruel heart.”

items.text: Early came evening, and ale was drunk, And among them long and loud they talked; They slumbered all when their beds they sought, But Gunnar alone was long awake.
lines: Early came evening, and ale was drunk,
And among them long and loud they talked;
They slumbered all when their beds they sought,
But Gunnar alone was long awake.

items.text: His feet were tossing, he talked to himself, And the slayer of hosts began to heed What the twain from the tree had told him then, The raven and eagle, as home they rode.
lines: His feet were tossing, he talked to himself,
And the slayer of hosts began to heed
What the twain from the tree had told him then,
The raven and eagle, as home they rode.

items.text: Brynhild awoke, the daughter of Buthli, The warrior’s daughter, ere dawn of day: “Love me or hate me, the harm is done, And my grief cries out, or else I die.”
lines: Brynhild awoke, the daughter of Buthli,
The warrior’s daughter, ere dawn of day:
“Love me or hate me, the harm is done,
And my grief cries out, or else I die.”

items.text: Silent were all who heard her speak, And nought of the heart of the queen they knew, Who wept such tears the thing to tell That laughing once of the men she had won.
lines: Silent were all who heard her speak,
And nought of the heart of the queen they knew,
Who wept such tears the thing to tell
That laughing once of the men she had won.

items.text: Brynhild spake:
“Gunnar, I dreamed a dream full grim: In the hall were corpses; cold was my bed; And, ruler, thou didst joyless ride, With fetters bound in the foemen’s throng.
lines: “Gunnar, I dreamed a dream full grim:
In the hall were corpses; cold was my bed;
And, ruler, thou didst joyless ride,
With fetters bound in the foemen’s throng.

items.text: “. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Utterly now your Niflung race All shall die; your oaths ye have broken.
lines: Utterly now your Niflung race
All shall die; your oaths ye have broken.

items.text: “Thou hast, Gunnar, the deed forgot, When blood in your footprints both ye mingled; All to him hast repaid with ill Who fain had made thee the foremost of kings.
lines: “Thou hast, Gunnar, the deed forgot,
When blood in your footprints both ye mingled;
All to him hast repaid with ill
Who fain had made thee the foremost of kings.

items.text: “Well did he prove, when proud he rode To win me then thy wife to be, How true the host-slayer ever had held The oaths he had made with the monarch young.
lines: “Well did he prove, when proud he rode
To win me then thy wife to be,
How true the host-slayer ever had held
The oaths he had made with the monarch young.

items.text: “The wound-staff then, all wound with gold, The hero let between us lie; With fire the edge was forged full keen, And with drops of venom the blade was damp.”
lines: “The wound-staff then, all wound with gold,
The hero let between us lie;
With fire the edge was forged full keen,
And with drops of venom the blade was damp.”

items.text: Here it is told in this poem about the death of Sigurth, and the story goes here that they slew him out of doors, but some say that they slew him in the house, on his bed while he was sleeping. But German men say that they killed him out of doors in the forest; and so it is told in the old Guthrun lay, that Sigurth and Gjuki’s sons had ridden to the council-place, and that he was slain there. But in this they are all agreed, that they deceived him in his trust of them, and fell upon him when he was lying down and unprepared.

Guthrun sat by the dead Sigurth; she did not weep as other women, but her heart was near to bursting with grief. The men and women came to her to console her, but that was not easy to do. It is told of men that Guthrun had eaten of Fafnir’s heart, and that she understood the speech of birds. This is a poem about Guthrun.
Then did Guthrun think to die, When she by Sigurth sorrowing sat; Tears she had not, nor wrung her hands, Nor ever wailed, as other women.
lines: Then did Guthrun think to die,
When she by Sigurth sorrowing sat;
Tears she had not, nor wrung her hands,
Nor ever wailed, as other women.

items.text: To her the warriors wise there came, Longing her heavy woe to lighten; Grieving could not Guthrun weep, So sad her heart, it seemed, would break.
lines: To her the warriors wise there came,
Longing her heavy woe to lighten;
Grieving could not Guthrun weep,
So sad her heart, it seemed, would break.

items.text: Then the wives of the warriors came, Gold-adorned, and Guthrun sought; Each one then of her own grief spoke, The bitterest pain she had ever borne.
lines: Then the wives of the warriors came,
Gold-adorned, and Guthrun sought;
Each one then of her own grief spoke,
The bitterest pain she had ever borne.

items.text: Then spake Gjaflaug, Gjuki’s sister: “Most joyless of all on earth am I; Husbands five were from me taken, (Two daughters then, and sisters three,) Brothers eight, yet I have lived.”
lines: Then spake Gjaflaug, Gjuki’s sister:
“Most joyless of all on earth am I;
Husbands five were from me taken,
(Two daughters then, and sisters three,)
Brothers eight, yet I have lived.”

items.text: Grieving could not Guthrun weep, Such grief she had for her husband dead, And so grim her heart by the hero’s body.
lines: Grieving could not Guthrun weep,
Such grief she had for her husband dead,
And so grim her heart by the hero’s body.

items.text: Then Herborg spake, the queen of the Huns: “I have a greater grief to tell; My seven sons in the southern land, And my husband, fell in fight all eight. (Father and mother and brothers four Amid the waves the wind once smote, And the seas crashed through the sides of the ship.)
lines: Then Herborg spake, the queen of the Huns:
“I have a greater grief to tell;
My seven sons in the southern land,
And my husband, fell in fight all eight.
(Father and mother and brothers four
Amid the waves the wind once smote,
And the seas crashed through the sides of the ship.)

items.text: “The bodies all with my own hands then I decked for the grave, and the dead I buried; A half-year brought me this to bear; And no one came to comfort me.
lines: “The bodies all with my own hands then
I decked for the grave, and the dead I buried;
A half-year brought me this to bear;
And no one came to comfort me.

items.text: “Then bound I was, and taken in war, A sorrow yet in the same half-year; They bade me deck and bind the shoes Of the wife of the monarch every morn.
lines: “Then bound I was, and taken in war,
A sorrow yet in the same half-year;
They bade me deck and bind the shoes
Of the wife of the monarch every morn.

items.text: “In jealous rage her wrath she spake, And beat me oft with heavy blows; Never a better lord I knew, And never a woman worse I found.”
lines: “In jealous rage her wrath she spake,
And beat me oft with heavy blows;
Never a better lord I knew,
And never a woman worse I found.”

items.text: Grieving could not Guthrun weep, Such grief she had for her husband dead, And so grim her heart by the hero’s body.
lines: Grieving could not Guthrun weep,
Such grief she had for her husband dead,
And so grim her heart by the hero’s body.

items.text: Then spake Gollrond, Gjuki’s daughter: “Thy wisdom finds not, my foster-mother, The way to comfort the wife so young.” She bade them uncover the warrior’s corpse.
lines: Then spake Gollrond, Gjuki’s daughter:
“Thy wisdom finds not, my foster-mother,
The way to comfort the wife so young.”
She bade them uncover the warrior’s corpse.

items.text: The shroud she lifted from Sigurth, laying His well-loved head on the knees of his wife: “Look on thy loved one, and lay thy lips To his as if yet the hero lived.”
lines: The shroud she lifted from Sigurth, laying
His well-loved head on the knees of his wife:
“Look on thy loved one, and lay thy lips
To his as if yet the hero lived.”

items.text: Once alone did Guthrun look; His hair all clotted with blood beheld, The blinded eyes that once shone bright, The hero’s breast that the blade had pierced.
lines: Once alone did Guthrun look;
His hair all clotted with blood beheld,
The blinded eyes that once shone bright,
The hero’s breast that the blade had pierced.

items.text: Then Guthrun bent, on her pillow bowed, Her hair was loosened, her cheek was hot, And the tears like raindrops downward ran.
lines: Then Guthrun bent, on her pillow bowed,
Her hair was loosened, her cheek was hot,
And the tears like raindrops downward ran.

items.text: Then Guthrun, daughter of Gjuki, wept, And through her tresses flowed the tears; And from the court came the cry of geese, The birds so fair of the hero’s bride.
lines: Then Guthrun, daughter of Gjuki, wept,
And through her tresses flowed the tears;
And from the court came the cry of geese,
The birds so fair of the hero’s bride.

items.text: Then Gollrond spake, the daughter of Gjuki: “Never a greater love I knew Than yours among all men on earth; Nowhere wast happy, at home or abroad, Sister mine, with Sigurth away.”
lines: Then Gollrond spake, the daughter of Gjuki:
“Never a greater love I knew
Than yours among all men on earth;
Nowhere wast happy, at home or abroad,
Sister mine, with Sigurth away.”

items.text: Guthrun spake:
“So was my Sigurth o’er Gjuki’s sons As the spear-leek grown above the grass, Or the jewel bright borne on the band, The precious stone that princes wear.
lines: “So was my Sigurth o’er Gjuki’s sons
As the spear-leek grown above the grass,
Or the jewel bright borne on the band,
The precious stone that princes wear.

items.text: “To the leader of men I loftier seemed And higher than all of Herjan’s maids; As little now as the leaf I am On the willow hanging; my hero is dead.
lines: “To the leader of men I loftier seemed
And higher than all of Herjan’s maids;
As little now as the leaf I am
On the willow hanging; my hero is dead.

items.text: “In his seat, in his bed, I see no more My heart’s true friend; the fault is theirs, The sons of Gjuki, for all my grief, That so their sister sorely weeps.
lines: “In his seat, in his bed, I see no more
My heart’s true friend; the fault is theirs,
The sons of Gjuki, for all my grief,
That so their sister sorely weeps.

items.text: “So shall your land its people lose As ye have kept your oaths of yore; Gunnar, no joy the gold shall give thee, (The rings shall soon thy slayers be,) Who swarest oaths with Sigurth once.
lines: “So shall your land its people lose
As ye have kept your oaths of yore;
Gunnar, no joy the gold shall give thee,
(The rings shall soon thy slayers be,)
Who swarest oaths with Sigurth once.

items.text: “In the court was greater gladness then The day my Sigurth Grani saddled, And went forth Brynhild’s hand to win, That woman ill, in an evil hour.”
lines: “In the court was greater gladness then
The day my Sigurth Grani saddled,
And went forth Brynhild’s hand to win,
That woman ill, in an evil hour.”

items.text: Then Brynhild spake, the daughter of Buthli: “May the witch now husband and children want Who, Guthrun, loosed thy tears at last, And with magic today hath made thee speak.”
lines: Then Brynhild spake, the daughter of Buthli:
“May the witch now husband and children want
Who, Guthrun, loosed thy tears at last,
And with magic today hath made thee speak.”

items.text: Then Gollrond, daughter of Gjuki, spake: “Speak not such words, thou hated woman; Bane of the noble thou e’er hast been, (Borne thou art on an evil wave, Sorrow hast brought to seven kings,) And many a woman hast loveless made.”
lines: Then Gollrond, daughter of Gjuki, spake:
“Speak not such words, thou hated woman;
Bane of the noble thou e’er hast been,
(Borne thou art on an evil wave,
Sorrow hast brought to seven kings,)
And many a woman hast loveless made.”

items.text: Then Brynhild, daughter of Buthli, spake: “Atli is guilty of all the sorrow, (Son of Buthli and brother of mine,) When we saw in the hall of the Hunnish race The flame of the snake’s bed flash round the hero; (For the journey since full sore have I paid, And ever I seek the sight to forget.)”
lines: Then Brynhild, daughter of Buthli, spake:
“Atli is guilty of all the sorrow,
(Son of Buthli and brother of mine,)
When we saw in the hall of the Hunnish race
The flame of the snake’s bed flash round the hero;
(For the journey since full sore have I paid,
And ever I seek the sight to forget.)”

items.text: By the pillars she stood, and gathered her strength, From the eyes of Brynhild, Buthli’s daughter, Fire there burned, and venom she breathed, When the wounds she saw on Sigurth then.
lines: By the pillars she stood, and gathered her strength,
From the eyes of Brynhild, Buthli’s daughter,
Fire there burned, and venom she breathed,
When the wounds she saw on Sigurth then.

items.text: Guthrun went thence away to a forest in the waste, and journeyed all the way to Denmark, and was there seven half-years with Thora, daughter of Hokon. Brynhild would not live after Sigurth. She had eight of her thralls slain and five serving-women. Then she killed herself with a sword, as is told in the Short Lay of Sigurth.
Of old did Sigurth Gjuki seek, The Volsung young, in battles victor; Well he trusted the brothers twain, With mighty oaths among them sworn.
lines: Of old did Sigurth Gjuki seek,
The Volsung young, in battles victor;
Well he trusted the brothers twain,
With mighty oaths among them sworn.

items.text: A maid they gave him, and jewels many, Guthrun the young, the daughter of Gjuki; They drank and spake full many a day, Sigurth the young and Gjuki’s sons.
lines: A maid they gave him, and jewels many,
Guthrun the young, the daughter of Gjuki;
They drank and spake full many a day,
Sigurth the young and Gjuki’s sons.

items.text: Thereafter went they Brynhild to woo, And so with them did Sigurth ride, The Volsung young, in battle valiant,— Himself would have had her if all he had seen.
lines: Thereafter went they Brynhild to woo,
And so with them did Sigurth ride,
The Volsung young, in battle valiant,—
Himself would have had her if all he had seen.

items.text: The southern hero his naked sword, Fair-flashing, let between them lie; (Nor would he come the maid to kiss;) The Hunnish king in his arms ne’er held The maiden he gave to Gjuki’s sons.
lines: The southern hero his naked sword,
Fair-flashing, let between them lie;
(Nor would he come the maid to kiss;)
The Hunnish king in his arms ne’er held
The maiden he gave to Gjuki’s sons.

items.text: Ill she had known not in all her life, And nought of the sorrows of men she knew; Blame she had not, nor dreamed she should bear it, But cruel the fates that among them came.
lines: Ill she had known not in all her life,
And nought of the sorrows of men she knew;
Blame she had not, nor dreamed she should bear it,
But cruel the fates that among them came.

items.text: By herself at the end of day she sat, And in open words her heart she uttered: “I shall Sigurth have, the hero young, E’en though within my arms he die.
lines: By herself at the end of day she sat,
And in open words her heart she uttered:
“I shall Sigurth have, the hero young,
E’en though within my arms he die.

items.text: “The word I have spoken; soon shall I rue it, His wife is Guthrun, and Gunnar’s am I; Ill Norns set for me long desire.”
lines: “The word I have spoken; soon shall I rue it,
His wife is Guthrun, and Gunnar’s am I;
Ill Norns set for me long desire.”

items.text: Oft did she go with grieving heart On the glacier’s ice at even-tide, When Guthrun then to her bed was gone, And the bedclothes Sigurth about her laid.
lines: Oft did she go with grieving heart
On the glacier’s ice at even-tide,
When Guthrun then to her bed was gone,
And the bedclothes Sigurth about her laid.

items.text: “(Now Gjuki’s child to her lover goes,) And the Hunnish king with his wife is happy; Joyless I am and mateless ever, Till cries from my heavy heart burst forth.”
lines: “(Now Gjuki’s child to her lover goes,)
And the Hunnish king with his wife is happy;
Joyless I am and mateless ever,
Till cries from my heavy heart burst forth.”

items.text: In her wrath to battle she roused herself: “Gunnar, now thou needs must lose Lands of mine and me myself, No joy shall I have with the hero ever.
lines: In her wrath to battle she roused herself:
“Gunnar, now thou needs must lose
Lands of mine and me myself,
No joy shall I have with the hero ever.

items.text: “Back shall I fare where first I dwelt, Among the kin that come of my race, To wait there, sleeping my life away, If Sigurth’s death thou shalt not dare, (And best of heroes thou shalt not be.)
lines: “Back shall I fare where first I dwelt,
Among the kin that come of my race,
To wait there, sleeping my life away,
If Sigurth’s death thou shalt not dare,
(And best of heroes thou shalt not be.)

items.text: “The son shall fare with his father hence, And let not long the wolf-cub live; Lighter to pay is the vengeance-price After the deed if the son is dead.”
lines: “The son shall fare with his father hence,
And let not long the wolf-cub live;
Lighter to pay is the vengeance-price
After the deed if the son is dead.”

items.text: Sad was Gunnar, and bowed with grief, Deep in thought the whole day through; Yet from his heart it was ever hid What deed most fitting he should find, (Or what thing best for him should be, Or if he should seek the Volsung to slay, For with mighty longing Sigurth he loved.)
lines: Sad was Gunnar, and bowed with grief,
Deep in thought the whole day through;
Yet from his heart it was ever hid
What deed most fitting he should find,
(Or what thing best for him should be,
Or if he should seek the Volsung to slay,
For with mighty longing Sigurth he loved.)

items.text: Much he pondered for many an hour; Never before was the wonder known That a queen should thus her kingdom leave; In counsel then did he Hogni call, (For him in truest trust he held.)
lines: Much he pondered for many an hour;
Never before was the wonder known
That a queen should thus her kingdom leave;
In counsel then did he Hogni call,
(For him in truest trust he held.)

items.text: “More than all to me is Brynhild, Buthli’s child, the best of women; My very life would I sooner lose Than yield the love of yonder maid.
lines: “More than all to me is Brynhild,
Buthli’s child, the best of women;
My very life would I sooner lose
Than yield the love of yonder maid.

items.text: “Wilt thou the hero for wealth betray? ’Twere good to have the gold of the Rhine, And all the hoard in peace to hold, And waiting fortune thus to win.”
lines: “Wilt thou the hero for wealth betray?
’Twere good to have the gold of the Rhine,
And all the hoard in peace to hold,
And waiting fortune thus to win.”

items.text: Few the words of Hogni were: “Us it beseems not so to do, To cleave with swords the oaths we swore, The oaths we swore and all our vows.
lines: Few the words of Hogni were:
“Us it beseems not so to do,
To cleave with swords the oaths we swore,
The oaths we swore and all our vows.

items.text: “We know no mightier men on earth The while we four o’er the folk hold sway, And while the Hunnish hero lives, Nor higher kinship the world doth hold.
lines: “We know no mightier men on earth
The while we four o’er the folk hold sway,
And while the Hunnish hero lives,
Nor higher kinship the world doth hold.

items.text: “If sons we five shall soon beget, Great, methinks, our race shall grow; Well I see whence lead the ways; Too bitter far is Brynhild’s hate.”
lines: “If sons we five shall soon beget,
Great, methinks, our race shall grow;
Well I see whence lead the ways;
Too bitter far is Brynhild’s hate.”

items.text: Gunnar spake:
“Gotthorm to wrath we needs must rouse, Our younger brother, in rashness blind; He entered not in the oaths we swore, The oaths we swore and all our vows.”
lines: “Gotthorm to wrath we needs must rouse,
Our younger brother, in rashness blind;
He entered not in the oaths we swore,
The oaths we swore and all our vows.”

items.text: It was easy to rouse the reckless one. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . The sword in the heart of Sigurth stood.
lines: It was easy to rouse the reckless one.
The sword in the heart of Sigurth stood.

items.text: In vengeance the hero rose in the hall, And hurled his sword at the slayer bold; At Gotthorm flew the glittering steel Of Gram full hard from the hand of the king.
lines: In vengeance the hero rose in the hall,
And hurled his sword at the slayer bold;
At Gotthorm flew the glittering steel
Of Gram full hard from the hand of the king.

items.text: The foeman cleft asunder fell, Forward hands and head did sink, And legs and feet did backward fall.
lines: The foeman cleft asunder fell,
Forward hands and head did sink,
And legs and feet did backward fall.

items.text: Guthrun soft in her bed had slept, Safe from care at Sigurth’s side; She woke to find her joy had fled, In the blood of the friend of Freyr she lay.
lines: Guthrun soft in her bed had slept,
Safe from care at Sigurth’s side;
She woke to find her joy had fled,
In the blood of the friend of Freyr she lay.

items.text: So hard she smote her hands together That the hero rose up, iron-hearted: “Weep not, Guthrun, grievous tears, Bride so young, for thy brothers live.
lines: So hard she smote her hands together
That the hero rose up, iron-hearted:
“Weep not, Guthrun, grievous tears,
Bride so young, for thy brothers live.

items.text: “Too young, methinks, is my son as yet, He cannot flee from the home of his foes; Fearful and deadly the plan they found, The counsel new that now they have heeded.
lines: “Too young, methinks, is my son as yet,
He cannot flee from the home of his foes;
Fearful and deadly the plan they found,
The counsel new that now they have heeded.

items.text: “No son will ride, though seven thou hast, To the Thing as the son of their sister rides; Well I see who the ill has worked, On Brynhild alone lies the blame for all.
lines: “No son will ride, though seven thou hast,
To the Thing as the son of their sister rides;
Well I see who the ill has worked,
On Brynhild alone lies the blame for all.

items.text: “Above all men the maiden loved me, Yet false to Gunnar I ne’er was found; I kept the oaths and the kinship I swore; Of his queen the lover none may call me.”
lines: “Above all men the maiden loved me,
Yet false to Gunnar I ne’er was found;
I kept the oaths and the kinship I swore;
Of his queen the lover none may call me.”

items.text: In a swoon she sank when Sigurth died; So hard she smote her hands together That all the cups in the cupboard rang, And loud in the courtyard cried the geese.
lines: In a swoon she sank when Sigurth died;
So hard she smote her hands together
That all the cups in the cupboard rang,
And loud in the courtyard cried the geese.

items.text: Then Brynhild, daughter of Buthli, laughed, Only once, with all her heart, When as she lay full loud she heard The grievous wail of Gjuki’s daughter.
lines: Then Brynhild, daughter of Buthli, laughed,
Only once, with all her heart,
When as she lay full loud she heard
The grievous wail of Gjuki’s daughter.

items.text: Then Gunnar, monarch of men, spake forth: “Thou dost not laugh, thou lover of hate, In gladness there, or for aught of good; Why has thy face so white a hue, Mother of ill? Foredoomed thou art.
lines: Then Gunnar, monarch of men, spake forth:
“Thou dost not laugh, thou lover of hate,
In gladness there, or for aught of good;
Why has thy face so white a hue,
Mother of ill? Foredoomed thou art.

items.text: “A worthier woman wouldst thou have been If before thine eyes we had Atli slain; If thy brother’s bleeding body hadst seen And the bloody wounds that thou shouldst bind.”
lines: “A worthier woman wouldst thou have been
If before thine eyes we had Atli slain;
If thy brother’s bleeding body hadst seen
And the bloody wounds that thou shouldst bind.”

items.text: Brynhild spake:
“None mock thee, Gunnar! thou hast mightily fought, But thy hatred little doth Atli heed; Longer than thou, methinks, shall he live, And greater in might shall he ever remain.
lines: “None mock thee, Gunnar! thou hast mightily fought,
But thy hatred little doth Atli heed;
Longer than thou, methinks, shall he live,
And greater in might shall he ever remain.

items.text: “To thee I say, and thyself thou knowest, That all these ills thou didst early shape; No bonds I knew, nor sorrow bore, And wealth I had in my brother’s home.
lines: “To thee I say, and thyself thou knowest,
That all these ills thou didst early shape;
No bonds I knew, nor sorrow bore,
And wealth I had in my brother’s home.

items.text: “Never a husband sought I to have, Before the Gjukungs fared to our land; Three were the kings on steeds that came,— Need of their journey never there was.
lines: “Never a husband sought I to have,
Before the Gjukungs fared to our land;
Three were the kings on steeds that came,—
Need of their journey never there was.

items.text: “To the hero great my troth I gave Who gold-decked sat on Grani’s back; Not like to thine was the light of his eyes, (Nor like in form and face are ye,) Though kingly both ye seemed to be.
lines: “To the hero great my troth I gave
Who gold-decked sat on Grani’s back;
Not like to thine was the light of his eyes,
(Nor like in form and face are ye,)
Though kingly both ye seemed to be.

items.text: “And so to me did Atli say That share in our wealth I should not have, Of gold or lands, if my hand I gave not; (More evil yet, the wealth I should yield,) The gold that he in my childhood gave me, (The wealth from him in my youth I had.)
lines: “And so to me did Atli say
That share in our wealth I should not have,
Of gold or lands, if my hand I gave not;
(More evil yet, the wealth I should yield,)
The gold that he in my childhood gave me,
(The wealth from him in my youth I had.)

items.text: “Oft in my mind I pondered much If still I should fight, and warriors fell, Brave in my byrnie, my brother defying; That would wide in the world be known, And sorrow for many a man would make.
lines: “Oft in my mind I pondered much
If still I should fight, and warriors fell,
Brave in my byrnie, my brother defying;
That would wide in the world be known,
And sorrow for many a man would make.

items.text: “But the bond at last I let be made, For more the hoard I longed to have, The rings that the son of Sigmund won; No other’s treasure e’er I sought.
lines: “But the bond at last I let be made,
For more the hoard I longed to have,
The rings that the son of Sigmund won;
No other’s treasure e’er I sought.

items.text: “One alone of all I loved, Nor changing heart I ever had; All in the end shall Atli know, When he hears I have gone on the death-road hence.”
lines: “One alone of all I loved,
Nor changing heart I ever had;
All in the end shall Atli know,
When he hears I have gone on the death-road hence.”

items.text: “Never a wife of fickle will Yet to another man should yield. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . So vengeance for all my ills shall come.”
lines: “Never a wife of fickle will
Yet to another man should yield.
So vengeance for all my ills shall come.”

items.text: Up rose Gunnar, the people’s ruler, And flung his arms round her neck so fair; And all who came, of every kind, Sought to hold her with all their hearts.
lines: Up rose Gunnar, the people’s ruler,
And flung his arms round her neck so fair;
And all who came, of every kind,
Sought to hold her with all their hearts.

items.text: But back she cast all those who came, Nor from the long road let them hold her; In counsel then did he Hogni call: “Of wisdom now full great is our need.
lines: But back she cast all those who came,
Nor from the long road let them hold her;
In counsel then did he Hogni call:
“Of wisdom now full great is our need.

items.text: “Let the warriors here in the hall come forth, Thine and mine, for the need is mighty, If haply the queen from death they may hold, Till her fearful thoughts with time shall fade.”
lines: “Let the warriors here in the hall come forth,
Thine and mine, for the need is mighty,
If haply the queen from death they may hold,
Till her fearful thoughts with time shall fade.”

items.text: (Few the words of Hogni were:) “From the long road now shall ye hold her not, That born again she may never be! Foul she came from her mother forth, And born she was for wicked deeds, (Sorrow to many a man to bring.)”
lines: (Few the words of Hogni were:)
“From the long road now shall ye hold her not,
That born again she may never be!
Foul she came from her mother forth,
And born she was for wicked deeds,
(Sorrow to many a man to bring.)”

items.text: From the speaker gloomily Gunnar turned, For the jewel-bearer her gems was dividing; On all her wealth her eyes were gazing, On the bond-women slain and the slaughtered slaves.
lines: From the speaker gloomily Gunnar turned,
For the jewel-bearer her gems was dividing;
On all her wealth her eyes were gazing,
On the bond-women slain and the slaughtered slaves.

items.text: Her byrnie of gold she donned, and grim Was her heart ere the point of her sword had pierced it; On the pillow at last her head she laid, And, wounded, her plan she pondered o’er.
lines: Her byrnie of gold she donned, and grim
Was her heart ere the point of her sword had pierced it;
On the pillow at last her head she laid,
And, wounded, her plan she pondered o’er.

items.text: “Hither I will that my women come Who gold are fain from me to get; Necklaces fashioned fair to each Shall I give, and cloth, and garments bright.”
lines: “Hither I will that my women come
Who gold are fain from me to get;
Necklaces fashioned fair to each
Shall I give, and cloth, and garments bright.”

items.text: Silent were all as so she spake, And all together answer made: “Slain are enough; we seek to live, Not thus thy women shall honor win.”
lines: Silent were all as so she spake,
And all together answer made:
“Slain are enough; we seek to live,
Not thus thy women shall honor win.”

items.text: Long the woman, linen-decked, pondered,— —Young she was,— and weighed her words: “For my sake now shall none unwilling Or loath to die her life lay down.
lines: Long the woman, linen-decked, pondered,—
—Young she was,— and weighed her words:
“For my sake now shall none unwilling
Or loath to die her life lay down.

items.text: “But little of gems to gleam on your limbs Ye then shall find when forth ye fare To follow me, or of Menja’s wealth. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: “But little of gems to gleam on your limbs
Ye then shall find when forth ye fare
To follow me, or of Menja’s wealth.

items.text: “Sit now, Gunnar! for I shall speak Of thy bride so fair and so fain to die; Thy ship in harbor home thou hast not, Although my life I now have lost.
lines: “Sit now, Gunnar! for I shall speak
Of thy bride so fair and so fain to die;
Thy ship in harbor home thou hast not,
Although my life I now have lost.

items.text: “Thou shalt Guthrun requite more quick than thou thinkest, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Though sadly mourns the maiden wise Who dwells with the king, o’er her husband dead.
lines: “Thou shalt Guthrun requite more quick than thou
thinkest,
Though sadly mourns the maiden wise
Who dwells with the king, o’er her husband dead.

items.text: “A maid shall then the mother bear; Brighter far than the fairest day Svanhild shall be, or the beams of the sun.
lines: “A maid shall then the mother bear;
Brighter far than the fairest day
Svanhild shall be, or the beams of the sun.

items.text: “Guthrun a noble husband thou givest, Yet to many a warrior woe will she bring, Not happily wedded she holds herself; Her shall Atli hither seek, (Buthli’s son, and brother of mine.)
lines: “Guthrun a noble husband thou givest,
Yet to many a warrior woe will she bring,
Not happily wedded she holds herself;
Her shall Atli hither seek,
(Buthli’s son, and brother of mine.)

items.text: “Well I remember how me ye treated When ye betrayed me with treacherous wiles; . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Lost was my joy as long as I lived.
lines: “Well I remember how me ye treated
When ye betrayed me with treacherous wiles;
Lost was my joy as long as I lived.

items.text: “Oddrun as wife thou fain wouldst win, But Atli this from thee withholds; Yet in secret tryst ye twain shall love; She shall hold thee dear, as I had done If kindly fate to us had fallen.
lines: “Oddrun as wife thou fain wouldst win,
But Atli this from thee withholds;
Yet in secret tryst ye twain shall love;
She shall hold thee dear, as I had done
If kindly fate to us had fallen.

items.text: “Ill to thee shall Atli bring, When he casts thee down in the den of snakes.
lines: “Ill to thee shall Atli bring,
When he casts thee down in the den of snakes.

items.text: “But soon thereafter Atli too His life, methinks, as thou shalt lose, (His fortune lose and the lives of his sons;) Him shall Guthrun, grim of heart, With the biting blade in his bed destroy.
lines: “But soon thereafter Atli too
His life, methinks, as thou shalt lose,
(His fortune lose and the lives of his sons;)
Him shall Guthrun, grim of heart,
With the biting blade in his bed destroy.

items.text: “It would better beseem thy sister fair To follow her husband first in death, If counsel good to her were given, Or a heart akin to mine she had.
lines: “It would better beseem thy sister fair
To follow her husband first in death,
If counsel good to her were given,
Or a heart akin to mine she had.

items.text: “Slowly I speak,— but for my sake Her life, methinks, she shall not lose; She shall wander over the tossing waves, To where Jonak rules his father’s realm.
lines: “Slowly I speak,— but for my sake
Her life, methinks, she shall not lose;
She shall wander over the tossing waves,
To where Jonak rules his father’s realm.

items.text: “Sons to him she soon shall bear, Heirs therewith of Jonak’s wealth; But Svanhild far away is sent, The child she bore to Sigurth brave.
lines: “Sons to him she soon shall bear,
Heirs therewith of Jonak’s wealth;
But Svanhild far away is sent,
The child she bore to Sigurth brave.

items.text: “Bikki’s word her death shall be, For dreadful the wrath of Jormunrek; So slain is all of Sigurth’s race, And greater the woe of Guthrun grows.
lines: “Bikki’s word her death shall be,
For dreadful the wrath of Jormunrek;
So slain is all of Sigurth’s race,
And greater the woe of Guthrun grows.

items.text: “Yet one boon I beg of thee, The last of boons in my life it is: Let the pyre be built so broad in the field That room for us all will ample be, (For us who slain with Sigurth are.)
lines: “Yet one boon I beg of thee,
The last of boons in my life it is:
Let the pyre be built so broad in the field
That room for us all will ample be,
(For us who slain with Sigurth are.)

items.text: “With shields and carpets cover the pyre, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Shrouds full fair, and fallen slaves, And besides the Hunnish hero burn me.
lines: “With shields and carpets cover the pyre,
Shrouds full fair, and fallen slaves,
And besides the Hunnish hero burn me.

items.text: “Besides the Hunnish hero there Slaves shall burn, full bravely decked, Two at his head and two at his feet, A brace of hounds and a pair of hawks, For so shall all be seemly done.
lines: “Besides the Hunnish hero there
Slaves shall burn, full bravely decked,
Two at his head and two at his feet,
A brace of hounds and a pair of hawks,
For so shall all be seemly done.

items.text: “Let between us lie once more The steel so keen, as so it lay When both within one bed we were, And wedded mates by men were called.
lines: “Let between us lie once more
The steel so keen, as so it lay
When both within one bed we were,
And wedded mates by men were called.

items.text: “The door of the hall shall strike not the heel Of the hero fair with flashing rings, If hence my following goes with him; Not mean our faring forth shall be.
lines: “The door of the hall shall strike not the heel
Of the hero fair with flashing rings,
If hence my following goes with him;
Not mean our faring forth shall be.

items.text: “Bond-women five shall follow him, And eight of my thralls, well-born are they, Children with me, and mine they were As gifts that Buthli his daughter gave.
lines: “Bond-women five shall follow him,
And eight of my thralls, well-born are they,
Children with me, and mine they were
As gifts that Buthli his daughter gave.

items.text: “Much have I told thee, and more would say If fate more space for speech had given; My voice grows weak, my wounds are swelling; Truth I have said, and so I die.”
lines: “Much have I told thee, and more would say
If fate more space for speech had given;
My voice grows weak, my wounds are swelling;
Truth I have said, and so I die.”

items.text: After the death of Brynhild there were made two bale-fires, the one for Sigurth, and that burned first, and on the other was Brynhild burned, and she was on a wagon which was covered with a rich cloth. Thus it is told, that Brynhild went in the wagon on Hel-way, and passed by a house where dwelt a certain giantess. The giantess spake:
“Thou shalt not further forward fare, My dwelling ribbed with rocks across; More seemly it were at thy weaving to stay, Than another’s husband here to follow.
lines: “Thou shalt not further forward fare,
My dwelling ribbed with rocks across;
More seemly it were at thy weaving to stay,
Than another’s husband here to follow.

items.text: “What wouldst thou have from Valland here, Fickle of heart, in this my house? Gold-goddess, now, if thou wouldst know, Heroes’ blood from thy hands hast washed.”
lines: “What wouldst thou have from Valland here,
Fickle of heart, in this my house?
Gold-goddess, now, if thou wouldst know,
Heroes’ blood from thy hands hast washed.”

items.text: Brynhild spake:
“Chide me not, woman from rocky walls, Though to battle once I was wont to go; Better than thou I shall seem to be, When men us two shall truly know.”
lines: “Chide me not, woman from rocky walls,
Though to battle once I was wont to go;
Better than thou I shall seem to be,
When men us two shall truly know.”

items.text: The giantess spake:
“Thou wast, Brynhild, Buthli’s daughter, For the worst of evils born in the world; To death thou hast given Gjuki’s children, And laid their lofty house full low.”
lines: “Thou wast, Brynhild, Buthli’s daughter,
For the worst of evils born in the world;
To death thou hast given Gjuki’s children,
And laid their lofty house full low.”

items.text: Brynhild spake:
“Truth from the wagon here I tell thee, Witless one, if know thou wilt How the heirs of Gjuki gave me to be Joyless ever, a breaker of oaths.
lines: “Truth from the wagon here I tell thee,
Witless one, if know thou wilt
How the heirs of Gjuki gave me to be
Joyless ever, a breaker of oaths.

items.text: “Hild the helmed in Hlymdalir They named me of old, all they who knew me. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: “Hild the helmed in Hlymdalir
They named me of old, all they who knew me.

items.text: “The monarch bold the swan-robes bore Of the sisters eight beneath an oak; Twelve winters I was, if know thou wilt, When oaths I yielded the king so young.
lines: “The monarch bold the swan-robes bore
Of the sisters eight beneath an oak;
Twelve winters I was, if know thou wilt,
When oaths I yielded the king so young.

items.text: “Next I let the leader of Goths, Hjalmgunnar the old, go down to hell, And victory brought to Autha’s brother; For this was Othin’s anger mighty.
lines: “Next I let the leader of Goths,
Hjalmgunnar the old, go down to hell,
And victory brought to Autha’s brother;
For this was Othin’s anger mighty.

items.text: “He beset me with shields in Skatalund, Red and white, their rims o’erlapped; He bade that my sleep should broken be By him who fear had nowhere found.
lines: “He beset me with shields in Skatalund,
Red and white, their rims o’erlapped;
He bade that my sleep should broken be
By him who fear had nowhere found.

items.text: “He let round my hall, that southward looked, The branches’ foe high-leaping burn; Across it he bade the hero come Who brought me the gold that Fafnir guarded.
lines: “He let round my hall, that southward looked,
The branches’ foe high-leaping burn;
Across it he bade the hero come
Who brought me the gold that Fafnir guarded.

items.text: “On Grani rode the giver of gold, Where my foster-father ruled his folk; Best of all he seemed to be, The prince of the Danes, when the people met.
lines: “On Grani rode the giver of gold,
Where my foster-father ruled his folk;
Best of all he seemed to be,
The prince of the Danes, when the people met.

items.text: “Happy we slept, one bed we had, As he my brother born had been; Eight were the nights when neither there Loving hand on the other laid.
lines: “Happy we slept, one bed we had,
As he my brother born had been;
Eight were the nights when neither there
Loving hand on the other laid.

items.text: “Yet Guthrun reproached me, Gjuki’s daughter, That I in Sigurth’s arms had slept; Then did I hear what I would were hid, That they had betrayed me in taking a mate.
lines: “Yet Guthrun reproached me, Gjuki’s daughter,
That I in Sigurth’s arms had slept;
Then did I hear what I would were hid,
That they had betrayed me in taking a mate.

items.text: “Ever with grief and all too long Are men and women born in the world; But yet we shall live our lives together, Sigurth and I. Sink down, Giantess!”
lines: “Ever with grief and all too long
Are men and women born in the world;
But yet we shall live our lives together,
Sigurth and I. Sink down, Giantess!”

items.text: Gunnar and Hogni then took all the gold that Fafnir had had. There was strife between the Gjukungs and Atli, for he held the Gjukungs guilty of Brynhild’s death. It was agreed that they should give him Guthrun as wife, and they gave her a draught of forgetfulness to drink before she would consent to be wedded to Atli. The sons of Atli were Erp and Eitil, and Svanhild was the daughter of Sigurth and Guthrun. King Atli invited Gunnar and Hogni to come to him, and sent as messenger Vingi or Knefröth. Guthrun was aware of treachery, and sent with him a message in runes that they should not come, and as a token she sent to Hogni the ring Andvaranaut and tied a wolf’s hair in it. Gunnar had sought Oddrun, Atli’s sister, for his wife, but had her not; then he married Glaumvor, and Hogni’s wife was Kostbera; their sons were Solar and Snævar and Gjuki. And when the Gjukungs came to Atli, then Guthrun besought her sons to plead for the lives of both the Gjukungs, but they would not do it. Hogni’s heart was cut out, and Gunnar was cast into the serpent’s den. He smote on the harp and put the serpents to sleep, but an adder stung him in the liver.
NOTE

Prose. Niflungs: regarding the mistaken application of this name to the sons of Gjuki, who were Burgundians, cf. Brot, 17 and note. Draught of forgetfulness: according to the Volsungasaga Grimhild, Guthrun’s mother, administered this, just as she did the similar draught which made Sigurth forget Brynhild. Erp and Eitil: Guthrun kills her two sons by Atli as part of her revenge; the annotator here explains her act further by saying that Guthrun asked her sons to intercede with their father in favor of Guthrun’s brothers, but that they refused, a detail which he appears to have invented, as it is found nowhere else. Svanhild: cf. Sigurtharkvitha en skamma, 54 and note. Vingi or Knefröth: Atlakvitha (stanza 1) calls the messenger Knefröth; Atlamol (stanza 4) speaks of two messengers, but names only one of them, Vingi. The annotator has here tried, unsuccessfully, to combine the two accounts. Andvaranaut: regarding the origin of Andvari’s ring cf. Reginsmol, prose after stanzas 4 and 5 and notes; Sigurth gave the ring to Guthrun. Here again the annotator is combining two stories; in Atlakvitha (stanza 8) Guthrun sends a ring (not Andvaranaut) with a wolf’s hair; in Atlamol (stanza 4) she sends a message written in runes. The messenger obscures these runes, and Kostbera, Hogni’s wife, who attempts to decipher them, is not clear as to their meaning, though she suspects danger. Oddrun: cf. Sigurtharkvitha en skamma, 57 and note. Glaumvor: almost nothing is told of Gunnar’s second wife, though she appears frequently in the Atlamol. Kostbera (or Bera), Hogni’s wife, is known only as skilled in runes. Her brother was Orkning. The sons of Hogni and Kostbera, according to the Atlamol (stanza 28), were Solar and Snævar; the third son, Gjuki, named after his grandfather, seems to be an invention of the annotator’s. Adder: according to Oddrunargratr (stanza 30) Atli’s mother assumed this form in order to complete her son’s vengeance.
King Thjothrek was with Atli, and had lost most of his men. Thjothrek and Guthrun lamented their griefs together. She spoke to him, saying:
A maid of maids my mother bore me, Bright in my bower, my brothers I loved, Till Gjuki dowered me with gold, Dowered with gold, and to Sigurth gave me.
lines: A maid of maids my mother bore me,
Bright in my bower, my brothers I loved,
Till Gjuki dowered me with gold,
Dowered with gold, and to Sigurth gave me.

items.text: So Sigurth rose o’er Gjuki’s sons As the leek grows green above the grass, Or the stag o’er all the beasts doth stand, Or as glow-red gold above silver gray.
lines: So Sigurth rose o’er Gjuki’s sons
As the leek grows green above the grass,
Or the stag o’er all the beasts doth stand,
Or as glow-red gold above silver gray.

items.text: Till my brothers let me no longer have The best of heroes my husband to be; Sleep they could not, or quarrels settle, Till Sigurth they at last had slain.
lines: Till my brothers let me no longer have
The best of heroes my husband to be;
Sleep they could not, or quarrels settle,
Till Sigurth they at last had slain.

items.text: From the Thing ran Grani with thundering feet, But thence did Sigurth himself come never; Covered with sweat was the saddle-bearer, Wont the warrior’s weight to bear.
lines: From the Thing ran Grani with thundering feet,
But thence did Sigurth himself come never;
Covered with sweat was the saddle-bearer,
Wont the warrior’s weight to bear.

items.text: Weeping I sought with Grani to speak, With tear-wet cheeks for the tale I asked; The head of Grani was bowed to the grass, The steed knew well his master was slain.
lines: Weeping I sought with Grani to speak,
With tear-wet cheeks for the tale I asked;
The head of Grani was bowed to the grass,
The steed knew well his master was slain.

items.text: Long I waited and pondered well Ere ever the king for tidings I asked. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: Long I waited and pondered well
Ere ever the king for tidings I asked.

items.text: His head bowed Gunnar, but Hogni told The news full sore of Sigurth slain: “Hewed to death at our hands he lies, Gotthorm’s slayer, given to wolves.
lines: His head bowed Gunnar, but Hogni told
The news full sore of Sigurth slain:
“Hewed to death at our hands he lies,
Gotthorm’s slayer, given to wolves.

items.text: “On the southern road thou shalt Sigurth see, Where hear thou canst the ravens cry; The eagles cry as food they crave, And about thy husband wolves are howling.”
lines: “On the southern road thou shalt Sigurth see,
Where hear thou canst the ravens cry;
The eagles cry as food they crave,
And about thy husband wolves are howling.”

items.text: “Why dost thou, Hogni, such a horror Let me hear, all joyless left? Ravens yet thy heart shall rend In a land that never thou hast known.”
lines: “Why dost thou, Hogni, such a horror
Let me hear, all joyless left?
Ravens yet thy heart shall rend
In a land that never thou hast known.”

items.text: Few the words of Hogni were, Bitter his heart from heavy sorrow: “Greater, Guthrun, thy grief shall be If the ravens so my heart shall rend.”
lines: Few the words of Hogni were,
Bitter his heart from heavy sorrow:
“Greater, Guthrun, thy grief shall be
If the ravens so my heart shall rend.”

items.text: From him who spake I turned me soon, In the woods to find what the wolves had left; Tears I had not, nor wrung my hands, Nor wailing went, as other women, (When by Sigurth slain I sat).
lines: From him who spake I turned me soon,
In the woods to find what the wolves had left;
Tears I had not, nor wrung my hands,
Nor wailing went, as other women,
(When by Sigurth slain I sat).

items.text: Never so black had seemed the night As when in sorrow by Sigurth I sat; The wolves . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: Never so black had seemed the night
As when in sorrow by Sigurth I sat;
The wolves . . . . . . . . . . . .

items.text: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Best of all methought ’twould be If I my life could only lose, Or like to birch-wood burned might be.
lines: Best of all methought ’twould be
If I my life could only lose,
Or like to birch-wood burned might be.

items.text: From the mountain forth five days I fared, Till Hoalf’s hall so high I saw; Seven half-years with Thora I stayed, Hokon’s daughter, in Denmark then.
lines: From the mountain forth five days I fared,
Till Hoalf’s hall so high I saw;
Seven half-years with Thora I stayed,
Hokon’s daughter, in Denmark then.

items.text: With gold she broidered, to bring me joy, Southern halls and Danish swans; On the tapestry wove we warrior’s deeds, And the hero’s thanes on our handiwork; (Flashing shields and fighters armed, Sword-throng, helm-throng, the host of the king).
lines: With gold she broidered, to bring me joy,
Southern halls and Danish swans;
On the tapestry wove we warrior’s deeds,
And the hero’s thanes on our handiwork;
(Flashing shields and fighters armed,
Sword-throng, helm-throng, the host of the king).

items.text: Sigmund’s ship by the land was sailing, Golden the figure-head, gay the beaks; On board we wove the warriors faring, Sigar and Siggeir, south to Fjon.
lines: Sigmund’s ship by the land was sailing,
Golden the figure-head, gay the beaks;
On board we wove the warriors faring,
Sigar and Siggeir, south to Fjon.

items.text: Then Grimhild asked, the Gothic queen, Whether willingly would I . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: Then Grimhild asked, the Gothic queen,
Whether willingly would I . . . . . .

items.text: Her needlework cast she aside, and called Her sons to ask, with stern resolve, Who amends to their sister would make for her son, Or the wife requite for her husband killed.
lines: Her needlework cast she aside, and called
Her sons to ask, with stern resolve,
Who amends to their sister would make for her son,
Or the wife requite for her husband killed.

items.text: Ready was Gunnar gold to give, Amends for my hurt, and Hogni too; Then would she know who now would go, The horse to saddle, the wagon to harness, (The horse to ride, the hawk to fly, And shafts from bows of yew to shoot).
lines: Ready was Gunnar gold to give,
Amends for my hurt, and Hogni too;
Then would she know who now would go,
The horse to saddle, the wagon to harness,
(The horse to ride, the hawk to fly,
And shafts from bows of yew to shoot).

items.text: (Valdar, king of the Danes, was come, With Jarizleif, Eymoth, and Jarizskar). In like princes came they all, The long-beard men, with mantles red, Short their mail-coats, mighty their helms, Swords at their belts, and brown their hair.
lines: (Valdar, king of the Danes, was come,
With Jarizleif, Eymoth, and Jarizskar).
In like princes came they all,
The long-beard men, with mantles red,
Short their mail-coats, mighty their helms,
Swords at their belts, and brown their hair.

items.text: Each to give me gifts was fain, Gifts to give, and goodly speech, Comfort so for my sorrows great To bring they tried, but I trusted them not.
lines: Each to give me gifts was fain,
Gifts to give, and goodly speech,
Comfort so for my sorrows great
To bring they tried, but I trusted them not.

items.text: A draught did Grimhild give me to drink, Bitter and cold; I forgot my cares; For mingled therein was magic earth, Ice-cold sea, and the blood of swine.
lines: A draught did Grimhild give me to drink,
Bitter and cold; I forgot my cares;
For mingled therein was magic earth,
Ice-cold sea, and the blood of swine.

items.text: In the cup were runes of every kind, Written and reddened, I could not read them; A heather-fish from the Haddings’ land, An ear uncut, and the entrails of beasts.
lines: In the cup were runes of every kind,
Written and reddened, I could not read them;
A heather-fish from the Haddings’ land,
An ear uncut, and the entrails of beasts.

items.text: Much evil was brewed within the beer, Blossoms of trees, and acorns burned, Dew of the hearth, and holy entrails, The liver of swine,— all grief to allay.
lines: Much evil was brewed within the beer,
Blossoms of trees, and acorns burned,
Dew of the hearth, and holy entrails,
The liver of swine,— all grief to allay.

items.text: Then I forgot, when the draught they gave me, There in the hall, my husband’s slaying; On their knees the kings all three did kneel, Ere she herself to speak began:
lines: Then I forgot, when the draught they gave me,
There in the hall, my husband’s slaying;
On their knees the kings all three did kneel,
Ere she herself to speak began:

items.text: “Guthrun, gold to thee I give, The wealth that once thy father’s was, Rings to have, and Hlothver’s halls, And the hangings all that the monarch had.
lines: “Guthrun, gold to thee I give,
The wealth that once thy father’s was,
Rings to have, and Hlothver’s halls,
And the hangings all that the monarch had.

items.text: “Hunnish women, skilled in weaving, Who gold make fair to give thee joy, And the wealth of Buthli thine shall be, Gold-decked one, as Atli’s wife.”
lines: “Hunnish women, skilled in weaving,
Who gold make fair to give thee joy,
And the wealth of Buthli thine shall be,
Gold-decked one, as Atli’s wife.”

items.text: Guthrun spake:
“A husband now I will not have, Nor wife of Brynhild’s brother be; It beseems me not with Buthli’s son Happy to be, and heirs to bear.”
lines: “A husband now I will not have,
Nor wife of Brynhild’s brother be;
It beseems me not with Buthli’s son
Happy to be, and heirs to bear.”

items.text: Grimhild spake:
“Seek not on men to avenge thy sorrows, Though the blame at first with us hath been; Happy shalt be as if both still lived, Sigurth and Sigmund, if sons thou bearest.”
lines: “Seek not on men to avenge thy sorrows,
Though the blame at first with us hath been;
Happy shalt be as if both still lived,
Sigurth and Sigmund, if sons thou bearest.”

items.text: Guthrun spake:
“Grimhild, I may not gladness find, Nor hold forth hopes to heroes now, Since once the raven and ravening wolf Sigurth’s heart’s-blood hungrily lapped.”
lines: “Grimhild, I may not gladness find,
Nor hold forth hopes to heroes now,
Since once the raven and ravening wolf
Sigurth’s heart’s-blood hungrily lapped.”

items.text: Grimhild spake:
“Noblest of birth is the ruler now I have found for thee, and foremost of all; Him shalt thou have while life thou hast, Or husbandless be if him thou wilt choose not.”
lines: “Noblest of birth is the ruler now
I have found for thee, and foremost of all;
Him shalt thou have while life thou hast,
Or husbandless be if him thou wilt choose not.”

items.text: Guthrun spake:
“Seek not so eagerly me to send To be a bride of yon baneful race; On Gunnar first his wrath shall fall, And the heart will he tear from Hogni’s breast.”
lines: “Seek not so eagerly me to send
To be a bride of yon baneful race;
On Gunnar first his wrath shall fall,
And the heart will he tear from Hogni’s breast.”

items.text: Weeping Grimhild heard the words That fate full sore for her sons foretold, (And mighty woe for them should work;) “Lands I give thee, with all that live there, (Vinbjorg is thine, and Valbjorg too,) Have them forever, but hear me, daughter.”
lines: Weeping Grimhild heard the words
That fate full sore for her sons foretold,
(And mighty woe for them should work;)
“Lands I give thee, with all that live there,
(Vinbjorg is thine, and Valbjorg too,)
Have them forever, but hear me, daughter.”

items.text: So must I do as the kings besought, And against my will for my kinsmen wed; Ne’er with my husband joy I had, And my sons by my brothers’ fate were saved not.
lines: So must I do as the kings besought,
And against my will for my kinsmen wed;
Ne’er with my husband joy I had,
And my sons by my brothers’ fate were saved not.

items.text: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . I could not rest till of life I had robbed The warrior bold, the maker of battles.
lines: I could not rest till of life I had robbed
The warrior bold, the maker of battles.

items.text: Soon on horseback each hero was, And the foreign women in wagons faring; A week through lands so cold we went, And a second week the waves we smote, (And a third through lands that water lacked).
lines: Soon on horseback each hero was,
And the foreign women in wagons faring;
A week through lands so cold we went,
And a second week the waves we smote,
(And a third through lands that water lacked).

items.text: The warders now on the lofty walls Opened the gates, and in we rode.
lines: The warders now on the lofty walls
Opened the gates, and in we rode.

items.text: Atli woke me, for ever I seemed Of bitterness full for my brothers’ death.
lines: Atli woke me, for ever I seemed
Of bitterness full for my brothers’ death.

items.text: Atli spake:
“Now from sleep the Norns have waked me With visions of terror,— to thee will I tell them; Methought thou, Guthrun, Gjuki’s daughter, With poisoned blade didst pierce my body.”
lines: “Now from sleep the Norns have waked me
With visions of terror,— to thee will I tell them;
Methought thou, Guthrun, Gjuki’s daughter,
With poisoned blade didst pierce my body.”

items.text: Guthrun spake:
“Fire a dream of steel shall follow And willful pride one of woman’s wrath; A baneful sore I shall burn from thee, And tend and heal thee, though hated thou art.”
lines: “Fire a dream of steel shall follow
And willful pride one of woman’s wrath;
A baneful sore I shall burn from thee,
And tend and heal thee, though hated thou art.”

items.text: Atli spake:
“Of plants I dreamed, in the garden drooping, That fain would I have full high to grow; Plucked by the roots, and red with blood, They brought them hither, and bade me eat.
lines: “Of plants I dreamed, in the garden drooping,
That fain would I have full high to grow;
Plucked by the roots, and red with blood,
They brought them hither, and bade me eat.

items.text: “I dreamed my hawks from my hand had flown, Eager for food, to an evil house; I dreamed their hearts with honey I ate, Soaked in blood, and heavy my sorrow.
lines: “I dreamed my hawks from my hand had flown,
Eager for food, to an evil house;
I dreamed their hearts with honey I ate,
Soaked in blood, and heavy my sorrow.

items.text: “Hounds I dreamed from my hand I loosed, Loud in hunger and pain they howled; Their flesh methought was eagles’ food, And their bodies now I needs must eat.”
lines: “Hounds I dreamed from my hand I loosed,
Loud in hunger and pain they howled;
Their flesh methought was eagles’ food,
And their bodies now I needs must eat.”

items.text: Guthrun spake:
“Men shall soon of sacrifice speak, And off the heads of beasts shall hew; Die they shall ere day has dawned, A few nights hence, and the folk shall have them.”
lines: “Men shall soon of sacrifice speak,
And off the heads of beasts shall hew;
Die they shall ere day has dawned,
A few nights hence, and the folk shall have them.”

items.text: Atli spake:
“On my bed I sank, nor slumber sought, Weary with woe,— full well I remember.” . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: “On my bed I sank, nor slumber sought,
Weary with woe,— full well I remember.”

items.text: Herkja was the name of a serving-woman of Atli’s; she had been his concubine. She told Atli that she had seen Thjothrek and Guthrun both together. Atli was greatly angered thereby. Then Guthrun said:
“What thy sorrow, Atli, Buthli’s son? Is thy heart heavy-laden? Why laughest thou never? It would better befit the warrior far To speak with men, and me to look on.”
lines: “What thy sorrow, Atli, Buthli’s son?
Is thy heart heavy-laden? Why laughest thou never?
It would better befit the warrior far
To speak with men, and me to look on.”

items.text: Atli spake:
