“It troubles me, Guthrun, Gjuki’s daughter, What Herkja here in the hall hath told me, That thou in the bed with Thjothrek liest, Beneath the linen in lovers’ guise.”
lines: “It troubles me, Guthrun, Gjuki’s daughter,
What Herkja here in the hall hath told me,
That thou in the bed with Thjothrek liest,
Beneath the linen in lovers’ guise.”

items.text: Guthrun spake:
“This shall I with oaths now swear, Swear by the sacred stone so white, That nought was there with Thjothmar’s son That man or woman may not know.
lines: “This shall I with oaths now swear,
Swear by the sacred stone so white,
That nought was there with Thjothmar’s son
That man or woman may not know.

items.text: “Nor ever once did my arms embrace The hero brave, the leader of hosts; In another manner our meeting was, When our sorrows we in secret told.
lines: “Nor ever once did my arms embrace
The hero brave, the leader of hosts;
In another manner our meeting was,
When our sorrows we in secret told.

items.text: “With thirty warriors Thjothrek came, Nor of all his men doth one remain; Thou hast murdered my brothers and mail-clad men, Thou hast murdered all the men of my race.
lines: “With thirty warriors Thjothrek came,
Nor of all his men doth one remain;
Thou hast murdered my brothers and mail-clad men,
Thou hast murdered all the men of my race.

items.text: “Gunnar comes not, Hogni I greet not, No longer I see my brothers loved; My sorrow would Hogni avenge with the sword, Now myself for my woes I shall payment win.
lines: “Gunnar comes not, Hogni I greet not,
No longer I see my brothers loved;
My sorrow would Hogni avenge with the sword,
Now myself for my woes I shall payment win.

items.text: “Summon Saxi, the southrons’ king, For he the boiling kettle can hallow.” Seven hundred there were in the hall, Ere the queen her hand in the kettle thrust.
lines: “Summon Saxi, the southrons’ king,
For he the boiling kettle can hallow.”
Seven hundred there were in the hall,
Ere the queen her hand in the kettle thrust.

items.text: To the bottom she reached with hand so bright, And forth she brought the flashing stones: “Behold, ye warriors, well am I cleared Of sin by the kettle’s sacred boiling.”
lines: To the bottom she reached with hand so bright,
And forth she brought the flashing stones:
“Behold, ye warriors, well am I cleared
Of sin by the kettle’s sacred boiling.”

items.text: Then Atli’s heart in happiness laughed, When Guthrun’s hand unhurt he saw; “Now Herkja shall come the kettle to try, She who grief for Guthrun planned.”
lines: Then Atli’s heart in happiness laughed,
When Guthrun’s hand unhurt he saw;
“Now Herkja shall come the kettle to try,
She who grief for Guthrun planned.”

items.text: Ne’er saw man sight more sad than this, How burned were the hands of Herkja then; In a bog so foul the maid they flung, And so was Guthrun’s grief requited.
lines: Ne’er saw man sight more sad than this,
How burned were the hands of Herkja then;
In a bog so foul the maid they flung,
And so was Guthrun’s grief requited.

items.text: Heithrek was the name of a king, whose daughter was called Borgny. Vilmund was the name of the man who was her lover. She could not give birth to a child until Oddrun, Atli’s sister, had come to her; Oddrun had been beloved of Gunnar, son of Gjuki. About this story is the following poem.
I have heard it told in olden tales How a maiden came to Morningland; No one of all on earth above To Heithrek’s daughter help could give.
lines: I have heard it told in olden tales
How a maiden came to Morningland;
No one of all on earth above
To Heithrek’s daughter help could give.

items.text: This Oddrun learned, the sister of Atli, That sore the maiden’s sickness was; The bit-bearer forth from his stall she brought, And the saddle laid on the steed so black.
lines: This Oddrun learned, the sister of Atli,
That sore the maiden’s sickness was;
The bit-bearer forth from his stall she brought,
And the saddle laid on the steed so black.

items.text: She let the horse go o’er the level ground, Till she reached the hall that loftily rose, (And in she went from the end of the hall;) From the weary steed the saddle she took; Hear now the speech that first she spake:
lines: She let the horse go o’er the level ground,
Till she reached the hall that loftily rose,
(And in she went from the end of the hall;)
From the weary steed the saddle she took;
Hear now the speech that first she spake:

items.text: “What news on earth, . . . . . . . . Or what has happened in Hunland now?”
lines: “What news on earth, . . . . . . . .
Or what has happened in Hunland now?”

items.text: A serving-maid spake:
“Here Borgny lies in bitter pain, Thy friend, and, Oddrun, thy help would find.”
lines: “Here Borgny lies in bitter pain,
Thy friend, and, Oddrun, thy help would find.”

items.text: Oddrun spake:
“Who worked this woe for the woman thus, Or why so sudden is Borgny sick?”
lines: “Who worked this woe for the woman thus,
Or why so sudden is Borgny sick?”

items.text: The serving-maid spake:
“Vilmund is he, the heroes’ friend, Who wrapped the woman in bedclothes warm, (For winters five, yet her father knew not).”
lines: “Vilmund is he, the heroes’ friend,
Who wrapped the woman in bedclothes warm,
(For winters five, yet her father knew not).”

items.text: Then no more they spake, methinks; She went at the knees of the woman to sit; With magic Oddrun and mightily Oddrun Chanted for Borgny potent charms.
lines: Then no more they spake, methinks;
She went at the knees of the woman to sit;
With magic Oddrun and mightily Oddrun
Chanted for Borgny potent charms.

items.text: At last were born a boy and girl, Son and daughter of Hogni’s slayer; Then speech the woman so weak began, Nor said she aught ere this she spake:
lines: At last were born a boy and girl,
Son and daughter of Hogni’s slayer;
Then speech the woman so weak began,
Nor said she aught ere this she spake:

items.text: “So may the holy ones thee help, Frigg and Freyja and favoring gods, As thou hast saved me from sorrow now.”
lines: “So may the holy ones thee help,
Frigg and Freyja and favoring gods,
As thou hast saved me from sorrow now.”

items.text: Oddrun spake:

“I came not hither to help thee thus Because thou ever my aid didst earn; I fulfilled the oath that of old I swore, That aid to all I should ever bring, (When they shared the wealth the warriors had).”
lines: “I came not hither to help thee thus
Because thou ever my aid didst earn;
I fulfilled the oath that of old I swore,
That aid to all I should ever bring,
(When they shared the wealth the warriors had).”

items.text: Borgny spake:
“Wild art thou, Oddrun, and witless now, That so in hatred to me thou speakest; I followed thee where thou didst fare, As we had been born of brothers twain.”
lines: “Wild art thou, Oddrun, and witless now,
That so in hatred to me thou speakest;
I followed thee where thou didst fare,
As we had been born of brothers twain.”

items.text: Oddrun spake:
“I remember the evil one eve thou spakest, When a draught I gave to Gunnar then; Thou didst say that never such a deed By maid was done save by me alone.”
lines: “I remember the evil one eve thou spakest,
When a draught I gave to Gunnar then;
Thou didst say that never such a deed
By maid was done save by me alone.”

items.text: Then the sorrowing woman sat her down To tell the grief of her troubles great.
lines: Then the sorrowing woman sat her down
To tell the grief of her troubles great.

items.text: “Happy I grew in the hero’s hall As the warriors wished, and they loved me well; Glad I was of my father’s gifts, For winters five, while my father lived.
lines: “Happy I grew in the hero’s hall
As the warriors wished, and they loved me well;
Glad I was of my father’s gifts,
For winters five, while my father lived.

items.text: “These were the words the weary king, Ere he died, spake last of all: He bade me with red gold dowered to be, And to Grimhild’s son in the South be wedded.
lines: “These were the words the weary king,
Ere he died, spake last of all:
He bade me with red gold dowered to be,
And to Grimhild’s son in the South be wedded.

items.text: “But Brynhild the helm he bade to wear, A wish-maid bright he said she should be; For a nobler maid would never be born On earth, he said, if death should spare her.
lines: “But Brynhild the helm he bade to wear,
A wish-maid bright he said she should be;
For a nobler maid would never be born
On earth, he said, if death should spare her.

items.text: “At her weaving Brynhild sat in her bower, Lands and folk alike she had; The earth and heaven high resounded When Fafnir’s slayer the city saw.
lines: “At her weaving Brynhild sat in her bower,
Lands and folk alike she had;
The earth and heaven high resounded
When Fafnir’s slayer the city saw.

items.text: “Then battle was fought with the foreign swords, And the city was broken that Brynhild had; Not long thereafter, but all too soon, Their evil wiles full well she knew.
lines: “Then battle was fought with the foreign swords,
And the city was broken that Brynhild had;
Not long thereafter, but all too soon,
Their evil wiles full well she knew.

items.text: “Woeful for this her vengeance was, As so we learned to our sorrow all; In every land shall all men hear How herself at Sigurth’s side she slew.
lines: “Woeful for this her vengeance was,
As so we learned to our sorrow all;
In every land shall all men hear
How herself at Sigurth’s side she slew.

items.text: “Love to Gunnar then I gave, To the breaker of rings, as Brynhild might; To Atli rings so red they offered, And mighty gifts to my brother would give.
lines: “Love to Gunnar then I gave,
To the breaker of rings, as Brynhild might;
To Atli rings so red they offered,
And mighty gifts to my brother would give.

items.text: “Fifteen dwellings fain would he give For me, and the burden that Grani bore; But Atli said he would never receive Marriage gold from Gjuki’s son.
lines: “Fifteen dwellings fain would he give
For me, and the burden that Grani bore;
But Atli said he would never receive
Marriage gold from Gjuki’s son.

items.text: “Yet could we not our love o’ercome, And my head I laid on the hero’s shoulder; Many there were of kinsmen mine Who said that together us they had seen.
lines: “Yet could we not our love o’ercome,
And my head I laid on the hero’s shoulder;
Many there were of kinsmen mine
Who said that together us they had seen.

items.text: “Atli said that never I Would evil plan, or ill deed do; But none may this of another think, Or surely speak, when love is shared.
lines: “Atli said that never I
Would evil plan, or ill deed do;
But none may this of another think,
Or surely speak, when love is shared.

items.text: “Soon his men did Atli send, In the murky wood on me to spy; Thither they came where they should not come, Where beneath one cover close we lay.
lines: “Soon his men did Atli send,
In the murky wood on me to spy;
Thither they came where they should not come,
Where beneath one cover close we lay.

items.text: “To the warriors ruddy rings we offered, That nought to Atli e’er they should say; But swiftly home they hastened thence, And eager all to Atli told.
lines: “To the warriors ruddy rings we offered,
That nought to Atli e’er they should say;
But swiftly home they hastened thence,
And eager all to Atli told.

items.text: “But close from Guthrun kept they hid What first of all she ought to have known. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: “But close from Guthrun kept they hid
What first of all she ought to have known.

items.text: “Great was the clatter of gilded hoofs When Gjuki’s sons through the gateway rode; The heart they hewed from Hogni then, And the other they cast in the serpents’ cave.
lines: “Great was the clatter of gilded hoofs
When Gjuki’s sons through the gateway rode;
The heart they hewed from Hogni then,
And the other they cast in the serpents’ cave.

items.text: “The hero wise on his harp then smote, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . For help from me in his heart yet hoped The high-born king, might come to him.
lines: “The hero wise on his harp then smote,
For help from me in his heart yet hoped
The high-born king, might come to him.

items.text: “Alone was I gone to Geirmund then, The draught to mix and ready to make; Sudden I heard from Hlesey clear How in sorrow the strings of the harp resounded.
lines: “Alone was I gone to Geirmund then,
The draught to mix and ready to make;
Sudden I heard from Hlesey clear
How in sorrow the strings of the harp resounded.

items.text: “I bade the serving-maids ready to be, For I longed the hero’s life to save; Across the sound the boats we sailed, Till we saw the whole of Atli’s home.
lines: “I bade the serving-maids ready to be,
For I longed the hero’s life to save;
Across the sound the boats we sailed,
Till we saw the whole of Atli’s home.

items.text: “Then crawling the evil woman came, Atli’s mother— may she ever rot! And hard she bit to Gunnar’s heart, So I could not help the hero brave.
lines: “Then crawling the evil woman came,
Atli’s mother— may she ever rot!
And hard she bit to Gunnar’s heart,
So I could not help the hero brave.

items.text: “Oft have I wondered how after this, Serpents’-bed goddess! I still might live, For well I loved the warrior brave, The giver of swords, as my very self.
lines: “Oft have I wondered how after this,
Serpents’-bed goddess! I still might live,
For well I loved the warrior brave,
The giver of swords, as my very self.

items.text: “Thou didst see and listen, the while I said The mighty grief that was mine and theirs; Each man lives as his longing wills,— Oddrun’s lament is ended now.”
lines: “Thou didst see and listen, the while I said
The mighty grief that was mine and theirs;
Each man lives as his longing wills,—
Oddrun’s lament is ended now.”

items.text: Guthrun, Gjuki’s daughter, avenged her brothers, as has become well known. She slew first Atli’s sons, and thereafter she slew Atli, and burned the hall with his whole company. Concerning this was the following poem made:
Atli sent of old to Gunnar A keen-witted rider, Knefröth did men call him; To Gjuki’s home came he and to Gunnar’s dwelling, With benches round the hearth, and to the beer so sweet.
lines: Atli sent of old to Gunnar
A keen-witted rider, Knefröth did men call him;
To Gjuki’s home came he and to Gunnar’s dwelling,
With benches round the hearth, and to the beer so sweet.

items.text: Then the followers, hiding their falseness, all drank Their wine in the war-hall, of the Huns’ wrath wary; And Knefröth spake loudly, his words were crafty, The hero from the south, on the high bench sitting:
lines: Then the followers, hiding their falseness, all drank
Their wine in the war-hall, of the Huns’ wrath wary;
And Knefröth spake loudly, his words were crafty,
The hero from the south, on the high bench sitting:

items.text: “Now Atli has sent me his errand to ride, On my bit-champing steed through Myrkwood the secret, To bid you, Gunnar, to his benches to come, With helms round the hearth, and Atli’s home seek.
lines: “Now Atli has sent me his errand to ride,
On my bit-champing steed through Myrkwood the secret,
To bid you, Gunnar, to his benches to come,
With helms round the hearth, and Atli’s home seek.

items.text: “Shields shall ye choose there, and shafts made of ash-wood, Gold-adorned helmets, and slaves out of Hunland, Silver-gilt saddle-cloths, shirts of bright scarlet, With lances and spears too, and bit-champing steeds.
lines: “Shields shall ye choose there, and shafts made of
ash-wood,
Gold-adorned helmets, and slaves out of Hunland,
Silver-gilt saddle-cloths, shirts of bright scarlet,
With lances and spears too, and bit-champing steeds.

items.text: “The field shall be given you of wide Gnitaheith, With loud-ringing lances, and stems gold-o’erlaid, Treasures full huge, and the home of Danp, And the mighty forest that Myrkwood is called.”
lines: “The field shall be given you of wide Gnitaheith,
With loud-ringing lances, and stems gold-o’erlaid,
Treasures full huge, and the home of Danp,
And the mighty forest that Myrkwood is called.”

items.text: His head turned Gunnar, and to Hogni he said: “What thy counsel, young hero, when such things we hear? No gold do I know on Gnitaheith lying So fair that other its equal we have not.
lines: His head turned Gunnar, and to Hogni he said:
“What thy counsel, young hero, when such things we hear?
No gold do I know on Gnitaheith lying
So fair that other its equal we have not.

items.text: “We have seven halls, each of swords is full, (And all of gold is the hilt of each;) My steed is the swiftest, my sword is sharpest, My bows adorn benches, my byrnies are golden, My helm is the brightest that came from Kjar’s hall, (Mine own is better than all the Huns’ treasure.)”
lines: “We have seven halls, each of swords is full,
(And all of gold is the hilt of each;)
My steed is the swiftest, my sword is sharpest,
My bows adorn benches, my byrnies are golden,
My helm is the brightest that came from Kjar’s hall,
(Mine own is better than all the Huns’ treasure.)”

items.text: Hogni spake:

“What seeks she to say, that she sends us a ring, Woven with a wolf’s hair? methinks it gives warning; In the red ring a hair of the heath-dweller found I, Wolf-like shall our road be if we ride on this journey.”
lines: “What seeks she to say, that she sends us a ring,
Woven with a wolf’s hair? methinks it gives warning;
In the red ring a hair of the heath-dweller found I,
Wolf-like shall our road be if we ride on this journey.”

items.text: Not eager were his comrades, nor the men of his kin, The wise nor the wary, nor the warriors bold. But Gunnar spake forth as befitted a king, Noble in the beer-hall, and bitter his scorn:
lines: Not eager were his comrades, nor the men of his kin,
The wise nor the wary, nor the warriors bold.
But Gunnar spake forth as befitted a king,
Noble in the beer-hall, and bitter his scorn:

items.text: “Stand forth now, Fjornir! and hither on the floor The beakers all golden shalt thou bring to the warriors. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: “Stand forth now, Fjornir! and hither on the floor
The beakers all golden shalt thou bring to the warriors.

items.text: “The wolves then shall rule the wealth of the Niflungs, Wolves aged and grey-hued, if Gunnar is lost, And black-coated bears with rending teeth bite, And make glad the dogs, if Gunnar returns not.”
lines: “The wolves then shall rule the wealth of the Niflungs,
Wolves aged and grey-hued, if Gunnar is lost,
And black-coated bears with rending teeth bite,
And make glad the dogs, if Gunnar returns not.”

items.text: A following gallant fared forth with the ruler, Yet they wept as their home with the hero they left; And the little heir of Hogni called loudly: “Go safe now, ye wise ones, wherever ye will!”
lines: A following gallant fared forth with the ruler,
Yet they wept as their home with the hero they left;
And the little heir of Hogni called loudly:
“Go safe now, ye wise ones, wherever ye will!”

items.text: Then let the bold heroes their bit-champing horses On the mountains gallop, and through Myrkwood the secret; All Hunland was shaken where the hard-souled ones rode, On the whip-fearers fared they through fields that were green.
lines: Then let the bold heroes their bit-champing horses
On the mountains gallop, and through Myrkwood the secret;
All Hunland was shaken where the hard-souled ones rode,
On the whip-fearers fared they through fields that were
green.

items.text: Then they saw Atli’s halls, and his watch-towers high, On the walls so lofty stood the warriors of Buthli; The hall of the southrons with seats was surrounded, With targets bound and shields full bright.
lines: Then they saw Atli’s halls, and his watch-towers high,
On the walls so lofty stood the warriors of Buthli;
The hall of the southrons with seats was surrounded,
With targets bound and shields full bright.

items.text: Mid weapons and lances did Atli his wine In the war-hall drink, without were his watchmen, For Gunnar they waited, if forth he should go, With their ringing spears they would fight with the ruler.
lines: Mid weapons and lances did Atli his wine
In the war-hall drink, without were his watchmen,
For Gunnar they waited, if forth he should go,
With their ringing spears they would fight with the ruler.

items.text: This their sister saw, as soon as her brothers Had entered the hall,— little ale had she drunk: “Betrayed art thou, Gunnar! what guard hast thou, hero, ’Gainst the plots of the Huns? from the hall flee swiftly!
lines: This their sister saw, as soon as her brothers
Had entered the hall,— little ale had she drunk:
“Betrayed art thou, Gunnar! what guard hast thou, hero,
’Gainst the plots of the Huns? from the hall flee swiftly!

items.text: “Brother, ’twere far better to have come in byrnie, With thy household helmed, to see Atli’s home, And to sit in the saddle all day ’neath the sun, (That the sword-norns might weep for the death-pale warriors, And the Hunnish shield-maids might shun not the sword,) And send Atli himself to the den of the snakes; (Now the den of the snakes for thee is destined.)”
lines: “Brother, ’twere far better to have come in byrnie,
With thy household helmed, to see Atli’s home,
And to sit in the saddle all day ’neath the sun,
(That the sword-norns might weep for the death-pale warriors,
And the Hunnish shield-maids might shun not the sword,)
And send Atli himself to the den of the snakes;
(Now the den of the snakes for thee is destined.)”

items.text: Gunnar spake:
. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . “Too late is it, sister, to summon the Niflungs, Long is it to come to the throng of our comrades, The heroes gallant, from the hills of the Rhine.”
lines: “Too late is it, sister, to summon the Niflungs,
Long is it to come to the throng of our comrades,
The heroes gallant, from the hills of the Rhine.”

items.text: Then Gunnar they seized, and they set him in chains, The Burgundians’ king, and fast they bound him.
lines: Then Gunnar they seized, and they set him in chains,
The Burgundians’ king, and fast they bound him.

items.text: Hogni slew seven with sword so keen, And an eighth he flung in the fire hot; A hero should fight with his foemen thus, As Hogni strove in Gunnar’s behalf.
lines: Hogni slew seven with sword so keen,
And an eighth he flung in the fire hot;
A hero should fight with his foemen thus,
As Hogni strove in Gunnar’s behalf.

items.text: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . The leader they asked if his life he fain With gold would buy, the king of the Goths.
lines: The leader they asked if his life he fain
With gold would buy, the king of the Goths.

items.text: Gunnar spake:
“First the heart of Hogni shall ye lay in my hands, All bloody from the breast of the bold one cut With keen-biting sword, from the son of the king.”
lines: “First the heart of Hogni shall ye lay in my hands,
All bloody from the breast of the bold one cut
With keen-biting sword, from the son of the king.”

items.text: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . They cut out the heart from the breast of Hjalli, On a platter they bore it, and brought it to Gunnar.
lines: They cut out the heart from the breast of Hjalli,
On a platter they bore it, and brought it to Gunnar.

items.text: Then Gunnar spake forth, the lord of the folk: “Here have I the heart of Hjalli the craven, Unlike to the heart of Hogni the valiant, For it trembles still as it stands on the platter; Twice more did it tremble in the breast of the man.”
lines: Then Gunnar spake forth, the lord of the folk:
“Here have I the heart of Hjalli the craven,
Unlike to the heart of Hogni the valiant,
For it trembles still as it stands on the platter;
Twice more did it tremble in the breast of the man.”

items.text: Then Hogni laughed when they cut out the heart Of the living helm-hammerer; tears he had not. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . On a platter they bore it, and brought it to Gunnar.
lines: Then Hogni laughed when they cut out the heart
Of the living helm-hammerer; tears he had not.
On a platter they bore it, and brought it to Gunnar.

items.text: Then Gunnar spake forth, the spear of the Niflungs: “Here have I the heart of Hogni the valiant, Unlike to the heart of Hjalli the craven, Little it trembles as it lies on the platter, Still less did it tremble when it lay in his breast.
lines: Then Gunnar spake forth, the spear of the Niflungs:
“Here have I the heart of Hogni the valiant,
Unlike to the heart of Hjalli the craven,
Little it trembles as it lies on the platter,
Still less did it tremble when it lay in his breast.

items.text: “So distant, Atli, from all men’s eyes, Shalt thou be as thou . . . . . from the gold. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: “So distant, Atli, from all men’s eyes,
Shalt thou be as thou . . . . . from the gold.

items.text: “To no one save me is the secret known Of the Niflungs’ hoard, now Hogni is dead; Of old there were two, while we twain were alive, Now is none but I, for I only am living.
lines: “To no one save me is the secret known
Of the Niflungs’ hoard, now Hogni is dead;
Of old there were two, while we twain were alive,
Now is none but I, for I only am living.

items.text: “The swift Rhine shall hold the strife-gold of heroes, That once was the gods’, the wealth of the Niflungs, In the depths of the waters the death-rings shall glitter, And not shine on the hands of the Hunnish men.”
lines: “The swift Rhine shall hold the strife-gold of heroes,
That once was the gods’, the wealth of the Niflungs,
In the depths of the waters the death-rings shall glitter,
And not shine on the hands of the Hunnish men.”

items.text: Atli spake:
“Ye shall bring the wagon, for now is he bound.”
lines: “Ye shall bring the wagon, for now is he bound.”

items.text: On the long-maned Glaum rode Atli the great, About him were warriors . . . . . . . . But Guthrun, akin to the gods of slaughter, Yielded not to her tears in the hall of tumult.
lines: On the long-maned Glaum rode Atli the great,
About him were warriors . . . . . . . .
But Guthrun, akin to the gods of slaughter,
Yielded not to her tears in the hall of tumult.

items.text: Guthrun spake:

“It shall go with thee, Atli, as with Gunnar thou heldest The oaths ofttimes sworn, and of old made firm, By the sun in the south, by Sigtyr’s mountain, By the horse of the rest-bed, and the ring of Ull.”
lines: “It shall go with thee, Atli, as with Gunnar thou heldest
The oaths ofttimes sworn, and of old made firm,
By the sun in the south, by Sigtyr’s mountain,
By the horse of the rest-bed, and the ring of Ull.”

items.text: Then the champer of bits drew the chieftain great, The gold-guarder, down to the place of death. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: Then the champer of bits drew the chieftain great,
The gold-guarder, down to the place of death.

items.text: By the warriors’ host was the living hero Cast in the den where crawling about Within were serpents, but soon did Gunnar With his hand in wrath on the harp-strings smite; The strings resounded,— so shall a hero, A ring-breaker, gold from his enemies guard.
lines: By the warriors’ host was the living hero
Cast in the den where crawling about
Within were serpents, but soon did Gunnar
With his hand in wrath on the harp-strings smite;
The strings resounded,— so shall a hero,
A ring-breaker, gold from his enemies guard.

items.text: Then Atli rode on his earth-treading steed, Seeking his home, from the slaughter-place; There was clatter of hoofs of the steeds in the court, And the clashing of arms as they came from the field.
lines: Then Atli rode on his earth-treading steed,
Seeking his home, from the slaughter-place;
There was clatter of hoofs of the steeds in the court,
And the clashing of arms as they came from the field.

items.text: Out then came Guthrun to meeting with Atli, With a golden beaker as gift to the monarch: “Thou mayst eat now, chieftain, within thy dwelling, Blithely with Guthrun young beasts fresh slaughtered.”
lines: Out then came Guthrun to meeting with Atli,
With a golden beaker as gift to the monarch:
“Thou mayst eat now, chieftain, within thy dwelling,
Blithely with Guthrun young beasts fresh slaughtered.”

items.text: The wine-heavy ale-cups of Atli resounded, When there in the hall the Hunnish youths clamored, And the warriors bearded, the brave ones, entered.
lines: The wine-heavy ale-cups of Atli resounded,
When there in the hall the Hunnish youths clamored,
And the warriors bearded, the brave ones, entered.

items.text: Then in came the shining one, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . and drink she bore them; Unwilling and bitter brought she food to the warrior, Till in scorn to the white-faced Atli did she speak:
lines: Then in came the shining one, . . . . . . . .
. . . . . . . . and drink she bore them;
Unwilling and bitter brought she food to the warrior,
Till in scorn to the white-faced Atli did she speak:

items.text: “Thou giver of swords, of thy sons the hearts All heavy with blood in honey thou hast eaten; Thou shalt stomach, thou hero, the flesh of the slain, To eat at thy feast, and to send to thy followers.
lines: “Thou giver of swords, of thy sons the hearts
All heavy with blood in honey thou hast eaten;
Thou shalt stomach, thou hero, the flesh of the slain,
To eat at thy feast, and to send to thy followers.

items.text: “Thou shalt never call to thy knees again Erp or Eitil, when merry with ale; Thou shalt never see in their seats again The sharers of gold their lances shaping, (Clipping the manes or minding their steeds.)”
lines: “Thou shalt never call to thy knees again
Erp or Eitil, when merry with ale;
Thou shalt never see in their seats again
The sharers of gold their lances shaping,
(Clipping the manes or minding their steeds.)”

items.text: There was clamor on the benches, and the cry of men, The clashing of weapons, and weeping of the Huns, Save for Guthrun only, she wept not ever For her bear-fierce brothers, or the boys so dear, So young and so unhappy, whom with Atli she had.
lines: There was clamor on the benches, and the cry of men,
The clashing of weapons, and weeping of the Huns,
Save for Guthrun only, she wept not ever
For her bear-fierce brothers, or the boys so dear,
So young and so unhappy, whom with Atli she had.

items.text: Gold did she scatter, the swan-white one, And rings of red gold to the followers gave she; The fate she let grow, and the shining wealth go, Nor spared she the treasure of the temple itself.
lines: Gold did she scatter, the swan-white one,
And rings of red gold to the followers gave she;
The fate she let grow, and the shining wealth go,
Nor spared she the treasure of the temple itself.

items.text: Unwise then was Atli, he had drunk to wildness, No weapon did he have, and of Guthrun bewared not; Oft their play was better when both in gladness Each other embraced among princes all.
lines: Unwise then was Atli, he had drunk to wildness,
No weapon did he have, and of Guthrun bewared not;
Oft their play was better when both in gladness
Each other embraced among princes all.

items.text: With her sword she gave blood for the bed to drink, With her death-dealing hand, and the hounds she loosed, The thralls she awakened, and a firebrand threw In the door of the hall; so vengeance she had.
lines: With her sword she gave blood for the bed to drink,
With her death-dealing hand, and the hounds she loosed,
The thralls she awakened, and a firebrand threw
In the door of the hall; so vengeance she had.

items.text: To the flames she gave all who yet were within, And from Myrkheim had come from the murder of Gunnar; The timbers old fell, the temple was in flames, The dwelling of the Buthlungs, and the shield-maids burned, They were slain in the house, in the hot flames they sank.
lines: To the flames she gave all who yet were within,
And from Myrkheim had come from the murder of Gunnar;
The timbers old fell, the temple was in flames,
The dwelling of the Buthlungs, and the shield-maids burned,
They were slain in the house, in the hot flames they sank.

items.text: Now the tale is all told, nor in later time Will a woman in byrnie avenge so her brothers; The fair one to three of the kings of the folk Brought the doom of death ere herself she died.
lines: Now the tale is all told, nor in later time
Will a woman in byrnie avenge so her brothers;
The fair one to three of the kings of the folk
Brought the doom of death ere herself she died.

items.text: Still more is told in the Greenland ballad of Atli.
There are many who know how of old did men In counsel gather; little good did they get; In secret they plotted, it was sore for them later, And for Gjuki’s sons, whose trust they deceived.
lines: There are many who know how of old did men
In counsel gather; little good did they get;
In secret they plotted, it was sore for them later,
And for Gjuki’s sons, whose trust they deceived.

items.text: Fate grew for the princes, to death they were given; Ill counsel was Atli’s, though keenness he had; He felled his staunch bulwark, his own sorrow fashioned, Soon a message he sent that his kinsmen should seek him.
lines: Fate grew for the princes, to death they were given;
Ill counsel was Atli’s, though keenness he had;
He felled his staunch bulwark, his own sorrow fashioned,
Soon a message he sent that his kinsmen should seek him.

items.text: Wise was the woman, she fain would use wisdom, She saw well what meant all they said in secret; From her heart it was hid how help she might render, The sea they should sail, while herself she should go not.
lines: Wise was the woman, she fain would use wisdom,
She saw well what meant all they said in secret;
From her heart it was hid how help she might render,
The sea they should sail, while herself she should go not.

items.text: Runes did she fashion, but false Vingi made them, The speeder of hatred, ere to give them he sought; Then soon fared the warriors whom Atli had sent, And to Limafjord came, to the home of the kings.
lines: Runes did she fashion, but false Vingi made them,
The speeder of hatred, ere to give them he sought;
Then soon fared the warriors whom Atli had sent,
And to Limafjord came, to the home of the kings.

items.text: They were kindly with ale, and fires they kindled, They thought not of craft from the guests who had come; The gifts did they take that the noble one gave them, On the pillars they hung them, no fear did they harbor.
lines: They were kindly with ale, and fires they kindled,
They thought not of craft from the guests who had come;
The gifts did they take that the noble one gave them,
On the pillars they hung them, no fear did they harbor.

items.text: Forth did Kostbera, wife of Hogni, then come, Full kindly she was, and she welcomed them both; And glad too was Glaumvor, the wife of Gunnar, She knew well to care for the needs of the guests.
lines: Forth did Kostbera, wife of Hogni, then come,
Full kindly she was, and she welcomed them both;
And glad too was Glaumvor, the wife of Gunnar,
She knew well to care for the needs of the guests.

items.text: Then Hogni they asked if more eager he were, Full clear was the guile, if on guard they had been; Then Gunnar made promise, if Hogni would go, And Hogni made answer as the other counseled.
lines: Then Hogni they asked if more eager he were,
Full clear was the guile, if on guard they had been;
Then Gunnar made promise, if Hogni would go,
And Hogni made answer as the other counseled.

items.text: Then the famed ones brought mead, and fair was the feast, Full many were the horns, till the men had drunk deep; . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Then the mates made ready their beds for resting.
lines: Then the famed ones brought mead, and fair was the feast,
Full many were the horns, till the men had drunk deep;
Then the mates made ready their beds for resting.

items.text: Wise was Kostbera, and cunning in rune-craft, The letters would she read by the light of the fire; But full quickly her tongue to her palate clave, So strange did they seem that their meaning she saw not.
lines: Wise was Kostbera, and cunning in rune-craft,
The letters would she read by the light of the fire;
But full quickly her tongue to her palate clave,
So strange did they seem that their meaning she saw not.

items.text: Full soon then his bed came Hogni to seek, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . The clear-souled one dreamed, and her dream she kept not, To the warrior the wise one spake when she wakened:
lines: Full soon then his bed came Hogni to seek,
The clear-souled one dreamed, and her dream she kept not,
To the warrior the wise one spake when she wakened:

items.text: “Thou wouldst go hence, Hogni, but heed my counsel,— Known to few are the runes,— and put off thy faring; I have read now the runes that thy sister wrote, And this time the bright one did not bid thee to come.
lines: “Thou wouldst go hence, Hogni, but heed my counsel,—
Known to few are the runes,— and put off thy faring;
I have read now the runes that thy sister wrote,
And this time the bright one did not bid thee to come.

items.text: “Full much do I wonder, nor well can I see, Why the woman wise so wildly hath written; But to me it seems that the meaning beneath Is that both shall be slain if soon ye shall go. But one rune she missed, or else others have marred it.”
lines: “Full much do I wonder, nor well can I see,
Why the woman wise so wildly hath written;
But to me it seems that the meaning beneath
Is that both shall be slain if soon ye shall go.
But one rune she missed, or else others have marred it.”

items.text: Hogni spake:
“All women are fearful; not so do I feel, Ill I seek not to find till I soon must avenge it; The king now will give us the glow-ruddy gold; I never shall fear, though of dangers I know.”
lines: “All women are fearful; not so do I feel,
Ill I seek not to find till I soon must avenge it;
The king now will give us the glow-ruddy gold;
I never shall fear, though of dangers I know.”

items.text: Kostbera spake:
“In danger ye fare, if forth ye go thither, No welcoming friendly this time shall ye find; For I dreamed now, Hogni, and nought will I hide, Full evil thy faring, if rightly I fear.
lines: “In danger ye fare, if forth ye go thither,
No welcoming friendly this time shall ye find;
For I dreamed now, Hogni, and nought will I hide,
Full evil thy faring, if rightly I fear.

items.text: “Thy bed-covering saw I in the flames burning, And the fire burst high through the walls of my home.”
lines: “Thy bed-covering saw I in the flames burning,
And the fire burst high through the walls of my home.”

items.text: Hogni spake:
“Yon garment of linen lies little of worth, It will soon be burned, so thou sawest the bed-cover.”
lines: “Yon garment of linen lies little of worth,
It will soon be burned, so thou sawest the bed-cover.”

items.text: Kostbera spake:
“A bear saw I enter, the pillars he broke, And he brandished his claws so that craven we were; With his mouth seized he many, and nought was our might, And loud was the tumult, not little it was.”
lines: “A bear saw I enter, the pillars he broke,
And he brandished his claws so that craven we were;
With his mouth seized he many, and nought was our might,
And loud was the tumult, not little it was.”

items.text: Hogni spake:
“Now a storm is brewing, and wild it grows swiftly, A dream of an ice-bear means a gale from the east.”
lines: “Now a storm is brewing, and wild it grows swiftly,
A dream of an ice-bear means a gale from the east.”

items.text: Kostbera spake:
“An eagle I saw flying from the end through the house, Our fate must be bad, for with blood he sprinkled us; . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . From the evil I fear that ’twas Atli’s spirit.”
lines: “An eagle I saw flying from the end through the house,
Our fate must be bad, for with blood he sprinkled us;
From the evil I fear that ’twas Atli’s spirit.”

items.text: Hogni spake:
“They will slaughter soon, and so blood do we see, Oft oxen it means when of eagles one dreams; True is Atli’s heart, whatever thou dreamest.” Then silent they were, and nought further they said.
lines: “They will slaughter soon, and so blood do we see,
Oft oxen it means when of eagles one dreams;
True is Atli’s heart, whatever thou dreamest.”
Then silent they were, and nought further they said.

items.text: The high-born ones wakened, and like speech they had, Then did Glaumvor tell how in terror she dreamed, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Gunnar two roads they should go.
lines: The high-born ones wakened, and like speech they had,
Then did Glaumvor tell how in terror she dreamed,
. . . . . Gunnar two roads they should go.

items.text: Glaumvor spake:
“A gallows saw I ready, thou didst go to thy hanging, Thy flesh serpents ate, and yet living I found thee; . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . The gods’ doom descended; now say what it boded.”
lines: “A gallows saw I ready, thou didst go to thy hanging,
Thy flesh serpents ate, and yet living I found thee;
The gods’ doom descended; now say what it boded.”

items.text: “A sword drawn bloody from thy garments I saw,— Such a dream is hard to a husband to tell,— A spear stood, methought, through thy body thrust, And at head and feet the wolves were howling.”
lines: “A sword drawn bloody from thy garments I saw,—
Such a dream is hard to a husband to tell,—
A spear stood, methought, through thy body thrust,
And at head and feet the wolves were howling.”

items.text: Gunnar spake:
“The hounds are running, loud their barking is heard, Oft hounds’ clamor follows the flying of spears.”
lines: “The hounds are running, loud their barking is heard,
Oft hounds’ clamor follows the flying of spears.”

items.text: Glaumvor spake:
“A river the length of the hall saw I run, Full swiftly it roared, o’er the benches it swept; O’er the feet did it break of ye brothers twain, The water would yield not; some meaning there was.”
lines: “A river the length of the hall saw I run,
Full swiftly it roared, o’er the benches it swept;
O’er the feet did it break of ye brothers twain,
The water would yield not; some meaning there was.”

items.text: “I dreamed that by night came dead women hither, Sad were their garments, and thee were they seeking; They bade thee come swiftly forth to their benches, And nothing, methinks, could the Norns avail thee.”
lines: “I dreamed that by night came dead women hither,
Sad were their garments, and thee were they seeking;
They bade thee come swiftly forth to their benches,
And nothing, methinks, could the Norns avail thee.”

items.text: Gunnar spake:
“Too late is thy speaking, for so is it settled; From the faring I turn not, the going is fixed, Though likely it is that our lives shall be short.”
lines: “Too late is thy speaking, for so is it settled;
From the faring I turn not, the going is fixed,
Though likely it is that our lives shall be short.”

items.text: Then bright shone the morning, the men all were ready, They said, and yet each would the other hold back; Five were the warriors, and their followers all But twice as many,— their minds knew not wisdom.
lines: Then bright shone the morning, the men all were ready,
They said, and yet each would the other hold back;
Five were the warriors, and their followers all
But twice as many,— their minds knew not wisdom.

items.text: Snævar and Solar, they were sons of Hogni, Orkning was he called who came with the others, Blithe was the shield-tree, the brother of Kostbera; The fair-decked ones followed, till the fjord divided them, Full hard did they plead, but the others would hear not.
lines: Snævar and Solar, they were sons of Hogni,
Orkning was he called who came with the others,
Blithe was the shield-tree, the brother of Kostbera;
The fair-decked ones followed, till the fjord divided them,
Full hard did they plead, but the others would hear not.

items.text: Then did Glaumvor speak forth, the wife of Gunnar, To Vingi she said that which wise to her seemed: “I know not if well thou requitest our welcome, Full ill was thy coming if evil shall follow.”
lines: Then did Glaumvor speak forth, the wife of Gunnar,
To Vingi she said that which wise to her seemed:
“I know not if well thou requitest our welcome,
Full ill was thy coming if evil shall follow.”

items.text: Then did Vingi swear, and full glib was his speech, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . “May giants now take me if lies I have told ye, And the gallows if hostile thought did I have.”
lines: Then did Vingi swear, and full glib was his speech,
“May giants now take me if lies I have told ye,
And the gallows if hostile thought did I have.”

items.text: Then did Bera speak forth, and fair was her thought, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . “May ye sail now happy, and victory have, To fare as I bid ye, may nought your way bar.”
lines: Then did Bera speak forth, and fair was her thought,
“May ye sail now happy, and victory have,
To fare as I bid ye, may nought your way bar.”

items.text: Then Hogni made answer,— dear held he his kin,— courage, ye wise ones, whatsoever may come; Though many may speak, yet is evil oft mighty, And words avail little to lead one homeward.
lines: Then Hogni made answer,— dear held he his kin,—
courage, ye wise ones, whatsoever may come;
Though many may speak, yet is evil oft mighty,
And words avail little to lead one homeward.

items.text: They tenderly looked till each turned on his way, Then with changing fate were their farings divided.
lines: They tenderly looked till each turned on his way,
Then with changing fate were their farings divided.

items.text: Full stoutly they rowed, and the keel clove asunder, Their backs strained at the oars, and their strength was fierce; The oar-loops were burst, the thole-pins were broken, Nor the ship made they fast ere from her they fared.
lines: Full stoutly they rowed, and the keel clove asunder,
Their backs strained at the oars, and their strength was
fierce;
The oar-loops were burst, the thole-pins were broken,
Nor the ship made they fast ere from her they fared.

items.text: Not long was it after— the end must I tell— That the home they beheld that Buthli once had; Loud the gates resounded when Hogni smote them; Vingi spake then a word that were better unsaid:
lines: Not long was it after— the end must I tell—
That the home they beheld that Buthli once had;
Loud the gates resounded when Hogni smote them;
Vingi spake then a word that were better unsaid:

items.text: “Go ye far from the house, for false is its entrance, Soon shall I burn you, ye are swiftly smitten; I bade ye come fairly, but falseness was under, Now bide ye afar while your gallows I fashion.”
lines: “Go ye far from the house, for false is its entrance,
Soon shall I burn you, ye are swiftly smitten;
I bade ye come fairly, but falseness was under,
Now bide ye afar while your gallows I fashion.”

items.text: Then Hogni made answer, his heart yielded little, And nought did he fear that his fate held in store: “Seek not to affright us, thou shalt seldom succeed; If thy words are more, then the worse grows thy fate.”
lines: Then Hogni made answer, his heart yielded little,
And nought did he fear that his fate held in store:
“Seek not to affright us, thou shalt seldom succeed;
If thy words are more, then the worse grows thy fate.”

items.text: Then Vingi did they smite, and they sent him to hell, With their axes they clove him while the death-rattle came.
lines: Then Vingi did they smite, and they sent him to hell,
With their axes they clove him while the death-rattle came.

items.text: Atli summoned his men, in mail-coats they hastened, All ready they came, and between was the courtyard.
lines: Atli summoned his men, in mail-coats they hastened,
All ready they came, and between was the courtyard.

items.text: Then came they to words, and full wrathful they were: “Long since did we plan how soon we might slay you.”
lines: Then came they to words, and full wrathful they were:
“Long since did we plan how soon we might slay you.”

items.text: Hogni spake:
“Little it matters if long ye have planned it; For unarmed do ye wait, and one have we felled, We smote him to hell, of your host was he once.”
lines: “Little it matters if long ye have planned it;
For unarmed do ye wait, and one have we felled,
We smote him to hell, of your host was he once.”

items.text: Then wild was their anger when all heard his words; Their fingers were swift on their bowstrings to seize, Full sharply they shot, by their shields were they guarded.
lines: Then wild was their anger when all heard his words;
Their fingers were swift on their bowstrings to seize,
Full sharply they shot, by their shields were they guarded.

items.text: In the house came the word how the heroes without Fought in front of the hall; they heard a thrall tell it; Grim then was Guthrun, the grief when she heard, With necklaces fair, and she flung them all from her, (The silver she hurled so the rings burst asunder.)
lines: In the house came the word how the heroes without
Fought in front of the hall; they heard a thrall tell it;
Grim then was Guthrun, the grief when she heard,
With necklaces fair, and she flung them all from her,
(The silver she hurled so the rings burst asunder.)

items.text: Then out did she go, she flung open the doors, All fearless she went, and the guests did she welcome; To the Niflungs she went— her last greeting it was,— In her speech truth was clear, and much would she speak.
lines: Then out did she go, she flung open the doors,
All fearless she went, and the guests did she welcome;
To the Niflungs she went— her last greeting it was,—
In her speech truth was clear, and much would she speak.

items.text: “For your safety I sought that at home ye should stay; None escapes his fate, so ye hither must fare.” Full wisely she spake, if yet peace they might win, But to nought would they hearken, and “No” said they all.
lines: “For your safety I sought that at home ye should stay;
None escapes his fate, so ye hither must fare.”
Full wisely she spake, if yet peace they might win,
But to nought would they hearken, and “No” said they all.

items.text: Then the high-born one saw that hard was their battle, In fierceness of heart she flung off her mantle; Her naked sword grasped she her kin’s lives to guard, Not gentle her hands in the hewing of battle.
lines: Then the high-born one saw that hard was their battle,
In fierceness of heart she flung off her mantle;
Her naked sword grasped she her kin’s lives to guard,
Not gentle her hands in the hewing of battle.

items.text: Then the daughter of Gjuki two warriors smote down, Atli’s brother she slew, and forth then they bore him; (So fiercely she fought that his feet she clove off;) Another she smote so that never he stood, To hell did she send him,— her hands trembled never.
lines: Then the daughter of Gjuki two warriors smote down,
Atli’s brother she slew, and forth then they bore him;
(So fiercely she fought that his feet she clove off;)
Another she smote so that never he stood,
To hell did she send him,— her hands trembled never.

items.text: Full wide was the fame of the battle they fought, ’Twas the greatest of deeds of the sons of Gjuki; Men say that the Niflungs, while themselves they were living, With their swords fought mightily, mail-coats they sundered, And helms did they hew, as their hearts were fearless.
lines: Full wide was the fame of the battle they fought,
’Twas the greatest of deeds of the sons of Gjuki;
Men say that the Niflungs, while themselves they were living,
With their swords fought mightily, mail-coats they sundered,
And helms did they hew, as their hearts were fearless.

items.text: All the morning they fought until midday shone, (All the dusk as well and the dawning of day,) When the battle was ended, the field flowed with blood; Ere they fell, eighteen of their foemen were slain, By the two sons of Bera and her brother as well.
lines: All the morning they fought until midday shone,
(All the dusk as well and the dawning of day,)
When the battle was ended, the field flowed with blood;
Ere they fell, eighteen of their foemen were slain,
By the two sons of Bera and her brother as well.

items.text: Then the warrior spake, and wild was his anger: “This is evil to see, and thy doing is all; Once we were thirty, we thanes keen for battle, Now eleven are left, and great is our lack.
lines: Then the warrior spake, and wild was his anger:
“This is evil to see, and thy doing is all;
Once we were thirty, we thanes keen for battle,
Now eleven are left, and great is our lack.

items.text: “There were five of us brothers when Buthli we lost, Now Hel has the half, and two smitten lie here; A great kinship had I,— the truth may I hide not,— From a wife bringing slaughter small joy could I win.
lines: “There were five of us brothers when Buthli we lost,
Now Hel has the half, and two smitten lie here;
A great kinship had I,— the truth may I hide not,—
From a wife bringing slaughter small joy could I win.

items.text: We lay seldom together since to me thou wast given, Now my kin all are gone, of my gold am I robbed; Nay, and worst, thou didst send my sister to hell.”
lines: We lay seldom together since to me thou wast given,
Now my kin all are gone, of my gold am I robbed;
Nay, and worst, thou didst send my sister to hell.”

items.text: Guthrun spake:

“Hear me now, Atli! the first evil was thine; My mother didst thou take, and for gold didst murder her, My sister’s daughter thou didst starve in a prison. A jest does it seem that thy sorrow thou tellest, And good do I find it that grief to thee comes.”
lines: “Hear me now, Atli! the first evil was thine;
My mother didst thou take, and for gold didst murder her,
My sister’s daughter thou didst starve in a prison.
A jest does it seem that thy sorrow thou tellest,
And good do I find it that grief to thee comes.”

items.text: Atli spake:
“Go now, ye warriors, and make greater the grief Of the woman so fair, for fain would I see it; So fierce be thy warring that Guthrun shall weep, I would gladly behold her happiness lost.
lines: “Go now, ye warriors, and make greater the grief
Of the woman so fair, for fain would I see it;
So fierce be thy warring that Guthrun shall weep,
I would gladly behold her happiness lost.

items.text: “Seize ye now Hogni, and with knives shall ye hew him, His heart shall ye cut out, this haste ye to do; And grim-hearted Gunnar shall ye bind on the gallows, Swift shall ye do it, to serpents now cast him.”
lines: “Seize ye now Hogni, and with knives shall ye hew him,
His heart shall ye cut out, this haste ye to do;
And grim-hearted Gunnar shall ye bind on the gallows,
Swift shall ye do it, to serpents now cast him.”

items.text: Hogni spake:

“Do now as thou wilt, for glad I await it, Brave shalt thou find me, I have faced worse before; We held thee at bay while whole we were fighting, Now with wounds are we spent, so thy will canst thou work.”
lines: “Do now as thou wilt, for glad I await it,
Brave shalt thou find me, I have faced worse before;
We held thee at bay while whole we were fighting,
Now with wounds are we spent, so thy will canst thou work.”

items.text: Then did Beiti speak, he was Atli’s steward: “Let us seize now Hjalli, and Hogni spare we! Let us fell the sluggard, he is fit for death, He has lived too long, and lazy men call him.”
lines: Then did Beiti speak, he was Atli’s steward:
“Let us seize now Hjalli, and Hogni spare we!
Let us fell the sluggard, he is fit for death,
He has lived too long, and lazy men call him.”

items.text: Afraid was the pot-watcher, he fled here and yon, And crazed with his terror he climbed in the corners: “Ill for me is this fighting, if I pay for your fierceness, And sad is the day to die leaving my swine And all the fair victuals that of old did I have.”
lines: Afraid was the pot-watcher, he fled here and yon,
And crazed with his terror he climbed in the corners:
“Ill for me is this fighting, if I pay for your fierceness,
And sad is the day to die leaving my swine
And all the fair victuals that of old did I have.”

items.text: They seized Buthli’s cook, and they came with the knife, The frightened thrall howled ere the edge did he feel; He was willing, he cried, to dung well the courtyard, Do the basest of work, if spare him they would; Full happy were Hjalli if his life he might have.
lines: They seized Buthli’s cook, and they came with the knife,
The frightened thrall howled ere the edge did he feel;
He was willing, he cried, to dung well the courtyard,
Do the basest of work, if spare him they would;
Full happy were Hjalli if his life he might have.

items.text: Then fain was Hogni— there are few would do thus— To beg for the slave that safe hence he should go; “I would find it far better this knife-play to feel, Why must we all hark to this howling longer?”
lines: Then fain was Hogni— there are few would do thus—
To beg for the slave that safe hence he should go;
“I would find it far better this knife-play to feel,
Why must we all hark to this howling longer?”

items.text: Then the brave one they seized; to the warriors bold No chance was there left to delay his fate longer; Loud did Hogni laugh, all the sons of day heard him, So valiant he was that well he could suffer.
lines: Then the brave one they seized; to the warriors bold
No chance was there left to delay his fate longer;
Loud did Hogni laugh, all the sons of day heard him,
So valiant he was that well he could suffer.

items.text: A harp Gunnar seized, with his toes he smote it; So well did he strike that the women all wept, And the men, when clear they heard it, lamented; Full noble was his song, the rafters burst asunder.
lines: A harp Gunnar seized, with his toes he smote it;
So well did he strike that the women all wept,
And the men, when clear they heard it, lamented;
Full noble was his song, the rafters burst asunder.

items.text: Then the heroes died ere the day was yet come; Their fame did they leave ever lofty to live. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
lines: Then the heroes died ere the day was yet come;
Their fame did they leave ever lofty to live.

items.text: Full mighty seemed Atli as o’er them he stood, The wise one he blamed, and his words reproached her: “It is morning, Guthrun; now thy dear ones dost miss, But the blame is part thine that thus it has chanced.”
lines: Full mighty seemed Atli as o’er them he stood,
The wise one he blamed, and his words reproached her:
“It is morning, Guthrun; now thy dear ones dost miss,
But the blame is part thine that thus it has chanced.”

items.text: Guthrun spake:
“Thou art joyous, Atli, for of evil thou tellest, But sorrow is thine if thou mightest all see; Thy heritage heavy here can I tell thee, Sorrow never thou losest unless I shall die.”
lines: “Thou art joyous, Atli, for of evil thou tellest,
But sorrow is thine if thou mightest all see;
Thy heritage heavy here can I tell thee,
Sorrow never thou losest unless I shall die.”

items.text: Atli spake:

“Not free of guilt am I; a way shall I find That is better by far,— oft the fairest we shunned;— With slaves I console thee, with gems fair to see, And with silver snow-white, as thyself thou shalt choose.”
lines: “Not free of guilt am I; a way shall I find
That is better by far,— oft the fairest we shunned;—
With slaves I console thee, with gems fair to see,
And with silver snow-white, as thyself thou shalt choose.”

items.text: Guthrun spake:

“No hope shall this give thee, thy gifts I shall take not, Requital I spurned when my sorrows were smaller; Once grim did I seem, but now greater my grimness, There was nought seemed too hard while Hogni was living.
lines: “No hope shall this give thee, thy gifts I shall take
not,
Requital I spurned when my sorrows were smaller;
Once grim did I seem, but now greater my grimness,
There was nought seemed too hard while Hogni was living.

items.text: “Our childhood did we have in a single house, We played many a game, in the grove did we grow; Then did Grimhild give us gold and necklaces; Thou shalt ne’er make amends for my brother’s murder, Nor ever shalt win me to think it was well.
lines: “Our childhood did we have in a single house,
We played many a game, in the grove did we grow;
Then did Grimhild give us gold and necklaces;
Thou shalt ne’er make amends for my brother’s murder,
Nor ever shalt win me to think it was well.

items.text: “But the fierceness of men rules the fate of women, The tree-top bows low if bereft of its leaves, The tree bends over if the roots are cleft under it; Now mayest thou, Atli, o’er all things here rule.”
lines: “But the fierceness of men rules the fate of women,
The tree-top bows low if bereft of its leaves,
The tree bends over if the roots are cleft under it;
Now mayest thou, Atli, o’er all things here rule.”

items.text: Full heedless the warrior was that he trusted her, So clear was her guile if on guard he had been; But crafty was Guthrun, with cunning she spake, Her glance she made pleasant, with two shields she played.
lines: Full heedless the warrior was that he trusted her,
So clear was her guile if on guard he had been;
But crafty was Guthrun, with cunning she spake,
Her glance she made pleasant, with two shields she played.

items.text: The beer then she brought for her brothers’ death-feast, And a feast Atli made for his followers dead; No more did they speak, the mead was made ready, Soon the men were gathered with mighty uproar.
lines: The beer then she brought for her brothers’ death-feast,
And a feast Atli made for his followers dead;
No more did they speak, the mead was made ready,
Soon the men were gathered with mighty uproar.

items.text: Thus bitterly planned she, and Buthli’s race threatened, And terrible vengeance on her husband would take; The little ones called she, on a block she laid them; Afraid were the proud ones, but their tears did not fall; To their mother’s arms went they, and asked what she would.
lines: Thus bitterly planned she, and Buthli’s race threatened,
And terrible vengeance on her husband would take;
The little ones called she, on a block she laid them;
Afraid were the proud ones, but their tears did not fall;
To their mother’s arms went they, and asked what she would.

items.text: Guthrun spake:
“Nay, ask me no more! You both shall I murder, For long have I wished your lives to steal from you.”
lines: “Nay, ask me no more! You both shall I murder,
For long have I wished your lives to steal from you.”

items.text: The boys spake:
“Slay thy boys as thou wilt, for no one may bar it, Short the angry one’s peace if all thou shalt do.”
lines: “Slay thy boys as thou wilt, for no one may bar it,
Short the angry one’s peace if all thou shalt do.”

items.text: Then the grim one slew both of the brothers young, Full hard was her deed when their heads she smote off; Fain was Atli to know whither now they were gone, The boys from their sport, for nowhere he spied them.
lines: Then the grim one slew both of the brothers young,
Full hard was her deed when their heads she smote off;
Fain was Atli to know whither now they were gone,
The boys from their sport, for nowhere he spied them.

items.text: Guthrun spake:

“My fate shall I seek, all to Atli saying, The daughter of Grimhild the deed from thee hides not; No joy thou hast, Atli, if all thou shalt hear, Great sorrow didst wake when my brothers thou slewest.
lines: “My fate shall I seek, all to Atli saying,
The daughter of Grimhild the deed from thee hides not;
No joy thou hast, Atli, if all thou shalt hear,
Great sorrow didst wake when my brothers thou slewest.

items.text: “I have seldom slept since the hour they were slain, Baleful were my threats, now I bid thee recall them; Thou didst say it was morning,— too well I remember,— Now is evening come, and this question thou askest.
lines: “I have seldom slept since the hour they were slain,
Baleful were my threats, now I bid thee recall them;
Thou didst say it was morning,— too well I remember,—
Now is evening come, and this question thou askest.

items.text: “Now both of thy sons thou hast lost . . . . . . . . . . . as thou never shouldst do; The skulls of thy boys thou as beer-cups didst have, And the draught that I made thee was mixed with their blood.
lines: “Now both of thy sons thou hast lost . . .
. . . . . . . . as thou never shouldst do;
The skulls of thy boys thou as beer-cups didst have,
And the draught that I made thee was mixed with their blood.

items.text: “I cut out their hearts, on a spit I cooked them, I came to thee with them, and calf’s flesh I called them; Alone didst thou eat them, nor any didst leave, Thou didst greedily bite, and thy teeth were busy.
lines: “I cut out their hearts, on a spit I cooked them,
I came to thee with them, and calf’s flesh I called them;
Alone didst thou eat them, nor any didst leave,
Thou didst greedily bite, and thy teeth were busy.

items.text: “Of thy sons now thou knowest; few suffer more sorrow; My guilt have I told, fame it never shall give me.”
lines: “Of thy sons now thou knowest; few suffer more sorrow;
My guilt have I told, fame it never shall give me.”

items.text: Atli spake:

“Grim wast thou, Guthrun, in so grievous a deed, My draught with the blood of thy boys to mingle; Thou hast slain thine own kin, most ill it beseemed thee, And little for me twixt my sorrows thou leavest.”
lines: “Grim wast thou, Guthrun, in so grievous a deed,
My draught with the blood of thy boys to mingle;
Thou hast slain thine own kin, most ill it beseemed thee,
And little for me twixt my sorrows thou leavest.”

items.text: Guthrun spake:

“Still more would I seek to slay thee thyself, Enough ill comes seldom to such as thou art; Thou didst folly of old, such that no one shall find In the whole world of men a match for such madness. Now this that of late we learned hast thou added, Great evil hast grasped, and thine own death-feast made.”
lines: “Still more would I seek to slay thee thyself,
Enough ill comes seldom to such as thou art;
Thou didst folly of old, such that no one shall find
In the whole world of men a match for such madness.
Now this that of late we learned hast thou added,
Great evil hast grasped, and thine own death-feast made.”

items.text: Atli spake:
“With fire shall they burn thee, and first shall they stone thee, So then hast thou earned what thou ever hast sought for.”
lines: “With fire shall they burn thee, and first shall they
stone thee,
So then hast thou earned what thou ever hast sought for.”

items.text: Guthrun spake:
“Such woes for thyself shalt thou say in the morning, From a finer death I to another light fare.”
lines: “Such woes for thyself shalt thou say in the morning,
From a finer death I to another light fare.”

items.text: Together they sat and full grim were their thoughts, Unfriendly their words, and no joy either found; In Hniflung grew hatred, great plans did he have, To Guthrun his anger against Atli was told.
lines: Together they sat and full grim were their thoughts,
Unfriendly their words, and no joy either found;
In Hniflung grew hatred, great plans did he have,
To Guthrun his anger against Atli was told.

items.text: To her heart came ever the fate of Hogni, She told him ’twere well if he vengeance should win; So was Atli slain,— ’twas not slow to await,— Hogni’s son slew him, and Guthrun herself.
lines: To her heart came ever the fate of Hogni,
She told him ’twere well if he vengeance should win;
So was Atli slain,— ’twas not slow to await,—
Hogni’s son slew him, and Guthrun herself.

items.text: Then the warrior spake, as from slumber he wakened, Soon he knew for his wounds would the bandage do nought: “Now the truth shalt thou say: who has slain Buthli’s son? Full sore am I smitten, nor hope can I see.”
lines: Then the warrior spake, as from slumber he wakened,
Soon he knew for his wounds would the bandage do nought:
“Now the truth shalt thou say: who has slain Buthli’s son?
Full sore am I smitten, nor hope can I see.”

items.text: Guthrun spake:
“Ne’er her deed from thee hides the daughter of Grimhild, I own to the guilt that is ending thy life, And the son of Hogni; ’tis so thy wounds bleed.”
lines: “Ne’er her deed from thee hides the daughter of Grimhild,
I own to the guilt that is ending thy life,
And the son of Hogni; ’tis so thy wounds bleed.”

items.text: Atli spake:
“To murder hast thou fared, though foul it must seem; Ill thy friend to betray who trusted thee well.
lines: “To murder hast thou fared, though foul it must seem;
Ill thy friend to betray who trusted thee well.

items.text: “Not glad went I hence thy hand to seek, Guthrun, In thy widowhood famed, but haughty men found thee; My belief did not lie, as now we have learned; I brought thee home hither, and a host of men with us.
lines: “Not glad went I hence thy hand to seek, Guthrun,
In thy widowhood famed, but haughty men found thee;
My belief did not lie, as now we have learned;
I brought thee home hither, and a host of men with us.

items.text: “Most noble was all when of old we journeyed, Great honor did we have of heroes full worthy; Of cattle had we plenty, and greatly we prospered, Mighty was our wealth, and many received it.
lines: “Most noble was all when of old we journeyed,
Great honor did we have of heroes full worthy;
Of cattle had we plenty, and greatly we prospered,
Mighty was our wealth, and many received it.

items.text: “To the famed one as bride-gift I gave jewels fair, I gave thirty slaves, and handmaidens seven; There was honor in such gifts, yet the silver was greater.
lines: “To the famed one as bride-gift I gave jewels fair,
I gave thirty slaves, and handmaidens seven;
There was honor in such gifts, yet the silver was greater.

items.text: “But all to thee was as if nought it were worth, While the land lay before thee that Buthli had left me; Thou in secret didst work so the treasure I won not; My mother full oft to sit weeping didst make, No wedded joy found I in fullness of heart.”
lines: “But all to thee was as if nought it were worth,
While the land lay before thee that Buthli had left me;
Thou in secret didst work so the treasure I won not;
My mother full oft to sit weeping didst make,
No wedded joy found I in fullness of heart.”

items.text: Guthrun spake:

“Thou liest now, Atli, though little I heed it; If I seldom was kindly, full cruel wast thou; Ye brothers fought young, quarrels brought you to battle, And half went to hell of the sons of thy house, And all was destroyed that should e’er have done good.
lines: “Thou liest now, Atli, though little I heed it;
If I seldom was kindly, full cruel wast thou;
Ye brothers fought young, quarrels brought you to battle,
And half went to hell of the sons of thy house,
And all was destroyed that should e’er have done good.

items.text: “My two brothers and I were bold in our thoughts, From the land we went forth, with Sigurth we fared; Full swiftly we sailed, each one steering his ship, So our fate sought we e’er till we came to the East.
lines: “My two brothers and I were bold in our thoughts,
From the land we went forth, with Sigurth we fared;
Full swiftly we sailed, each one steering his ship,
So our fate sought we e’er till we came to the East.

items.text: “First the king did we slay, and the land we seized, The princes did us service, for such was their fear; From the forest we called them we fain would have guiltless, And rich made we many who of all were bereft.
lines: “First the king did we slay, and the land we seized,
The princes did us service, for such was their fear;
From the forest we called them we fain would have guiltless,
And rich made we many who of all were bereft.

items.text: “Slain was the Hun-king, soon happiness vanished, In her grief the widow so young sat weeping; Yet worse seemed the sorrow to seek Atli’s house, A hero was my husband, and hard was his loss.
lines: “Slain was the Hun-king, soon happiness vanished,
In her grief the widow so young sat weeping;
Yet worse seemed the sorrow to seek Atli’s house,
A hero was my husband, and hard was his loss.

items.text: “From the Thing thou camst never, for thus have we heard, Having won in thy quarrels, or warriors smitten; Full yielding thou wast, never firm was thy will, In silence didst suffer, . . . . . . . .”
lines: “From the Thing thou camst never, for thus have we heard,
Having won in thy quarrels, or warriors smitten;
Full yielding thou wast, never firm was thy will,
In silence didst suffer, . . . . . . . .”

items.text: Atli spake:
“Thou liest now, Guthrun, but little of good Will it bring to either, for all have we lost; But, Guthrun, yet once be thou kindly of will, For the honor of both, when forth I am borne.”
lines: “Thou liest now, Guthrun, but little of good
Will it bring to either, for all have we lost;
But, Guthrun, yet once be thou kindly of will,
For the honor of both, when forth I am borne.”

items.text: Guthrun spake:
“A ship will I buy, and a bright-hued coffin, I will wax well the shroud to wind round thy body, For all will I care as if dear were we ever.”
lines: “A ship will I buy, and a bright-hued coffin,
I will wax well the shroud to wind round thy body,
For all will I care as if dear were we ever.”

items.text: Then did Atli die, and his heirs’ grief doubled; The high-born one did as to him she had promised; Then sought Guthrun the wise to go to her death, But for days did she wait, and ’twas long ere she died.
lines: Then did Atli die, and his heirs’ grief doubled;
The high-born one did as to him she had promised;
Then sought Guthrun the wise to go to her death,
But for days did she wait, and ’twas long ere she died.

items.text: Full happy shall he be who such offspring has, Or children so gallant, as Gjuki begot; Forever shall live, and in lands far and wide, Their valor heroic wherever men hear it.
lines: Full happy shall he be who such offspring has,
Or children so gallant, as Gjuki begot;
Forever shall live, and in lands far and wide,
Their valor heroic wherever men hear it.

items.text: Guthrun went forth to the sea after she had slain Atli. She went out into the sea and fain would drown herself, but she could not sink. The waves bore her across the fjord to the land of King Jonak; he took her as wife; their sons were Sorli and Erp and Hamther. There was brought up Svanhild, Sigurth’s daughter; she was married to the mighty Jormunrek. With him was Bikki, who counselled that Randver, the king’s son, should have her. This Bikki told to the king. The king had Randver hanged, and Svanhild trodden to death under horses’ feet. And when Guthrun learned this, she spake with her sons.
A word-strife I learned, most woeful of all, A speech from the fullness of sorrow spoken, When fierce of heart her sons to the fight Did Guthrun whet with words full grim.
lines: A word-strife I learned, most woeful of all,
A speech from the fullness of sorrow spoken,
When fierce of heart her sons to the fight
Did Guthrun whet with words full grim.

items.text: “Why sit ye idle, why sleep out your lives, Why grieve ye not in gladness to speak? Since Jormunrek your sister young Beneath the hoofs of horses hath trodden, (White and black on the battle-way, Gray, road-wonted, the steeds of the Goths.)
lines: “Why sit ye idle, why sleep out your lives,
Why grieve ye not in gladness to speak?
Since Jormunrek your sister young
Beneath the hoofs of horses hath trodden,
(White and black on the battle-way,
Gray, road-wonted, the steeds of the Goths.)

items.text: “Not like are ye to Gunnar of yore, Nor have ye hearts such as Hogni’s was; Vengeance for her ye soon would have If brave ye were as my brothers of old, Or hard your hearts as the Hunnish kings’.”
lines: “Not like are ye to Gunnar of yore,
Nor have ye hearts such as Hogni’s was;
Vengeance for her ye soon would have
If brave ye were as my brothers of old,
Or hard your hearts as the Hunnish kings’.”

items.text: Then Hamther spake, the high of heart: “Little the deed of Hogni didst love, When Sigurth they wakened from his sleep; Thy bed-covers white were red with blood Of thy husband, drenched with gore from his heart.
lines: Then Hamther spake, the high of heart:
“Little the deed of Hogni didst love,
When Sigurth they wakened from his sleep;
Thy bed-covers white were red with blood
Of thy husband, drenched with gore from his heart.

items.text: “Bloody revenge didst have for thy brothers, Evil and sore, when thy sons didst slay; Else yet might we all on Jormunrek Together our sister’s slaying avenge.
lines: “Bloody revenge didst have for thy brothers,
Evil and sore, when thy sons didst slay;
Else yet might we all on Jormunrek
Together our sister’s slaying avenge.

items.text: “. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . The gear of the Hunnish kings now give us! Thou hast whetted us so to the battle of swords.”
lines: The gear of the Hunnish kings now give us!
Thou hast whetted us so to the battle of swords.”

items.text: Laughing did Guthrun go to her chamber, The helms of the kings from the cupboards she took, And mail-coats broad, to her sons she bore them; On their horses’ backs the heroes leaped.
lines: Laughing did Guthrun go to her chamber,
The helms of the kings from the cupboards she took,
And mail-coats broad, to her sons she bore them;
On their horses’ backs the heroes leaped.

items.text: Then Hamther spake, the high of heart: “Homeward no more his mother to see Comes the spear-god, fallen mid Gothic folk; One death-draught thou for us all shalt drink, For Svanhild then and thy sons as well.”
lines: Then Hamther spake, the high of heart:
“Homeward no more his mother to see
Comes the spear-god, fallen mid Gothic folk;
One death-draught thou for us all shalt drink,
For Svanhild then and thy sons as well.”

items.text: Weeping Guthrun, Gjuki’s daughter, Went sadly before the gate to sit, And with tear-stained cheeks to tell the tale Of her mighty griefs, so many in kind.
lines: Weeping Guthrun, Gjuki’s daughter,
Went sadly before the gate to sit,
And with tear-stained cheeks to tell the tale
Of her mighty griefs, so many in kind.

items.text: “Three home-fires knew I, three hearths I knew, Home was I brought by husbands three; But Sigurth only of all was dear, He whom my brothers brought to his death.
lines: “Three home-fires knew I, three hearths I knew,
Home was I brought by husbands three;
But Sigurth only of all was dear,
He whom my brothers brought to his death.

items.text: “A greater sorrow I saw not nor knew, Yet more it seemed I must suffer yet When the princes great to Atli gave me.
lines: “A greater sorrow I saw not nor knew,
Yet more it seemed I must suffer yet
When the princes great to Atli gave me.

items.text: “The brave boys I summoned to secret speech; For my woes requital I might not win Till off the heads of the Hniflungs I hewed.
lines: “The brave boys I summoned to secret speech;
For my woes requital I might not win
Till off the heads of the Hniflungs I hewed.

items.text: “To the sea I went, my heart full sore For the Norns, whose wrath I would now escape; But the lofty billows bore me undrowned, Till to land I came, so I longer must live.
lines: “To the sea I went, my heart full sore
For the Norns, whose wrath I would now escape;
But the lofty billows bore me undrowned,
Till to land I came, so I longer must live.

items.text: “Then to the bed— of old was it better!— Of a King of the folk a third time I came; Boys I bore his heirs to be, Heirs so young, the sons of Jonak.
lines: “Then to the bed— of old was it better!—
Of a King of the folk a third time I came;
Boys I bore his heirs to be,
Heirs so young, the sons of Jonak.

items.text: “But round Svanhild handmaidens sat, She was dearest ever of all my children; So did Svanhild seem in my hall As the ray of the sun is fair to see.
lines: “But round Svanhild handmaidens sat,
She was dearest ever of all my children;
So did Svanhild seem in my hall
As the ray of the sun is fair to see.
